docs.text:
Cyberbotics Lab / Software platform

From method to experiment

Model the system.

Kinematics, dynamics and the numerical tools to reason about motion.

Compose the behavior.

State estimation, terrain queries, control algorithms and learned policies.

Run and understand.

Execution, world interfaces and recorded evidence of what happened.

docs.title: A shared foundation for robot behavior.
docs.text:
Cyber Suite connects robot models, numerical methods, sensing, control and execution in a modular C++ and Python package. Use a single building block or compose an experiment whose behavior you can inspect.

Explore the architecture → Learn with an example

docs.title: How you use the package
docs.text:
The C++ interface exposes cyber_suite::<module> targets through find_package(cyber_suite). Python exposes supported bindings and native tools through cyber_suite; learning integrations also use the separate cyber_suite_mjlab adapter. Robot models and other packaged data are found through the package's data resolver. See the package consumption boundary for the current installation and build contract.

Hard real-time control belongs in C++20. Python supports training, research and analysis, as well as components without hard real-time constraints. Module lifecycle and available bindings vary; each block's owner contract identifies its supported surface.

Modules provide reusable mechanisms. Projects choose behavior.

A robot project selects modules, connects them, supplies calibration and scenario settings, and defines the evidence needed to accept a result. Training recipes, robot-specific tuning and experiment outcomes stay with that project.

docs.title: See the pieces in an experiment
docs.text:
Digit is the most complete integration example, spanning model-based control, learned policies, CORTA and the Agility low-level interface. Unitree G1 is the focused starting point for a student project. Their guides distinguish implementation from demonstrated simulation and hardware behavior.

Explore Digit · Start a G1 project · TRON1 · Terrain mapping

New to robotics software? The illustrated handbook follows one command through the feedback loop, connects it to a recorded result and proposes a first exercise. The first simulation guide then takes you into a viewer.

These guides explain design and use. Owner contracts describe implemented behavior; validation records describe demonstrated limits. Consult repository status for the current project-wide summary.

docs.title: System architecture
docs.text:
Cyber Suite is a collection of reusable robotics mechanisms with explicit ownership boundaries. Its core package supplies models, numerical tools, sensing and state products, motion and control algorithms, world interfaces, execution and logging. Robot projects compose these capabilities into a particular behavior and evaluate that behavior under stated conditions.

You can use a robot model or a numerical solver on its own. An integrated experiment adds the connections: which measurements become state, which algorithm produces commands, which world receives them, and how the result is recorded.

docs.title: The module map
docs.text:
cyber_suite 13 modules · 5 capability groups Execution & observability Run the composition and inspect what happened. corta Plant-paced execution experimental corta_adapters External inputs & observers experimental logging Bounded telemetry & records experimental Sensing & state Turn measurements into usable state and geometry. estimation State & contact estimation candidate perception Terrain products & queries experimental Motion & control Represent motion and realize commands. locomotion Biped & contact primitives experimental control Feedback & whole-body control candidate policy Learned-policy deployment experimental World interfaces Exchange observations and actuator commands. sim MuJoCo, terrain & sensors candidate digit_hardware Digit low-level interface experimental Models & numerics Shared mathematical and computational building blocks. foundation Math, profiles & data lookup candidate robot Kinematics & dynamics candidate solvers QP problems & backends candidate Select a block to explore its responsibility and owner contract. Groups describe capabilities; placement does not imply a dependency or execution order.

This capability map includes every module with a MODULE.md contract. The build checks that inventory and reads lifecycle labels from the contracts. The categories are a reading aid, not a strict dependency graph: both an estimator and a controller can query a robot model, and observing telemetry does not make a viewer part of the control decision.

docs.title: Foundation
docs.text:
Shared mathematical utilities, strict profile reading and package-data lookup. For example, the same data resolver can locate a packaged robot asset from C++ or Python without hard-coding a neighboring source checkout. Foundation stays small; it does not own robot behavior or runtime scheduling.

Owner contract · Models and simulation

docs.title: Robot
docs.text:
Robot descriptions become a computational model: joint state, coordinate conventions, kinematics and dynamics. A controller can query a frame Jacobian or a mass matrix without owning URDF loading. A simulator is a separate world interface; a model calculation alone does not advance a physical experiment.

Owner contract · Models and simulation

docs.title: Solvers
docs.text:
QP problem containers, solution status and backend wrappers provide the numerical boundary. Control code supplies the costs and constraints; the solver reports the numerical result. A feasible QP does not by itself establish tracking quality or physical success.

Owner contract · Model-based walking

docs.title: Estimation
docs.text:
State and contact estimation turn measurements into evidence the control composition can use. For example, contact evidence can inform a walking composition, but the estimator does not own the decision that a foot may support the robot. Frames, timestamps and the distinction between measured and estimated quantities matter at this boundary.

Owner contract · State and perception

docs.title: Perception
docs.text:
Terrain products, geometric uncertainty and bounded queries describe the nearby world. The mapping application can inspect elevation or candidate support geometry without running a walking controller. Acquisition, scheduling and a planner's decision to use a product remain outside the perception core; geometric confidence alone does not certify a safe foothold.

Owner contract · State and perception · Mapping example

docs.title: Locomotion
docs.text:
Reusable biped, contact and numerical primitives support walking compositions, including reduced-order locomotion computations. A robot project connects those primitives to its state and chooses its planning policy. Robot-specific tuning, reference authoring and scenario acceptance are not hidden in a generic locomotion default.

Owner contract · Model-based walking

docs.title: Control
docs.text:
Feedback, joint servo and the TAC-QP whole-body core realize control requests. In a model-based composition, task references and constraints produce actuator commands using the robot's state and dynamics. The app selects the tasks and their meaning; control does not decide the experiment's walking strategy.

Owner contract · Model-based walking

docs.title: Policy
docs.text:
The learned-policy deployment boundary covers observation construction, action decoding, joint-PD realization, ONNX inference and bundle/parity tooling. It preserves the meaning of a trained policy when moving between training and execution. Training recipes belong to the app's learning project; this module does not imply an estimator or safety filter around every policy.

Owner contract · Policy deployment · Learning workflow

docs.title: Simulation
docs.text:
MuJoCo simulation, the terrain catalog, simulated sensors and optional viewer helpers provide an inspectable world. An experiment can change the terrain while keeping its robot model and controller configuration fixed. Simulation owns neither the controller nor the CORTA graph that an app may use to run it.

Owner contract · Models and simulation

docs.title: Digit hardware
docs.text:
Digit's Agility low-level interface supplies state/command mapping, limit handling, guarded command encoding and a live link for Agility simulation or the robot. The SDK-free pieces and optional live SDK path have different build requirements. The live vendor-SDK integration is root-build functionality, not a promise that every installed package includes hardware access. Hardware qualification remains an app-level validation question.

Owner contract · Digit integration

docs.title: CORTA
docs.text:
CORTA executes a Plant-paced composition with inline and deferred work, typed bounded messages, telemetry and replay mechanisms. A Plant exchanges observations and commands with the world. The runtime core stays independent of robot models, MuJoCo, Python and vendor SDKs; an app supplies the composition. Execution mechanisms do not establish hard real-time qualification on a particular machine.

Owner contract · Runtime and execution

docs.title: CORTA adapters
docs.text:
Adapters connect typed CORTA ingress and egress to external inputs and observers, such as keyboard, joystick, datagrams or visualization. Free-running external connections stay off the control tick. Adapters depend on CORTA; CORTA does not depend on an app's chosen adapter or operator-command semantics.

Owner contract · Runtime and execution

docs.title: Logging
docs.text:
Telemetry channels, records and bounded producer buffers make runtime behavior inspectable. File writing is separate from the producer path, so logging infrastructure need not place blocking disk I/O on a control tick. Logging records signals; scheduling and graph replay belong to the runtime.

Owner contract · Runtime and execution · Evaluating experiments

docs.title: What the package exports
docs.text:
Surface How a consumer uses it What stays with the consumer C++ find_package(cyber_suite) and exported cyber_suite::<module> targets Composition, application policy and robot-specific configuration Python Supported cyber_suite bindings and native tools; the separate cyber_suite_mjlab learning adapter Training recipes, analysis and experiment orchestration Data cyber_suite::data::resolve or cyber_suite.data.resolve App calibration and local experiment assets Contracts Each module's MODULE.md and each app's APP.md / VALIDATION.md Acceptance criteria and evidence for the intended use

The application consumption contract specifies the current build boundary. Available exports and optional dependencies vary by module; the capability map is not a promise that every module ships every interface.

docs.title: Boundaries worth understanding
docs.text: Boundary What it establishes Where to learn more Robot description → computations Joint names, coordinates, inertial and actuation assumptions Models and simulation Measurements → estimated state What the controller knows, in which frame and at what time State and perception Planning → reference execution Desired motion, reference coordinates and validity Model-based walking Graph → execution Rates, deferred work, observation/command exchange Runtime and execution Training → deployed policy Observation packing, action meaning and realization Policy deployment Experiment → conclusion Matched conditions, measurements and qualification limits Evaluate an experiment

docs.title: Follow a single experiment
docs.text:
For Digit model-based walking, a scenario selects ALIP or DCM, terrain and a velocity schedule. The app loads calibration profiles, constructs the graph and creates the Plant. Servo builds the state used by planning and control, the planner authors task references, and the whole-body controller turns them into actuator commands. The handbook follows that loop with diagrams and a measured example.

Changing to a learned policy changes the control composition: inference produces actions and the policy Servo realizes them according to the bundle's contract. It is not simply another footstep planner feeding the same whole-body controller. The robot boundary and execution infrastructure can still be shared. See policy deployment.

docs.title: Where a change belongs
docs.text:
A robot-neutral numerical improvement belongs in the module that owns it. A new experiment normally begins in app-owned configuration. A student project consumes the package through its published C++ and Python boundaries, using its own Pixi project. It should not reach into a neighboring source checkout to borrow private implementation files.

Robot descriptions live under assets/robots/<robot>/; app calibration lives with the app. The shared terrain catalog is owned by simulation. Keeping these homes distinct makes a question such as “did the new controller improve tracking?” answerable: the comparison can preserve the model and world while changing the intended behavior.

docs.title: Implementation and evidence are different
docs.text:
A module contract describes the implemented surface and lifecycle. An app contract describes the composition. Its validation document records what has been demonstrated, with conditions and limitations. A historical design can explain a decision without describing today's execution.

This website organizes the maintained reading paths; it does not promote modules to stable status or replace the owner contracts. The development workflow explains how a change is validated and integrated.

docs.title: How a Digit walking command becomes motion
docs.text:
You ask Digit to walk forward at 0.3 m/s. That request must become foot placements, body motion, joint torques and, eventually, new sensor readings. Follow that journey to understand where the main parts of Cyber Suite fit and where your own experiment would belong.

Digit is the worked example because it connects model-based walking, learned control, CORTA execution and the Agility deployment interface. G1 is a starting project students can extend using the same ownership principles. You can follow this chapter with basic programming and robotics knowledge; the planner and controller equations can come later.

After this chapter, you should be able to:

  • Explain the difference between a motion command, a task reference and an actuator command.
  • Trace the model-based and learned control paths without confusing their controllers.
  • Find the owner of a proposed change and name evidence that would evaluate it.

docs.title: The loop at a glance
docs.text:
Start at Desired motion, then follow the green arrows into planning, reference tracking and the Plant. Follow the blue arrows back: the robot's response changes what the controller does next. This is a simplified picture of the model-based graph, with the two feedback loops drawn explicitly.

Figure 1 · Structure from the reviewed code. Green arrows carry requests and commands; blue arrows return observations. The Plant may be MuJoCo or the LLAPI connection.

Open full-size diagram

Read the same request at three levels: “travel forward at 0.3 m/s” is a motion command; “move this foot along this trajectory” is a task reference; “apply these joint torques and drive settings” is an actuator command. Each arrow has a different meaning. A correct message at one boundary does not guarantee the desired physical response at the next.

Check your understanding: the robot misses a foot target. Where would you look first?

Compare the installed foot reference with measured foot motion at the Servo boundary. If the reference itself is unsuitable, follow it upstream to the planner. If the reference looks reasonable but the foot cannot follow it, inspect state estimates, contact constraints, actuator saturation and Plant actuation. The animation alone cannot distinguish these causes.

The app assembles this particular robot behavior. Shared modules provide reusable algorithms and infrastructure. A scenario selects the planner, world and motion schedule; profiles supply calibration. An artifact records what happened in one run. These four ideas help you navigate before learning individual classes.

docs.title: 1. Express the motion you want
docs.text:
The ALIP scenario requests forward velocity [0.3, 0.0] m/s with zero yaw rate on flat ground. It also selects the planner and simulation settings. The app combines that scenario with its profiles and command-line overrides to produce the resolved configuration.

A velocity request describes desired travel. Startup, step planning, actuator limits and the robot's actual state determine the resulting motion. An operator's keyboard or joystick can provide the command instead of a fixed schedule; that changes the command source while preserving the downstream ownership boundaries.

docs.title: 2. Estimate what the robot is doing
docs.text:
The Plant supplies encoder readings and measurements from the IMU (inertial measurement unit). In the usual closed-loop simulation composition, the estimator reconstructs the floating base's orientation, velocity and position in its qualified local frame. The dynamics support gate estimates support and contact capacity. The Servo combines these with robot-model queries to prepare the state used by planning and control.

The simulator also knows the exact simulated state. That truth is available for diagnostics and explicitly selected external-state modes; it is not the normal closed-loop estimator input. When comparing algorithms, preserve the state source. A controller that works on truth has demonstrated a different boundary from one that works on estimates.

docs.title: 3. Plan steps and author references
docs.text:
ALIP means angular-momentum linear inverted pendulum; DCM means divergent component of motion. They use reduced models of balance to choose stepping behavior. Their app adapters turn accepted plans into executable references for the feet, pelvis and body motion.

The shared walking coordinator tracks startup, walking, touchdown admission and stopping. It consumes the full-rate contact history supplied by Servo, so a 50 Hz planner can reason about contact evidence collected at 1 kHz. A reference preview contains a short future trajectory and task activation targets. It carries more than a single desired position.

ALIP and DCM have different reference-coordinate contracts. Their adapters and controller task geometry must agree. Replacing a planner therefore means respecting its reference contract, even though both fit the same overall application structure.

docs.title: 4. Turn references into actuator commands
docs.text:
Every millisecond, Servo samples the installed trajectories and asks the whole-body controller to realize them. TAC-QP is the repository's constrained whole-body quadratic-programming controller. It reconciles the body and foot objectives with the modeled dynamics and constraints such as contact, friction and actuator limits.

The model-based planner owns the walking sequence and reference meaning. Servo owns their execution against the current estimated state. This separation matters when diagnosing a problem: an unreachable foot target, poor tracking of a feasible target and incorrect contact estimation are different causes.

The outgoing command includes actuator torque and, when the drive model is active, drive-damping information. The Plant handles how that command reaches the simulated or external drives. The default MuJoCo actuation model includes drive behavior and command delay; requesting a torque does not mean it acts instantaneously.

docs.title: 5. Observe the response and repeat
docs.text:
The Plant advances simulation or exchanges data through the low-level interface, then returns a new observation. The next Servo tick reacts to it; the next planner update can revise future motion. Startup readiness, finite reference validity and measured stopping also belong to this loop.

A viewer displays selected observations. Watching the robot stay upright is useful, but does not establish velocity tracking, actuator margins or settled stopping. Use the recorded configuration and diagnostics to explain the behavior you see.

docs.title: Why the two rates matter
docs.text:
The canonical model-based composition releases the planner at 50 Hz, about once every 20 ms, while Servo executes at 1 kHz. Between planner releases, Servo keeps sampling the installed reference trajectory and reacting to fresh state. It does not wait for a new plan before every torque calculation.

Figure 2 · Scheduled rates, drawn schematically. A diamond releases planning work; it does not mean a new plan has already arrived. Reference adoption follows deferred completion.

Open full-size diagram

At 7 ms, there is no new planner release. What does Servo do?

It samples the installed reference at the current time, uses the fresh state and computes another actuator command. A trajectory describes how the target changes between planning updates. Holding the last torque for 20 ms would be a different controller.

Boundary What crosses it Why it matters Plant → Servo Sensor observation Defines what the controller can know Servo → planner Command, estimated state and contact history Gives planning a coherent view of execution Planner → Servo Finite reference preview and task targets Keeps planning decisions separate from fast execution Servo → Plant Actuator command Defines how control acts on the world

CORTA provides the runtime graph, timing declarations and bounded message exchange. The planner executes as deferred work; Servo runs inline with the Plant exchange. Copied values cross these boundaries rather than shared mutable planner/controller objects. The graph wiring is visible in the application entry point.

A configured rate is not a measured deadline guarantee. Running a simulation with 1 ms ticks does not prove every tick finishes within 1 ms on a real robot. Timing evidence and physical behavior evidence answer separate questions.

docs.title: What changes with a learned policy
docs.text:
Selecting planner: policy replaces both the model-based planner and its Servo with a policy inference worker and PolicyServo. The Plant, scenario machinery and CORTA execution framework remain shared. The normal learned path does not send its actions through the model-based whole-body controller.

Training → exported bundle → inference → joint targets → joint PD → Plant

Training is owned by Digit learning. The exported bundle specifies how observations are packed and actions are decoded. Deferred inference runs at the bundle's declared rate; the shipped walking policies use 50 Hz. PolicyServo adopts actions and realizes joint proportional-derivative (PD) control at 1 kHz, with damping placed according to the contract and Plant.

This gives you two useful research paths. You can investigate footstep planning and whole-body objectives in the model-based composition, or investigate observations, rewards and learned behavior in the learning composition. Compare them on matched scenarios while recording the model, state source, actuation assumptions and policy bundle.

Policy parity checks whether exported inference and action realization reproduce the trainer's recorded contract. Physical evaluation then asks whether the resulting robot tracks commands, respects limits and handles the tested scenarios. Passing one does not substitute for the other. See the policy deployment reference for the complete chain.

docs.title: Where simulation meets deployment
docs.text:
The MuJoCo Plant owns the simulated world, sensors and actuation. The LLAPI Plant connects the app to Agility's low-level API. A common observation/command boundary lets the control composition reach both, but the state source, timing, command acceptance and drive behavior must still be handled explicitly.

With the default LLAPI base-state selection, the app uses Agility's base estimate. The integration also handles operation-mode handover and drive damping. These details explain why a controller can behave differently after moving from the local simulator to Agility's simulator even when its planning algorithm is unchanged.

Digit has recorded model-based and learned-policy operation through LLAPI against Agility's simulator, plus model and drive-alignment investigations. Those results establish specific simulation and interface evidence. They do not establish complete simulator equivalence or qualify this application for physical-hardware operation. Use the current validation to identify the model revision, controller, conditions and remaining limitations behind any deployment claim.

docs.title: Read a real result
docs.text:
Question: if a run completes, did the robot do what we asked? Here is a small example from the recorded October 1 Arena campaign. Digit was asked to move sideways at 0.200 m/s on flat ground with nominal sensor noise. The cadence policy, ALIP and DCM each ran with seeds 0, 1 and 2. All nine selected runs completed.

Figure 3 · Recorded simulation, 2026-10-01. Each hollow circle is one run's steady-plateau velocity; each filled square is the median of three seeds. The dashed line is the command. This campaign predates the current drive model.

Open full-size plot

Read the plot in three passes:

  1. Find the request. The dashed line marks the same 0.200 m/s lateral command for all three controllers.
  2. Compare the response. The policy's median is 0.136 m/s, about 0.064 m/s below the command, or 32% slower. The ALIP and DCM medians lie closer to the command in this example.
  3. Limit the conclusion. Completion and tracking are different measurements. This plot does not show transient motion, stopping, actuator margins or the cause of the policy's error. It also does not establish which controller is best on other tasks or on today's code.
Before changing the policy, what evidence would you request?

Request time-aligned command and measured velocity, confirm the observation/action contract and actuation model, then inspect joint targets, tracking and saturation. Check whether the shortfall persists across the chosen evaluation scenarios. The result suggests a question to investigate; it does not yet tell you whether to change rewards, inference, state estimation or the Plant.

Inspect the numbers and reproduce the figure Controller Seed 0 (m/s) Seed 1 (m/s) Seed 2 (m/s) Median (m/s) Completed Cadence policy 0.129616 0.136660 0.136238 0.136238 3/3 ALIP 0.197065 0.200260 0.197787 0.197787 3/3 DCM 0.197195 0.208508 0.205089 0.205089 3/3

The published CSV contains exactly the nine runs shown above, selected from the complete Arena dataset using campaign=grid, condition=nominal, terrain=flat, motion=left_0.2 and config=policy|alip|dcm. No failed runs are removed from this selection. The original capsule and its manifest record the historical experiment and its source patch. The teaching-figure capsule, input specification and renderer record the selection and presentation. No simulation was rerun to make this plot.

# From the repository root; reads the retained compact data.
pixi run python notes/evidence/2026-10-18-handbook-walking/scripts/render.py

docs.title: Try it in simulation
docs.text:
Use the Digit project on the simulation host. This exercise assumes the repository and Pixi environment are already available; the running guide covers launch options and the remote guide explains display and port forwarding.

cd apps/digit
pixi run build --target digit_corta_walking
pixi run walk --config alip_walking --print-resolved-config
pixi run walk --config alip_walking --rerun-web \
  --log artifacts/handbook/alip-first-run.h5

The simulation and viewer server run on that host. For a remote session, open the viewer through the forwarding described in the remote guide. Use a fresh log name for each run. Preserve the first run as your baseline before changing configuration.

Before running, predict what the measured forward velocity will do during startup, steady walking and stopping. While it runs, connect the picture to the loop:

  1. Identify the forward command in the resolved configuration and compare it with measured forward velocity.
  2. Watch startup, stepping and the transition back toward standing. Identify which components own those decisions.
  3. Inspect tracking, contact/support and actuator diagnostics alongside the animation. Record a failure as an outcome to investigate.

After the run, the app-owned plotter can summarize the model-based walking log:

pixi run plot-walking artifacts/handbook/alip-first-run.h5 \
  -o artifacts/handbook/alip-first-run-plots

Changing --config to dcm_walking selects another canonical scenario, whose motion schedule also differs. To study the planner alone, retain the ALIP scenario and select --planner dcm, preserve the other settings and use another log path. The planner profile and reference contract still change deliberately. A useful comparison states exactly what was held fixed.

Your first deliverable can be one annotated plot of commanded versus measured velocity, with startup, steady walking and stopping marked, plus three sentences: what you expected, what happened, and which boundary you would inspect next. Record the model, state source, configuration and code revision beside it. Keep the plot in your project's ignored artifacts/ while exploring. This makes an agent task concrete without requiring you to understand every API first.

docs.title: Find the owner of your change
docs.text:
Your question Start here Evidence to inspect What command or world should I test? App scenarios and resolved configuration Same scenario, seed, model and actuation assumptions Why did the planner choose this step? App planner adapter, then modules/locomotion Plan, installed reference and touchdown history Why did the robot miss the target? Servo/reference binding, then modules/control Reference versus actual motion, constraints and actuator saturation Is the estimated state wrong? Estimation configuration, then modules/estimation Timestamp-matched estimate and diagnostic truth How should I change learned behavior? apps/digit/learning Fixed observation/action contract, baseline and physical evaluation Why does deployment behave differently? Plant configuration and modules/digit_hardware State source, drive realization, timing and command acceptance Open the implementation when you need the details
  • Graph composition: the actual systems and their connections.
  • Servo and control transaction: the fast model-based path.
  • ALIP adapter and DCM adapter: planner-owned behavior.
  • Reference binding: installing previews into controller tasks.
  • Policy controller: inference and policy realization.
  • MuJoCo Plant and LLAPI Plant: the two world boundaries.
  • App contract and validation: implemented behavior and its demonstrated limits.

docs.title: Turn your question into an agent task
docs.text:
Give the agent a question, an owner, a baseline, constraints and observable outcomes. You do not need to name every class before asking. You do need enough understanding to judge whether its proposed change answers your question.

Help me compare ALIP and DCM on the same flat Digit scenario. Explain the current planner/Servo boundary first. Preserve the model, actuation, estimator, command schedule and shared controller calibration; record the planner-specific profiles and reference contracts that change. Reproduce the baseline, then compare tracking, actuator saturation, stopping and failures using separate artifacts. Keep the experiment in app-owned configuration and report what the results establish.

Before accepting a result, ask yourself: did the agent change the component that owns the behavior, preserve the comparison, and show physical evidence for its conclusion?

Start a project with G1. Use the student-project guide to create a pinned, independent project. Digit supplies the integrated example; your G1 project owns its experiments, configuration and validation. Its learning contract is a starting point for learning work. Carry over the ownership and evaluation habits, and check which capabilities the G1 app actually implements before reusing a Digit workflow.

docs.title: Your first simulation
docs.text: The first goal is to connect a command, a visible response and an inspectable result. Start with one robot project and one known scenario. Keep that run as a baseline before changing configuration or asking an agent to improve behavior.

docs.title: Choose the execution host
docs.text:
These commands assume an available Cyber Suite checkout and Pixi. Ubuntu is the intended execution host. Run the commands in its local terminal or in a remote terminal connected from your own computer, and confirm the checkout before building:

hostname
pwd
git status --short --branch
pixi run --locked orient

Use command -v pixi to confirm that Pixi is available on the execution host. The development workflow explains project environments, and remote development explains local versus remote terminals and viewers. A connected SSH shell alone does not verify the GPU or display setup.

docs.title: Digit: follow the integrated example
docs.text:
From the repository root:

cd apps/digit
pixi run --locked build --target digit_corta_walking
pixi run --locked walk --config alip_walking --print-resolved-config
pixi run --locked walk --config alip_walking --rerun-web \
  --log artifacts/first-run/alip.h5

The build uses the project's installed-package boundary. The first environment installation may build dependencies; allow it to finish before launching. The second command prints the actual configuration. The final command runs the simulation and a browser viewer, normally on port 9090. Choose a fresh log path if you repeat it.

On a client connected through VS Code Remote - SSH, forward port 9090 in Ports and open its forwarded address. The simulation stays on Ubuntu. The Digit running guide covers alternate viewers, ports and scenario choices.

docs.title: G1: start with standing
docs.text:
In a new terminal at the repository root:

cd apps/unitree-g1
pixi run --locked stand --viser

The task builds the project and starts the simulation. Open the printed URL, normally port 8080; forward that port for a remote client browser. Then use the G1 running guide for walking and recording. Its walking acceptance can fail even when visible motion completes; read the reported outcome rather than judging only the animation.

docs.title: Explain what you saw
docs.text:
Locate the command and the measured response. Identify startup, steady motion and stopping. Record the code revision, resolved configuration and outcome beside the log. For Digit, generate the app's plots from the Digit project:

pixi run --locked plot-walking artifacts/first-run/alip.h5 \
  -o artifacts/first-run/alip-plots

Your first useful result is an annotated plot and a short explanation of what the command produced. The handbook supplies the conceptual loop; the evaluation guide helps turn the observation into a controlled comparison.

docs.title: If the run does not start
docs.text:
Symptom First check Build or package installation failed Read the first error and verify the owning manifest and supported host; do not launch an older binary as though it were the new build The viewer URL opens on Ubuntu but not your client Check the printed port and your client's forwarding address The viewer is visible but the outcome fails Inspect the app's reported acceptance and its validation limits A command behaves differently after pulling Rebuild and compare the resolved configuration and model identity

The documentation build does not run these robot scenarios. Current execution evidence lives in each app's validation record.

docs.title: G1 Student Projects
docs.text:
Unitree G1 is the student template selected by the maintainer. The maintained source is apps/unitree-g1; pixi run create-g1-project exports a committed revision into a new, independent project. It copies the existing 23-DoF standing, walking, viewer and learning code instead of maintaining a second implementation in a template folder. The source app contracts and validation limits travel with the project.

For work inside the parent repository, follow the development and project workflow. A standalone export becomes its own repository and owns its subsequent changes, validation and task notes.

docs.title: Create a project
docs.text:
From a Cyber Suite checkout, select a committed revision that is available from the repository every student can access:

pixi run create-g1-project /path/to/g1-project --revision COMMIT

The destination's parent must exist; the destination must not. The default dependency is ssh://git@github.com/ayonga/cyber-suite.git. Both the compiled package and the Python distribution pin the same full commit. An unpushed local commit can be exported for local validation but cannot be fetched by students until it is available at that URL.

For an existing student mirror, pass its Git and browser URLs explicitly:

pixi run create-g1-project /path/to/g1-project --revision COMMIT \
  --source-url ssh://git@HOST/OWNER/cyber-suite.git \
  --web-url https://HOST/OWNER/cyber-suite

The mirror must contain the selected Cyber Suite commit and its package sources. The exporter creates no remote repository and changes no visibility or access settings. Using the existing repository with authorized collaborators needs no separate mirror. Before distributing, verify collaborator access, the selected revision's availability, and the intended code/asset sharing terms. No top-level open-source license is supplied by this repository; the exporter does not invent one. Unitree's asset licenses and upstream provenance are retained verbatim.

docs.title: What is exported
docs.text:
The project contains its own pixi.toml, CMake source, walking and learning apps, app documentation, empty working-note home and a complete G1 asset snapshot under assets/robots/unitree_g1. SOURCE.json records the source revision, original file hashes and exported file hashes. The source lockfile is omitted because it contains monorepo path dependencies. Environments, builds, logs, checkpoints, private handoffs and Git history are excluded. Only files tracked at the selected commit are read; dirty and untracked source changes cannot silently enter an export.

Project documentation links that leave the exported project point to the pinned source revision. Historical validation remains inherited evidence. A new project records its own fresh results before treating a change as accepted.

docs.title: Validate and lock
docs.text:
Run from the exported project:

pixi run check
pixi run -e learn task-check --device cpu --num-envs 2 --steps 10 --ppo 1 \
  --out artifacts/learning-smoke
pixi run -e learn export-policy --checkpoint artifacts/learning-smoke/model_smoke.pt \
  --out artifacts/learning-bundle --fixture-steps 30
pixi run policy-parity artifacts/learning-bundle

Commit the generated pixi.lock alongside the project source and SOURCE.json, clone the project into a fresh directory, then repeat with --locked. check proves the installed-package C++ build, 23-DoF model parity and bounded standing acceptance. The learning smoke and policy parity check the Python-only environment, model/action/observation mapping and sampled export conventions. None qualifies a learned gait, hardware operation or real-time deadlines. Interactive standing uses pixi run stand --viser; see the exported running guide for local/remote viewers.

docs.title: Training assets
docs.text:
Learning does not depend on the C++ package or a nearby Cyber Suite checkout. Its G1 assets ship in the project at the same relative paths the shared resolver accepts. Pixi starts commands in the project folder, which is the first data search root. For direct invocation from another directory, set CYBER_SUITE_DATA_PATH to the project folder. The snapshot includes generated model views, every referenced mesh, raw upstream descriptions, licenses and checksums; it is pinned to the same source revision as the initial package dependencies.

When upgrading, update both Git dependency revisions together, deliberately review any asset changes, regenerate the lockfile and rerun the checks. SOURCE.json describes the initial export; subsequent project commits own intentional edits. A new robot follows the same data-search contract with its own project assets or an explicit CYBER_SUITE_DATA_PATH.

docs.title: Status and CI
docs.text:
Each app's APP.md and VALIDATION.md remain the project status authorities. Notes are working context. There is no duplicate per-project CURRENT.md to synchronize. Within Cyber Suite, root orientation discovers these contracts and active handoffs.

Project CI is optional. Run the standalone checks manually before integrating changes; existing root CI covers the root build and governance. A later project CI job can invoke the same pixi run --locked check command without introducing another acceptance definition. No CI workflow is generated by the template.

docs.title: Verified boundary
docs.text:
The 2026-10-17 Ubuntu validation exported G1 from c366b7e, created an independent Git project, committed its generated lockfile and ran pixi run --locked check from a fresh clone. Installed-package compilation, 32-sample model parity and 10 s standing acceptance passed. The Python-only learning environment passed a one-update CPU smoke, export and C++ parity using project-local assets and a non-editable Git-installed Python distribution. This first check used local file:// Git transport.

After publishing main, a new export pinned to 00b2d09ac4ce9da88b7ac6fe67965ec658f61a25 fetched both dependencies through the default GitHub SSH URL. A fresh clone with its committed lockfile passed the standalone C++ build, 32-sample model parity, 10 s standing acceptance and two-environment CPU learning mapping smoke. Python installation metadata confirms the remote URL and revision, and assets resolve inside that clone. This verifies remote transport with the maintainer's existing access; students still need their own repository access. Logs are under repository-root artifacts/robot_project_phase9/g1-remote-*; the owning walking and learning validation documents state the physical limits.

docs.title: Digit M0: a worked learning example
docs.text:
This page explains the September 2026 M0 baseline and its retained evidence. It is a worked example, not a summary of every current Digit policy. Later cadence, drive and task-space variants have different configurations; use the learning workflow for current entry points and the app contracts for their limits.

M0 trains a neural-network policy that makes Digit walk at a commanded forward speed, sideways speed and yaw rate on flat ground. This document explains how:

  • the learner;
  • what the policy sees and commands;
  • the rewards that shape the gait;
  • what training produced.

It explains; it does not define. The contract is the app's APP.md and the code it names, and the latest demonstrated result is in VALIDATION.md. Where they disagree with this page, they win.

The task is Digit-Velocity-Flat-1ms. It starts from mjlab's make_velocity_env_cfg() recipe, the one mjlab's Unitree G1 uses, and changes only what Digit needs:

  • joint reads through compiled-model addresses, because of Digit's ball-jointed rods;
  • Digit's posture tolerances;
  • a narrower lateral command range;
  • a self-collision penalty;
  • flat terrain;
  • the C++ plant's physics options.

docs.title: At a Glance
docs.text: Item M0 choice Learner PPO (RSL-RL), asymmetric actor–critic, 4096 parallel envs on one GPU Simulator mjlab on MuJoCo Warp; 1 ms physics step with the C++ plant's solver options Policy rate 50 Hz; each action is held for 20 physics steps Actor input 92 values: base velocities, gravity direction, 30 joint positions and velocities, last action, command Critic input The actor's 92 without noise, plus 12 privileged foot values Output 20 joint-position offsets from the standing pose, tracked by torque-limited PD Reward 4 Gaussian tracking and shaping terms, 9 active penalties (10 listed, one weighted 0) Episode 20 s; ends early when the torso tilts past 70° Budget 3000 iterations, 2.95e8 policy steps, 1 h 41 min on an RTX 4090

docs.title: How the Pieces Fit
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  subgraph ENV["mjlab environment, 4096 copies on the GPU"]
    CMD["Command sampler<br/>vx, vy, ωz"]
    SIM["MuJoCo Warp<br/>1 ms step"]
    PD["20 position actuators<br/>PD, torque-limited"]
    OBS["Observation terms<br/>+ uniform noise"]
    REW["14 reward terms<br/>weighted, × 0.02 s"]
    TERM["Termination<br/>tilt > 70° or 20 s"]
  end
  subgraph LEARN["RSL-RL PPO"]
    ACT["Actor MLP<br/>512-256-128, Gaussian"]
    CRIT["Critic MLP<br/>512-256-128"]
    BUF["Rollout buffer<br/>24 steps × 4096 envs"]
    UPD["GAE + clipped PPO update"]
  end
  CMD --> OBS
  SIM --> OBS
  OBS -- "92 noisy values" --> ACT
  OBS -- "104 clean values" --> CRIT
  ACT -- "action a, 20 values" --> PD
  PD -- "joint torque" --> SIM
  SIM --> REW --> BUF
  SIM --> TERM --> BUF
  CRIT -- "V(s)" --> BUF
  BUF --> UPD
  UPD -- "new weights" --> ACT
  UPD -- "new weights" --> CRIT

Only the actor is deployed. The critic exists to estimate returns during training, so it may see simulator quantities that the robot cannot measure.

docs.title: Timing
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
  participant P as Policy (50 Hz)
  participant A as Position actuators
  participant M as MuJoCo (1 kHz)
  P->>A: target = q_stand + s · a, held for 20 ms
  loop 20 physics steps
    A->>M: τ = clamp(kp (target − q) − kd q̇, ±τmax)
    M-->>A: q, q̇
  end
  M-->>P: next observation and reward

The PD law runs inside MuJoCo at every 1 ms physics step, as position actuators. The policy only moves the setpoint. The training timestep of 1 ms is a separate decision from the plant's 0.5 ms step; the learning roadmap records why.

docs.title: Observations
docs.text:
The actor sees 92 values, concatenated in this order. The noise is uniform, added during training only.

Term Size Definition Noise (±) Base linear velocity 3 Root velocity in the torso frame, from the simulator's true state 0.5 m/s Base angular velocity 3 Root angular velocity in the torso frame 0.2 rad/s Projected gravity 3 Unit gravity direction in the torso frame; its x and y parts encode tilt 0.05 Joint positions 30 \(q - q^{\text{stand}}\) for the 20 motors and 10 passive joints 0.01 rad Joint velocities 30 \(\dot q\) for the same 30 joints 1.5 rad/s Last action 20 The previous raw policy output \(a_{t-1}\) none Command 3 \((v_x^{\text{cmd}}, v_y^{\text{cmd}}, \omega_z^{\text{cmd}})\) in the torso frame none
  • Passive joints. They are the ten the LLAPI measures: shin, tarsus, heel spring, toe pitch and toe roll on each side. The ball-jointed rods are not observed.
  • Joint reads. All joint terms read each hinge at its compiled qpos and dof address (mdp.py). mjlab 1.6's name-based joint terms misread 17 of Digit's 20 motors.
  • No memory. There is no observation history, no gait clock and no phase variable. Rhythm comes from the dynamics and the rewards; the last action is the only memory.
  • No estimator in training. The base velocity is simulator truth, and the ±0.5 m/s noise is the only stand-in for estimation error. M1b has since run the policy on InEKF estimates in the C++ plant; see What M0 Does Not Cover.
  • Critic extras (12). Foot height above the ground, current air time, contact flags, and contact force (signed \(\log(1+|F|)\), 3 per foot), for both feet.

docs.title: Actions
docs.text:
The policy outputs 20 unbounded numbers, one per motor. Each becomes a joint-position target around the standing keyframe:

\[ q_i^{\text{target}} = q_i^{\text{stand}} + s_i\,a_i, \qquad s_i = \frac{0.25\,\tau_i^{\max}}{k_{p,i}} \]

A unit action therefore asks for 25% of the joint's torque limit at zero velocity. MuJoCo applies the PD law at every physics step:

\[ \tau_i = \operatorname{clamp}\!\left(k_{p,i}\,(q_i^{\text{target}} - q_i) - k_{d,i}\,\dot q_i,\; \pm\tau_i^{\max}\right), \qquad k_p = I_a\,\omega_n^2,\quad k_d = 2\zeta\,I_a\,\omega_n \]
  • Gains. \(I_a\) is the joint's reflected motor inertia (MJCF armature), with \(\omega_n = 2\pi \cdot 10\) Hz and \(\zeta = 2\) (RL_GAINS).
  • Torque units. \(\tau^{\max}\) is the joint-side limit, the MJCF motor's ctrlrange times its gear. The C++ plant expects motor-side torque, so a deployed policy must send \(\tau / \text{gear}\).

Left side, read back from the exported policy contract; the right side mirrors it.

Joint Standing angle (rad) \(k_p\) (Nm/rad) \(k_d\) (Nm·s/rad) \(\tau^{\max}\) (Nm) \(s\) (rad per unit action) hip roll 0.317 686 43.7 126.7 0.046 hip yaw 0.000 268 17.1 79.2 0.074 hip pitch 0.028 476 30.3 216.9 0.114 knee −0.053 476 30.3 231.3 0.122 toe A 0.061 143 9.1 42.0 0.074 toe B −0.101 143 9.1 42.0 0.074 shoulder roll −0.300 686 43.7 126.7 0.046 shoulder pitch 0.944 686 43.7 126.7 0.046 shoulder yaw 0.000 268 17.1 79.2 0.074 elbow 0.363 686 43.7 126.7 0.046

These gains are soft. At zero action Digit collapses, so the policy must learn to hold itself up as well as to walk. They are simulation starting values, not hardware gains.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
flowchart TD
  R["Every 3–8 s, per env: resample"] --> U["vx ~ U(−1, 1) m/s<br/>vy ~ U(−0.5, 0.5) m/s<br/>ωz ~ U(−0.5, 0.5) rad/s<br/>heading target ~ U(−π, π)"]
  U --> F{"forward env?<br/>p = 0.2"}
  F -- yes --> F1["vx = max(abs(vx), 0.3)<br/>vy = 0, ωz = 0"]
  F -- no --> H
  F1 --> H{"heading env?<br/>p = 0.3"}
  H -- yes --> H1["every step:<br/>ωz = clip(0.5 · heading error, ±0.5)"]
  H -- no --> S
  H1 --> S{"standing env?<br/>p = 0.1"}
  S -- yes --> S1["command = 0"]
  S -- no --> OUT["command in the torso frame"]
  S1 --> OUT
  • Independent flags. The three flags are separate coin flips. Standing overrides everything, and a heading env's yaw rate overrides the forward flag's zero.
  • Curriculum. mjlab's command curriculum would widen vx to (−1.5, 2.0) m/s and ωz to ±0.7 rad/s at iteration 5000, and vx to (−2, 3) m/s at 10,000. The 3000-iteration run never reached either stage, so the policy has only seen the ranges above.

docs.title: Rewards
docs.text:
At each policy step the reward is a weighted sum scaled by the step length \(\Delta t = 0.02\) s:

\[ r_t = \Delta t \sum_k w_k\, f_k(s_t, a_t) \]

The four positive terms are Gaussian kernels of an error, so each lies in \([0, 1]\) and is 1 only when the error is zero. A perfect 20 s episode would score \((2 + 2 + 1 + 1) \times 20 = 120\).

Term \(w\) \(f\) Linear velocity tracking 2.0 \(\exp\!\left(-\left(\lVert \mathbf v^{\text{cmd}}_{xy} - \mathbf v_{xy}\rVert^2 + v_z^2\right) / 0.25\right)\) Yaw-rate tracking 2.0 \(\exp\!\left(-\left((\omega^{\text{cmd}}_z - \omega_z)^2 + \omega_x^2 + \omega_y^2\right) / 0.5\right)\) Upright torso 1.0 \(\exp\!\left(-(g_x^2 + g_y^2) / 0.2\right)\), with \(g\) the unit gravity vector in the torso frame Posture 1.0 \(\exp\!\left(-\frac{1}{20}\sum_{j=1}^{20} (q_j - q_j^{\text{stand}})^2 / \sigma_j^2\right)\) over the motors

Velocities are the root body's, in the torso frame. The tracking terms also penalize vertical bounce and roll and pitch rates.

  • Tracking is forgiving near zero. At the gate's 0.2 m/s limit, linear tracking still pays 0.85 of its maximum, so the reward pushes hardest on large errors.
  • Upright. It falls to 0.5 at about 22° of tilt.
  • Posture tolerance depends on speed. With commanded speed \(c = \lVert \mathbf v^{\text{cmd}}_{xy}\rVert + |\omega^{\text{cmd}}_z|\):
Regime Condition \(\sigma_j\) Standing \(c < 0.05\) 0.05 rad on every joint, which holds the stance tightly Walking \(0.05 \le c < 1.5\) hip pitch 0.3, knee 0.35, toes 0.25, hip roll and yaw 0.15, shoulder pitch and roll 0.15, shoulder yaw 0.1, elbow 0.15 Running \(c \ge 1.5\) Looser; rare in the initial command range

The penalties shape the gait and discourage harmful motion. Foot terms apply only while the command is nonzero (\(c > 0.05\)), so standing still costs nothing.

Term \(w\) Cost \(f\) Foot clearance −2.0 \(\sum_{\text{feet}} \lvert h - 0.10\rvert \cdot \lVert \mathbf v_{xy}\rVert\): a moving foot should be 10 cm up Joint limits −1.0 Sum of motor excursions beyond 90% of each joint's range Self-collision −1.0 Number of the last 4 recorded substeps with a self-contact force above 10 N Foot swing height −0.25 At each touchdown, \((h^{\text{peak}}/0.10 - 1)^2\) Action rate −0.1 \(\lVert a_t - a_{t-1}\rVert^2\) Foot slip −0.1 \(\sum \lVert \mathbf v_{xy}\rVert^2\) over feet in contact Torso angular velocity −0.05 \(\omega_x^2 + \omega_y^2\) of the torso Angular momentum −0.02 \(\lVert \mathbf L\rVert^2\), whole-body angular momentum about the centre of mass Soft landing −1e‑5 Sum of contact force magnitudes at touchdown Air time 0 Disabled

Foot height \(h\) is measured by a ring of six rays around each sole centre; foot velocity is the sole site's.

At the end of training the positive terms earn 5.24 per second and the penalties cost 0.87, for a net 4.37 per second, or 87 per episode. Action rate accounts for 0.74 of the penalties. The others each cost under 0.08 per second: they are nearly satisfied, not ignored.

These are training rewards, measured on the stochastic policy. The action-rate term therefore includes exploration noise, which is still 0.46 action units at the end, as well as the mean policy's own changes.

docs.title: Episodes, Resets and Randomization
docs.text: Aspect Setting Length 20 s (1000 policy steps). A timeout is treated as truncation: PPO bootstraps the return with \(\gamma V\), so running out of time is not scored as failure. Failure Torso tilt above 70° ends the episode, with no extra penalty. It only forfeits future reward. Joint reset The IK standing keyframe, ball-joint quaternions included, with zero velocity. Joint angles are not randomized, because the closed chains would need a constraint solve. Base reset ±0.5 m in x and y, 1–5 cm above the keyframe height, any yaw Pushes Every 1–3 s, the base velocity jumps by up to ±0.5 m/s in x and y, ±0.4 m/s in z, ±0.52 rad/s in roll and pitch rate, and ±0.78 rad/s in yaw rate Foot friction 0.3–1.2 per env, drawn once at startup Torso centre of mass Offset by ±2.5 cm in x and y and ±3 cm in z, per env at startup Not randomized Masses, gains, motor strength, latency, joint friction. Encoder bias is off, because mjlab applies it per joint and would misread Digit.

docs.title: The Learner: PPO
docs.text:
Proximal Policy Optimization alternates between collecting experience with the current policy and taking a few conservative gradient steps on it. One iteration:

  1. Rollout. Each of the 4096 envs runs 24 policy steps, 98,304 transitions in all.
  2. Actions are sampled from \(a \sim \mathcal N(\mu_\theta(o), \operatorname{diag}\sigma^2)\).
  3. \(\sigma\) is a learned per-action vector, independent of the state, and starts at 1.
  4. The buffer stores the observations, action, log-probability, reward, done flag and critic value.
  5. Advantages by generalized advantage estimation, with \(\gamma = 0.99\) and \(\lambda = 0.95\):

$$ \delta_t = r_t + \gamma V(s_{t+1})(1 - d_t) - V(s_t), \qquad \hat A_t = \delta_t + \gamma\lambda(1 - d_t)\hat A_{t+1} $$ - The value target is \(\hat A_t + V(s_t)\). - Advantages are then normalized over the batch. - At 50 Hz, \(\gamma = 0.99\) is an effective horizon of about 100 steps, or 2 s.

  1. Update. 5 epochs over 4 minibatches of 24,576 transitions, with Adam. With \(\rho = \pi_\theta(a|o) / \pi_{\text{old}}(a|o)\) the loss is:

$$ L = -\min!\left(\rho \hat A,\; \operatorname{clip}(\rho, 0.8, 1.2)\,\hat A\right) + 1.0\,L_V^{\text{clipped}} - 0.01\,\mathcal H[\pi_\theta] $$

Gradient norms are clipped at 1.0, separately for the actor and critic.

  1. Adaptive learning rate. The rate starts at 1e‑3. After each minibatch:
  2. if the KL divergence from the old policy exceeds 0.02, the rate is divided by 1.5;
  3. below 0.005 it is multiplied by 1.5;
  4. it stays within 1e‑5 to 1e‑2.
Network Layers Activation Input normalization Actor 92 → 512 → 256 → 128 → 20 ELU Running mean and variance Critic 104 → 512 → 256 → 128 → 1 ELU Running mean and variance

The asymmetric critic sees clean observations and foot contact information. That lowers the variance of its value estimates, which makes the advantages the actor learns from less noisy, while the actor stays limited to what a robot can sense.

docs.title: What Training Produced
docs.text:
One run, training seed 42, on the RTX 4090. The per-iteration values are RSL-RL's running means over recently completed training episodes.

  • Iterations 0–400: staying up. Episodes lengthen slowly, to about 11 s. Upright and posture rise first, because not falling earns them without any tracking.
  • Iterations 400–480: the policy stops falling. Episodes reach 19 s and upright reaches 0.93.
  • Iterations 480–1200: tracking. Linear tracking climbs from 0.36 to 0.80 of its maximum, and exploration noise falls from 0.69 to 0.48. At iteration 600 the policy walks forward but not yet backward or sideways.
  • After 1200: diminishing returns. The return rises from 83 to 87 over the last 1800 iterations.

The gate (the Digit project's evaluate task) tests 45 fixed commands over the initial range, with eight replicates of 10 s each, and pushes. The rows above show the same progression:

  • Checkpoint 600 tracks only standing and slow forward walking (vy = 0, vx of 0 or 0.5 m/s). It falls 0.24–0.35 m/s short at 1 m/s forward. Backward and sideways errors are about the size of the command, and the gate fails.
  • Checkpoint 1200 is the first to pass, with a mean planar error of 0.098 m/s against the 0.1 m/s limit.
  • Checkpoint 2999 passes on two evaluation seeds. The mean planar error is 0.09 m/s, with no falls in 360 tracking runs and full survival of 0.5 m/s and 1 m/s kicks.

The largest remaining errors are:

  • 0.10–0.13 m/s under lateral commands;
  • up to 0.15 rad/s when turning in place.

The resulting gait takes about three steps per second, with no flight phase, and the foot apex reaches 85–111 mm at 0.5–1 m/s. VALIDATION.md holds the gate criteria and the gait table.

The capsule behind these figures is 2026-09-27-digit-m0-velocity-policy.

docs.title: What M0 Does Not Cover
docs.text:
• Transfer. Everything on this page is inside mjlab. M1 has since run the same policy in the C++ plant: the five flat scenarios complete on truth (M1a) and on InEKF estimates (M1b). The learning roadmap records that gate.
  • Estimation. Training sees true base velocity. In M1b, the policy's tracking on estimates was within 0.01 m/s of its truth runs. The simulated IMU is noiseless, so this says nothing about hardware estimation.
  • Small commands. In mjlab and in the plant, the policy barely responds to small lateral and yaw commands. The gate's grid tests only 0 and ±0.5 on those axes, so M0 could not see this; M1 found it.
  • Hardware realism. Training has no latency, actuator-dynamics, gain or mass randomization, and no terrain. The plant adds one 1 ms tick of action latency.
  • Variance. There is one training seed.
  • Range. Commands above 1 m/s forward, 0.5 m/s lateral or 0.5 rad/s yaw were never trained.
  • Reward interpretation. Tracking accuracy comes from the gate, not the training reward, because the tracking kernels barely distinguish 0 from 0.2 m/s of error.

docs.title: Reproduce
docs.text:
The commands below use the current Digit project entry points. Training today runs the current task definition; it does not automatically reproduce the September baseline. For a historical comparison, use the revision, configuration and reduced data recorded in the M0 evidence capsule, and keep a new run distinct from the recorded results.

# Train (CUDA workstation), evaluate, export: in the Digit project.
cd apps/digit
pixi run -e learn train Digit-Velocity-Flat-1ms --env.scene.num-envs 4096 \
  --agent.max-iterations 3000 --agent.run-name NAME
pixi run -e learn evaluate --run learning/checkpoints/runs/digit_velocity/RUN
pixi run -e learn export-policy --run learning/checkpoints/runs/digit_velocity/RUN
cd ../..

# Figures on this page, from the capsule's reduced data.
pixi run python apps/digit/notes/evidence/2026-09-27-digit-m0-velocity-policy/scripts/render.py

docs.title: Models and simulation
docs.text: A robot experiment depends on more than its controller. Geometry, inertia, joint coordinates, contacts, actuators and sensor behavior all affect the response. Cyber Suite keeps robot descriptions with their assets and exposes model computations through the robot module, while simulation owns the world and simulated measurements.

docs.title: Model computations and the simulated world
docs.text:
The robot module supplies kinematics and dynamics for estimation and control. The simulation module supplies MuJoCo integration, scene construction and terrain utilities. These roles are related but distinct: a controller can query a model to predict a foot's motion while the simulator evolves the robot under contact and actuation.

Parity checks ask whether corresponding computations agree under matched coordinates and assumptions. Matching joint names or loading both models successfully is insufficient. A useful check specifies the configuration, velocity, coordinate convention and quantity being compared. Robot-specific qualifications remain in the owning app's validation.

docs.title: Assets and calibration have different owners
docs.text:
Information Home Why Robot geometry, inertial properties and description files assets/robots/<robot>/ Shared robot identity Reusable terrain scenes modules/sim/terrains/ Simulator-owned data and geometry Controller and estimator tuning The app's config/ Values chosen for a particular behavior Command schedule and run choices App scenario Reproducible experiment definition Resolved configuration and outputs Run artifacts What this run actually used

For example, changing a Digit controller gain is an app-calibration change. Changing the shin damping in the robot model changes the physical assumptions for multiple consumers, including training. The latter requires checking the affected policies and comparisons rather than treating it as another gain adjustment.

docs.title: Terrain geometry is not terrain knowledge
docs.text:
The terrain catalog includes flat planes, oriented boxes for slopes and steps, and heightfields for continuous surfaces. A viewer can display that geometry even when a controller has no access to it. Selecting stairs therefore changes the world; it does not automatically provide foothold heights to the planner.

The terrain catalog explains scene ownership. The state and perception guide explains the additional sensing, mapping and adoption boundaries needed to use terrain information.

docs.title: An actuator command is not instantaneous torque
docs.text:
In Digit's deployment-oriented simulation, command delay and drive damping change the torque that reaches a joint. The LLAPI drive configuration is shared with the learning app. An ideal actuation experiment answers a different question from one using the drive model, even if the velocity command and planner are unchanged.

Before comparing results, record the model identity, actuation mode, delay assumptions, physics step, contact settings and state source. For a learned policy, also record the model and control contract used during training. Export parity cannot repair a mismatch in the simulated plant.

docs.title: A useful first experiment
docs.text:
Run one known scenario and save its resolved configuration. Change only the terrain selection or one explicitly chosen actuation assumption, then compare the observed behavior and outcome. Keep the original run. If the change causes a failure, identify which boundary changed before tuning the controller to hide the symptom.

Implementation details live in the robot contract and simulation contract. Digit's walking validation records the drive and simulator comparisons and their limits.

docs.title: Runtime and execution
docs.text: CORTA coordinates a robotics computation around a Plant observation/command exchange. It separates work that must participate in a tick from work that can finish on a deferred worker. Understanding this distinction explains how a planner, policy inference, fast controller and viewer can coexist without making every component run at the same rate.

docs.title: The Plant sets the world boundary
docs.text:
A Plant supplies observations and receives commands. In a simulator it advances the simulated world; an external Plant exchanges data through the device interface. The app supplies the observation and command types and chooses the Plant implementation. That boundary lets the computation remain recognizable across execution environments, but it does not prove their timing, sensors or actuators are equivalent.

For Digit, the composition is visible in the application entry point. Its model-based graph contains two message pairs: Plant ↔ Servo and Servo ↔ planner. The policy composition replaces the latter with Servo ↔ inference and uses a policy-specific Servo.

docs.title: Inline and deferred work
docs.text:
Inline work participates directly in the tick's execution order. Deferred work runs on a named worker and publishes results that become visible at a defined runtime boundary. A scheduled release is not the same event as completed work or an adopted result.

Digit's canonical model-based rates. Servo continues executing an installed trajectory between planner releases. Deferred completion and reference adoption are not assigned times in this schematic.

Open full-size diagram

The graph declares rates, workers and message storage. Copied values or bounded payload leases cross the graph's boundaries. This is different from letting a planning thread mutate a controller's live task objects. For a concrete example, a planner can publish a new preview while Servo continues sampling the previously installed one until the new preview is adopted.

docs.title: Input, output and observation
docs.text:
An operator device is an asynchronous input, not the clock-defining Plant. CORTA adapters handle transport and arrival off the tick path; the app decides what an operator command means. In Digit, supervision adds command shaping, modes and link-loss behavior. Reaching a viewer URL does not give that viewer ownership of the controller.

Telemetry and visualization are observation paths. Their job is to make the run inspectable. Logging has its own bounded producer/drain mechanisms, and viewer delivery may drop samples independently. A 50 Hz scene stream is useful for animation; it cannot establish a 1 kHz contact-force peak.

docs.title: What determinism and timing claims need
docs.text:
Logical execution, replay and wall-clock scheduling answer different questions. A replay checks the recorded decisions within its declared boundary. A configured 1 kHz graph states a period. Neither alone establishes that the whole deployed tick meets a one-millisecond deadline under the target scheduling policy.

Inspect computation duration, Plant exchange, queue/adoption age, overruns and termination behavior separately. The current CORTA contract records remaining boundary and scheduling limitations; the app's validation records scenario-specific measurements. A new transport or robot requires its own evidence.

docs.title: Read further
docs.text: The CORTA contract, adapter contract and logging contract hold implementation details. The CORTA design develops the execution rules; the adapter reference explains Plant, ingress/egress, state/events and observation boundaries with implemented examples. Their design requirements remain distinct from conformance and application timing evidence.

docs.title: Model-based walking
docs.text: Model-based walking separates choosing a feasible motion from realizing it with the full robot. A reduced balance model helps choose steps. The app turns those decisions into body and foot trajectories. A whole-body controller then tries to realize the trajectories under the modeled dynamics and constraints.

docs.title: The execution loop
docs.text:
Digit's model-based composition. A motion command, a task reference and an actuator command are three different contracts. Each needs its own evidence when diagnosing a failure.

Open full-size diagram

docs.title: What ALIP and DCM contribute
docs.text:
ALIP, the angular-momentum linear inverted pendulum model, describes balance through a reduced relationship between body position and angular momentum. DCM, the divergent component of motion, describes the unstable part of pendulum-like motion and how foot placement affects it. They provide different ways to reason about where and when to step.

Neither reduced model is the whole robot. Feet must lift and land, joint and actuator limits still apply, and the estimated state can be wrong. In Cyber Suite the numerical kernels belong to locomotion; robot-specific task mapping and reference authoring belong to the app adapters. The current locomotion contract names those boundaries.

docs.title: Coordination is more than a sequence timer
docs.text:
The walking coordinator handles startup, accepted contact transitions and stopping. A planner receives contact history collected at Servo rate and publishes references with finite validity. That lets a slower planning update reason about events observed between releases.

The controller executes the installed reference against current state. ALIP and DCM have different reference-coordinate contracts, so replacing one with the other deliberately changes more than a class name. Preserve the world, command schedule, estimator and shared calibration when comparing them, and report the planner-specific profiles and reference meanings that change.

docs.title: Whole-body control resolves competing objectives
docs.text:
The TAC-QP controller combines desired body and foot motion with modeled physical constraints. Its task objectives can compete: asking the torso to recover quickly can consume actuator authority needed to move a foot. A numerical solution, a small task residual and successful physical recovery are different outcomes.

Use the control contract for the implemented controller and constraint vocabulary. Fallback behavior is app-configured and may relax constraints in a declared order; a fallback activation must be reported rather than interpreted as proof that every original bound held.

docs.title: Diagnose from the boundary that failed
docs.text:
Observation First comparison Likely owner to inspect A foot target jumps Authored plan versus installed trajectory Planner adapter and reference binding A foot misses a sensible target Reference versus measured motion, effort and constraints Servo, controller and Plant A support transition happens too early Contact evidence versus admitted transition Estimation and walking coordination The run walks but never settles Stop command, balance state and stop acceptance Coordination and app completion logic

These are starting points, not diagnoses. A single screenshot rarely establishes the cause. Use time-aligned signals and a matched baseline; the evaluation guide shows how to turn that into an experiment.

Continue with the walking coordinator reference for lifecycle, contact history and robot-specific admission settings. The ALIP formulation and DCM formulation map their derivations and alternatives to the current kernels. The walking app contract and validation own integrated behavior and demonstrated limits.

docs.title: State and perception
docs.text: Control needs a description of the robot; perceptive planning also needs a description of the world. Both descriptions depend on measurements, coordinate frames, timestamps and uncertainty. A simulator can provide exact state for analysis, but that does not make exact state an ordinary controller input.

docs.title: Three views of the same run
docs.text:
View What it means What it is useful for Measurements Encoders, IMU and selected sensor products Inputs available to the chosen composition Estimated state Reconstructed base/joint/support information Planning and feedback control Simulation truth The simulator's internal state Diagnostics and explicitly selected truth-state experiments

An estimate-versus-truth plot is meaningful only after matching timestamps, frames and state definitions. A world-frame velocity supplied to a base-frame observation term is a contract error even when the values look numerically plausible.

docs.title: State and support estimation
docs.text:
The estimator reconstructs the floating base and other required state from the selected measurements. Contact/support estimation supplies evidence about which parts of the robot can support load. Those outputs feed the app's planning and controller composition; the estimator does not own the walking sequence.

Do not change state source midway through a comparison without recording it. A truth-state policy experiment, an internally estimated-state walk and an LLAPI run using Agility's estimate have different observation boundaries. The estimation contract and owning app validation identify what each composition currently supports.

docs.title: From sensor geometry to a terrain product
docs.text:
The perception module separates acquisition from mapping. Simulation or hardware owns the sensor measurements; reusable perception code registers them against pose history, fuses elevation and exposes bounded geometric products. The mapping app owns prescribed sensor motion and comparison with known terrain.

The useful chain is acquisition → time and frame registration → fusion → geometric queries → app adoption. Errors at earlier stages can look like planning errors later. A height query without a valid timestamp or coordinate convention is not enough for a controller to use it.

docs.title: Geometry is not contact authority
docs.text:
A flat-looking patch or a small height uncertainty does not establish friction, load capacity or safe support. Perception's geometric confidence and the controller's contact authority answer different questions. The app must explicitly decide how a map product changes planning or control, with validation at that boundary.

Digit's oracle-perception option is a bounded integration path; it is not equivalent to autonomous sensing and localization on hardware. The mapping project is a useful place to study geometry and recording independently of walking.

docs.title: A useful inspection workflow
docs.text:
First inspect a saved map and the corresponding sensor/pose inputs. Compare valid regions, height error, missing observations and registration errors against the known scene. Then test the downstream query or planning decision separately. A prettier visualization does not establish better footholds or fewer falls.

The perception contract describes the implemented products, and the recording contract defines what playback preserves. The mapping validation records the tested scenarios and remaining limits.

docs.title: Deploying A Learned Policy
docs.text: Any project, for any robot, can train a policy its own way and deploy it with the controller it chooses. The repository holds every project to two things: the robot's plant command boundary, and replay parity between what training computed and what deployment computes. Everything else here is a library a project may use, never a framework it must fit. The module contract is modules/policy/MODULE.md; the plan that produced this design is the deployment-layer plan.

docs.title: The Chain
docs.text:
A deployed learned controller is a chain of links. Each link has a kind, and the kind's owner implements it in both training and deployment.

Link What it does Implemented now Owner Plant boundary Reads sensors; enforces command limits, authority and staleness modules/digit_hardware The robot's hardware module (required) State source Supplies base and joint state MuJoCo truth, the InEKF Project Observation Turns state and commands into model inputs Seven proprioceptive terms and the velocity command modules/policy for these terms; project terms are reserved Model Evaluates the network One ONNX model, [1, N] to [1, M] modules/policy runtime Decode Turns model output into references joint_affine (joint targets) Module for joint_affine, project for its own Realization Turns references into actuator commands joint_pd, with each term placed in the controller or the actuator Module for joint_pd, project for its own (a posture task in TAC-QP, a task-space QP) Deployment additions Anything training never saw The TAC-QP torque filter (Experiment 0) Project, never in the contract

Four rules follow:

  1. The contract describes training as it was. It records every link from observation to realization as training computed it. A deployment-only addition, such as a safety filter, is the deploying app's choice; its scenarios validate it, not parity.
  2. The module is a library. modules/policy implements common kinds and never calls project code. A project's controller calls the library; there is no registry, plug-in loader or base class to inherit.
  3. Kinds are namespaced by owner. A bare kind (joint_pd) belongs to the module. A dotted kind (digit.pose_task) belongs to the project named before the dot: the loader keeps its parameters as YAML text, and its project parses and implements it.
  4. A kind moves into the module when a second project deploys it, the learning roadmap's rule that a contract stays candidate until a second consumer uses it, applied per kind.

docs.title: What A Project Must Do
docs.text:
1. Command through the robot's plant boundary. Every controller, learned or not, ends in the robot's hardware module, which owns the plant description, limits, authority and command staleness. A new robot's first hardware module defines these for it; a shared plant type across robots waits for a second hardware module.
  2. Ship a bundle that passes parity. Write policy_contract.yaml, the model and parity_fixture.npz, then run pixi run policy-parity BUNDLE. Every kind must have a stage: the module's kinds bring theirs, and a project kind brings a stage file (--stage KIND=FILE). A kind without one fails as unchecked.

A project that does not deploy owes nothing.

docs.title: Choosing A Realization
docs.text:
joint_pd covers a PD law split between host and drive. Its two placements and two clamps describe:

Plant Stiffness Damping Example Ideal simulator controller controller MuJoCo position actuators; TRON1, G1 and Digit without drives Drives that damp controller actuator Digit through Agility's LLAPI (-Drives tasks) Driver PD actuator actuator Motor drivers that take kp and kd per command

Delay is not in the contract: training randomizes it because the hardware has it, and deployment adds none. Provenance records it, as it records training noise.

A deploying app checks the placement against its plant. The Digit walking servo refuses a version 2 bundle whose damping placement differs from the plant's unless --realization-override is given, and records the override in its telemetry. A version 1 contract records no placement and is not refused.

When a policy's actions mean something else, for example joint targets realized as a posture task in a whole-body QP, keep joint_affine and write a project realization. When the decode differs too, for example task-space requests, write a project decode with its output size.
