One Runtime owns one graph and one logical clock. Multiple independent runtimes may coexist in one process, but they have no direct graph edges and never share ticks. External communication is divided by semantics, not by transport:

  1. Clock plane. A peer that paces or participates in the servo exchange is a Plant, Gateway, or Hardware boundary. A transport carrying that exchange is Plant implementation detail and never an adapter profile.
  2. Semantic bridge plane. Every other external value that may influence behavior crosses an asynchronous adapter thread and meets the graph only at an Ingress<T> or Egress<T> boundary.
  3. Observation plane. Telemetry, recording, introspection, and external visualization are observer-only. Enabling them cannot change graph-visible values, commands, or scheduling decisions.

CORTA implements no transport, discovery, QoS, distributed clock synchronization, RPC, or general message schema. A robot with perception, GPU, and control computers may use UDP, LCM, DDS, ROS 2, or another existing pipe. CORTA contributes the graph boundary; modules/corta_adapters contributes the off-thread adapter shape; the pipe remains an integration choice.

The latency floor of a semantic bridge is one receiver tick plus the queue handoff. A value that cannot tolerate that floor is clock-plane traffic and must not be routed through an adapter.

docs.title: 7.2 Unpaired graph boundaries
docs.text:
Ingress and egress are separate primitives. Core does not provide a paired channel, connection, topic, or endpoint abstraction.

  • Ingress: the existing initialized latest-value API and semantics remain unchanged. An adapter thread writes it with nonzero source timestamp identity; Runtime samples it once at the boundary transaction and records the graph-visible sample per [S-34]. The mailbox payload is ordinary fixed storage protected by the existing BoundaryCutoff: one producer writes under its producer guard and Runtime samples under its boundary guard. A fixed-size trivially copyable Value therefore need not fit one target atomic. Copies of one writer still must not publish concurrently.
  • Egress: a graph-owned sink reads a typed producer value after a successful ordinary Plant write, stamps the value's CORTA publication provenance, and performs one fixed-step, wait-free try_push into preallocated SPSC storage. The required atomics must be lock-free on the supported target. A full queue refuses the newest sample and increments its counter immediately. An adapter thread reads that storage. No encoder, allocator, transport callback, lock, retry, or syscall runs on the tick thread.

An egress is a real reader for C2 and for Block retention accounting. A Block egress queue contributes its complete retained-lease capacity to C16. A lease moved into adapter work remains external retention, so the adapter also declares its bounded in-flight count through the existing Graph::external_leases() contract; queue capacity plus that count appears in the pool plan. An egress enqueue refusal is counted and reportable; it cannot block the tick or change the graph transaction that produced the value.

Only the egress handoff is claimed wait-free. The whole boundary cutoff remains unqualified under S-23 because existing coherent publication sections can still spin behind a preempted producer.

Egress<T> v1 is C++ only. The Python frontend gains no binding until a real Python adapter consumer exists.

docs.title: 7.3 Adapter ownership and threading
docs.text:
One adapter owns one external connection and one SDK-owned thread. It may bind N ingress writers and M egress readers. Pairing happens only in that adapter; the graph primitives remain independent.

The adapter thread is free-running at the cadence dictated by its device or transport. It may block, allocate, encode, decode, reconnect, or call middleware APIs. It must never publish directly into graph-visible storage or read mutable graph state: input crosses IngressWriter<T> and output crosses an egress reader.

Adapters reuse CORTA's DeviceThread stop/join ordering. Their SDK configuration carries a ThreadPlacement; thread entry applies it through apply_thread_placement() and retains the resulting report. The application owns the actual affinity and priority policy. A ROS executor or Rerun serializer must be placed so it cannot preempt the tick thread, but a refused placement is reported rather than misrepresented as acquired. This is deployment evidence, not hard-real-time qualification.

Adapters expose requests, not safety authority. Keyboard, joystick, and remote "emergency stop" inputs remain application requests; safety policy and the hardware terminal path remain outside the adapter.

docs.title: 7.4 Delivery profiles
docs.text:
Only two asynchronous delivery profiles are admitted initially. Both are best-effort, bounded, and fully accounted.

LatestState. The adapter retains the newest value. A replacement counts as a coalescence/overwrite. This profile fits axes, desired modes represented as state, navigation goals, perception summaries, and state publication.

BoundedEvents<N>. The adapter retains a fixed rolling FIFO window of sequenced events and publishes a fixed-size batch value through ordinary Ingress<T>. The receiver processes only sequence numbers newer than its last accepted value. Because every latest batch repeats the retained window, Ingress coalescing does not silently turn distinct events into one state change. A receiver-visible sequence gap proves missed events; source-instance change starts a new sequence epoch. N is chosen per endpoint from the worst credible burst between receiver boundary samples, never from an average rate.

Overflow is explicitly drop-oldest: when N events are retained, evict exactly the oldest, count one overflow, insert the new event, and publish the resulting window. The fixed batch includes a populated count; unused slots are not interpreted as events.

The adapter counts local FIFO overflow/window eviction. The receiver counts sequence gaps. There is no acknowledgment, retry, RPC, or lossless promise. If a value cannot tolerate that behavior, it does not belong on an adapter. Where sensible, an adapter converts device events into state before ingress; for example, a mode-toggle event may update one LatestState current-mode value. Keystrokes, button transitions, and discrete operator requests that remain events use BoundedEvents<N> and are never coalesced as bare values.

ClockedExchange is not a delivery profile. It is categorically Plant traffic.

docs.title: 7.5 Time, identity, and restart
docs.text:
[S-28] Clock identity is two orthogonal fields. ClockDomainId identifies a shared, comparable time basis (e.g., a PTP domain, or a single host's monotonic clock). SourceInstanceId identifies the producing process/device/session. Zero in either required boundary identity is validation failure, not "unknown but usable." Timestamp comparison returns an optional result: it has a value iff the clock domains match, regardless of source instance; mismatched domains are incomparable rather than ordered by raw integers. Source instance supports provenance, restart detection, and staleness attribution. Runtimes never share ticks; cross-runtime data is interpreted via local visibility tick or source timestamps under a matching clock domain.

S-28 has executable evidence for nonzero identity validation, optional cross-domain comparison, source-instance restart detection, and receiver behavior across a sequence reset. That completion is a prerequisite only; no cross-process bridge is implemented or described as supported yet. It does not include clock-offset estimation.

docs.title: 7.6 Failure accounting
docs.text:
Every coalescence, queue overflow, malformed frame, schema rejection, disconnect/reconnect, source restart, and receiver-visible event gap is counted and reportable. A malformed or incompatible input is rejected before calling an ingress writer. A disconnected latest-state input remains held with visible age and generation; application code decides whether that age is acceptable. Adapters do not invent control fallback.

Transport CRC, schema mapping, authentication, and QoS remain transport-side. There is no unified wire envelope across semantic bridges, telemetry, and replay.

docs.title: 7.7 Determinism at this boundary
docs.text:
Cross-runtime inputs are external inputs, exactly like sensors: sampled at boundary transactions, recorded per tick, replayable from the log. [S-20] holds per runtime with these inputs included in the boundary sample sequence.

The required replay check records a receiver ingress run, replays the recorded graph-visible samples, and obtains identical downstream graph-visible behavior. It does not claim that the live sender or transport is deterministic.

docs.title: 7.8 Observation adapters
docs.text:
Rerun and similar viewers are observation-plane consumers. A telemetry router is the sole consumer of each SPSC telemetry ring. It preserves the storage path and may copy a record or converted batch into a separate bounded Rerun queue. Rerun backpressure drops and counts visualization copies; it never stalls storage or control. A typed VisualizationFrame egress is added only when a concrete visualization cannot be expressed at the telemetry converter.

The active adapter integrations are ordered deliberately: in-process loopback, POSIX keyboard input, then Rerun telemetry fan-out. All three are implemented. The maintained Digit walking app is the first integrated Rerun consumer and selects its servo and planner streams exactly at observer registration; its Python dashboard is process/blueprint setup, not a telemetry bridge. Joystick input, two-CORTA-app UDP LatestState, ROS 2 pub/sub, ROS 2 services/actions, ROS 1, HTTP, clock-offset estimation, endpoint manifests, and a unified wire envelope remain deferred until a concrete consumer reopens them.

docs.title: 8. Logging, telemetry, and replay
docs.text: Two facilities share the logger thread and nothing else. The replay stream records what is required to reconstruct graph-visible behavior; its schema is the graph, its consumer is the replay machinery. Telemetry records internal columnar diagnostics; its schema is per-system channel declarations, its consumer is offline analysis. The boundary rule of Section 2.3 decides which facility a signal belongs to.

docs.title: 8.1 The replay stream
docs.text:
Mandatory contents, recorded per tick with tick indices:

  1. the Plant observation and complete TickInfo;
  2. every graph-visible ingress sample with its visibility tick, generation, source timestamp, clock identity, and source instance;
  3. every deferred commitment tick ([S-16]);
  4. each producer/output ID, payload, generation, origin, trigger/publication/commit ticks, and transaction membership for every RecordOutput system ([S-40]);
  5. every Runtime-owned scheduling decision: dispatch, demand discarded/coalesced/serviced, predicate input/result with its PredicateContext, and cut injection;
  6. every ordinary Plant command, its Fresh/HoldLast/SafeCommand origin, and write result;
  7. every fault, Hold entry, reset request/result/effect tick/outcome, externally requested stop and its observed safe-point, fallback activation, terminal write_safe invocation/action kind and command payload where applicable, plus the termination reason;
  8. gap and incompleteness markers ([S-36]).

[S-40] Replay classes. The runtime does not decide what is recomputable; each system declares replay_class. Deterministic: recorded inputs suffice to regenerate its outputs (outputs may still be recorded for divergence checking). RecordOutput: outputs are always recorded and the system is an automatic authoritative cut. In authoritative replay, compile replaces the cut executor: Runtime does not call that object's configure, start, reset, update, or stop; it injects the recorded Startup transaction during startup (satisfying S-14/C9), an inline transaction at that system's compiled step-3 slot, and a deferred transaction at its recorded boundary commitment. Runtime emulates the cut's in-flight/demand state from its private event tape. The unused system object is destroyed normally. A separate comparison mode may execute the producer non-authoritatively and compare fresh outputs. Defaults: deferred and Python systems are RecordOutput; inline systems are Deterministic, with an explicit override for honestly nondeterministic inline code. Honesty of a Deterministic declaration is an application obligation; ctx.rng() ([S-42]) is what makes it achievable for stochastic-but-seedable systems.

Recording selection beyond the mandatory set is a reviewed per-edge verbosity declaration; there is no runtime "looks constant, suppress it" heuristic (an all-zero emergency channel is validation evidence, not noise). Queues are filled wait-free by the tick thread and drained by the logger; a slow disk degrades logging, never control.

[S-36] Overflow and completeness. Log queues are finite; under sustained overload, records are dropped by one fixed policy (drop-newest at enqueue), every drop is counted per stream, a gap marker is written as soon as capacity returns, and the log is marked replay_complete = false if any required replay record was dropped. Telemetry drops never affect replay_complete. Every replay-based claim in this document is conditional on replay_complete == true.

[S-43] Run manifest. Every log begins with a manifest: build identifier/VCS hash, compiled-graph fingerprint (systems, edges, attributes, per-residue orders, cut layout), Obs/Cmd and record schemas, required capacities, runtime options, run seed ([S-42]), MessageTraits schema versions, and floating-point environment flags. Compatibility has two classes. Graph identities/order, message/record schemas, cut layout, and required capacities are hard: a mismatch cannot be overridden because the tape cannot be mapped safely. Build identifier, floating-point flags, and runtime options that do not change topology, schemas, cut mapping, required capacity, or event interpretation are soft: an explicit counterfactual override may continue with a warning, but disables every bit-identical claim. Any option affecting those structural properties is hard regardless of its label. The [S-20] scope conditions thereby become auditable rather than aspirational.

docs.title: 8.2 Replay modes
docs.text:
1. Deterministic re-simulation: rerun the graph in simulation mode with the complete recorded boundary event stream, manifest seed, logical schedules, and declared cut outputs; reproduces bit-for-bit under the [S-20] scope conditions.
  2. Hardware log replay: ReplayPlant feeds recorded observations and TickInfo while Runtime follows recorded Runtime-owned events, commitment ticks, and cut transactions. Deterministic systems re-execute; every authoritative RecordOutput executor is bypassed per [S-40]. Downstream of the declared cuts, the graph re-executes against exactly what it saw on the robot. Requires replay_complete and hard-compatible structure.
  3. Cut-point replay: replace selected producers with their recorded outputs — recorded planner intent → controller, recorded terrain → controller, recorded policy → controller — so the consumer provably sees exactly what it saw live, while the code under study re-executes. Re-executing a replaced producer against the log and comparing its fresh outputs to the recorded ones is the companion comparison mode.
  4. Open-loop counterfactual replay: replay with modified code or parameters downstream of recorded inputs. Named open-loop deliberately: recorded future observations do not respond to a changed controller, so divergence is a signal about the change, not a physical closed-loop counterfactual.

Runtime owns the sole tick/event cursor; ReplayPlant owns only its observation cursor and command comparator. Runtime-owned decisions—demand/dispatch transitions, predicate result, commitment tick, fallback selection, and injected cut transactions—are authoritative: Runtime re-derives what it can, compares, flags divergence, and follows the tape. Arbitrary user-code state is not forceable. An unexpected deterministic-system exception, a missing recorded exception, or a different reset outcome is strict divergence and stops replay. An explicitly selected non-authoritative diagnostic mode may continue after divergence but makes no later alignment claim; reaching a cut does not reconstruct already-diverged downstream state unless that state is explicitly reset/rebuilt.

docs.title: 8.3 Telemetry
docs.text:
High-rate columnar diagnostics from inside systems — solver cost fractions, per-task tracking residuals, per-contact-point latent states, torque headroom, iteration counts — recorded for plotting and offline analysis. Telemetry is never consumed by any system and plays no role in replay; turning such signals into output ports would make the graph a logging manifest instead of a statement of the algorithm (Section 2.3).

  • Channels are declared once, recorded by handle. In start(), a system declares one named stream and its channels — stream = ctx.telemetry("components/control/tac_qp"), stream.scalar("cost_fraction"), stream.vector("sigma_support", n_points), or stream.matrix("preview", rows, cols) — and stores the returned handles. In update(), handle.record(value) performs one bounds-checked write into a preallocated row. No string hashing or schema mutation exists on the hot path. Payloads are scalars and small fixed-size vectors or matrices; images and grids are not telemetry. Python record conversion failures are observer-only: they leave the row incomplete and visible to completeness checks, but do not fault the system transaction.
  • The runtime stamps every record with tick and system. Records from deferred systems carry the job's trigger tick, so a planner's internals align with the plan its consumers later latched.
  • Per-stream rate divisors thin high-volume rows; a fixed-width row cannot omit one channel. Records flow through per-system ring buffers drained by the logger thread: wait-free, zero steady-state allocation (under the Section 12.2 probe), with drops counted and reported per [S-36] (never affecting replay_complete).
  • On disk, the application-owned storage session writes the declared streams. The maintained Python loader, cyber_suite.corta.telemetry.load(path), returns Stream objects whose numpy channel arrays remain in sample order beside their explicit tick_index; a dense tick axis is opt-in. Live viewers (PlotJuggler, Rerun, …) attach as adapters at the converter/storage level and are never runtime features (Section 14).
  • Runtime counters — demand generated/discarded/serviced, vetoes, coalesced ingress arrivals, drops, budget exceedances, pool occupancy, migration-parity counters — are monotonic integer telemetry channels, not a separate facility; Section 12.4 reads their end-of-run values from the telemetry output.
  • [S-30] Telemetry purity: record() has no effect on any state visible to [S-20], and channel configuration has no semantic effect anywhere. The bit-identical claim is scoped to simulation and replay, where the commitment schedule is fixed: there, a run with all telemetry disabled is bit-identical on every edge to the same run with every channel enabled (conformance-verified). On live hardware, recording cost can perturb timing and thereby move deferred commitment ticks; the perturbation is visible in the recorded ticks and has no effect outside them.

[S-30] combined with replay yields the design's most valuable diagnostic property: replaying with richer telemetry than the original run recorded. Record lean on the robot, inside the tick budget; reproduce the run via mode 8.2(2); re-execute with every channel enabled. Because the computation downstream of the declared replay cuts ([S-40]) is bit-identical, the regenerated internals there are the true internals of the hardware run. This dissolves the standing tension between "log everything" and the 1 ms budget.

docs.title: 9. Compile-time and startup checks
docs.text:
All setup validation uses one CompileErrorCode vocabulary with structured offending system/port identity. C1–C8 and C10–C18 run in compile() and throw CompileError. C9 necessarily runs after lazy start(); Runtime catches the same C9-coded setup failure, performs startup unwind, and returns/caches Fault with both its code and structured CompileLocation in RunReport rather than letting an exception escape step() or run(). C14 is advisory in full: its due-set feasibility verdict never throws, and its runtime-overhead term is additionally reported as unqualified until a calibrated cost profile is supplied. Malformed C14 declarations and every other failed check are errors.

class CompileError : public std::runtime_error {
 public:
  CompileError(CompileErrorCode, CompileLocation, std::string message);
  CompileErrorCode code() const noexcept;
  const CompileLocation& location() const noexcept; // structured system/port/source IDs
};

Graph, rate, trait, capacity, Plant-descriptor, and time-mode validators all use this type and code set. The post-start C9 path preserves its canonical code in RunReport; other Runtime faults, Plant I/O failures, and replay divergence remain run-report/fault kinds, not CompileError.

# Check Catches C1 Single writer per input port ([S-4]) Ownership ambiguity two writers cannot resolve C2 Every declared input is connected and every output has a system reader or explicit record tap Missing edges; graph ports that are really undeclared telemetry C3 Harmonic rates: every_ticks(k) divides the base, 0 ≤ phase < k; frequency_hz divides evenly ([S-1]) Undefined "same tick" semantics C4 The immediate inline subgraph is acyclic Algebraic loops; cycles must be broken by declaring at least one unit-delay edge C5 Unit-delay declared only on inline→inline edges Meaningless declarations (deferred edges are delayed by construction) C6 Topological order of inline systems, per due-set, deterministic tie-break by declaration order ([S-11]) Timing-dependent same-tick delivery C7 Python systems are deferred ([S-26]) Interpreter on the servo path C8 Deferred systems declare worker, overrun policy, independent job_budget, and logical completion latency Undefined scheduling, measurement, or simulation behavior C9 Post-start() publication check: every connected output published, with Initial metadata ([S-14]) First-tick null reads; fake tick-0 provenance C10 Complete MessageTraits<T> declared for every port type; inline Value types are real-time-copy-safe; materialization and logical-capacity checks installable at every slot/publish ([S-5]) Undeclared storage/version/capacity; unsafe or unbounded payloads C11 Graph is consumed by compile() and later use is rejected ([S-8]) Post-compile mutation bypassing C1–C18 C12 Every latency callback returns PositiveTicks; finite schedules declare RepeatLast or Error exhaustion ([S-17]) Same-dispatch publication; ambiguous schedule exhaustion C13 The Plant command sink's producer is an inline system due every tick ([S-9] step 5, Section 5.2) Ticks without a freshly filtered command C14 Enumerate every due set in at most one base-rate second; report whether each declared system+Plant sum fits the base period without rejecting, and include Runtime overhead only from an explicit calibrated cost profile ([S-35]). Rejects only malformed declarations: negative terms, overflowing arithmetic, incomplete cost-model provenance Silent over-subscription; unqualified runtime-overhead margins; unusable budget declarations C15 A Fatal error policy requires a registered application fault handler ([S-19]) Fatal faults with nowhere to go C16 Block pools sized to the exact graph-retention bound plus declared external_leases (slack explicit); theorem is scoped to declared retention ([S-38]) Pool exhaustion by graph construction; undeclared external retention remains a runtime fault C17 A command fallback policy — HoldLast(max_ticks) or SafeCommand — is declared ([S-44]) Ticks with no defined command value C18 Plant descriptor/kind/time-mode/advancement matrix is legal; Hardware/Gateway declare positive read timeout and miss threshold; claimed write budget is positive ([S-41], [S-46], [S-47]) Illegal logical/wall binding, silent peer hangs, unbounded missed exchanges, unmeasurable writes

docs.title: 10. Public API sketch
docs.text:
Illustrative, not final; semantics are binding, names are not.

// ---- the fused inline control stack (safety split out, Section 11) ----
class ControlStack final : public corta::System {
 public:
  corta::Input<RobotObservation>  obs   {this, "obs"};
  corta::Input<FootstepIntent>    intent{this, "intent"};   // deferred producer
  corta::Input<TerrainField>      sdf   {this, "sdf"};      // deferred producer, Block storage
  corta::Input<PolicyCommand>     mod   {this, "mod"};      // Python producer
  corta::Output<ActuatorCommand>  cmd   {this, "cmd"};
  corta::Output<ControlStatus>    status{this, "status"};

  corta::telemetry::Scalar qp_cost;   // channel handle; declared in start() via ctx.telemetry()

  explicit ControlStack(const RobotModel& model);            // const shared resource: allowed

  void start(corta::StartContext&) override;                 // publishes cmd, status once ([S-14]);
                                                             // declares telemetry channels
  void update(corta::UpdateContext& ctx) override {
    // internal composition is plain C++: estimator -> CCC -> reference -> TAC-QP
    const auto& plan = intent.value();
    const int age = ctx.tick() - intent.trigger_tick();      // plan age in ticks
    if (intent.origin() != corta::Origin::Update) { /* startup/reset fallback, [S-14], [S-39] */ }
    // ... staleness policy, act-once via intent.generation(), etc.
    cmd.publish(computed_command);                           // staged; commits per [S-33]
    status.publish(current_status);
    qp_cost.record(cost_fraction);                           // telemetry, Section 8.3
  }
};

class SafetyFilter final : public corta::System {            // separate inline system, Section 11
 public:
  corta::Input<ActuatorCommand>  cmd_in {this, "cmd_in"};
  corta::Input<RobotObservation> obs    {this, "obs"};
  corta::Output<ActuatorCommand> cmd_out{this, "cmd_out"};
  // start() publishes a safe initial command; update() clamps/filters every tick
};

// ---- application main --------------------------------------------------
int main(int argc, char** argv) {
  corta::Graph<RobotObservation, ActuatorCommand> g(1000);
  auto& ctrl    = g.add<ControlStack>(corta::inl().frequency_hz(1000), robot_model);
  auto& safety  = g.add<SafetyFilter>(corta::inl().frequency_hz(1000), limits);
  auto& planner = g.add<FootstepPlanner>(corta::deferred().frequency_hz(100)
                       .worker("planner").overrun(corta::Overrun::Latest)
                       .latency(8).job_budget(2ms));
  auto& terrain = g.add<TerrainField>(corta::deferred().frequency_hz(100)
                       .worker("terrain").overrun(corta::Overrun::Skip)
                       .latency(50).job_budget(8ms)
                       .dispatch_if(corta::input_advanced("frame")));
  auto& nav     = g.add<Navigation>(corta::deferred().frequency_hz(2)
                       .worker("misc").overrun(corta::Overrun::Skip)
                       .latency(200).job_budget(20ms));
  auto& policy  = g.add_python("policy_module", "Policy");   // deferred, python worker

  g.connect(g.plant().obs, ctrl.obs);
  g.connect(g.plant().obs, safety.obs);
  g.connect(ctrl.cmd,      safety.cmd_in);                   // inline -> inline, same tick
  g.connect(safety.cmd_out, g.plant().cmd);                  // check C13
  g.connect(ctrl.status,   planner.status);
  g.connect(planner.intent, ctrl.intent);
  g.connect(terrain.sdf,   ctrl.sdf);                        // Block: one pooled payload, two leases
  g.connect(terrain.sdf,   planner.sdf);
  g.connect(nav.goal,      planner.goal);
  g.connect(policy.out("command"), ctrl.mod);
  // camera device thread -> ingress mailbox -> terrain.frame, per [S-34]

  auto plant = choose_plant(argv);   // MuJoCoPlant | DigitGateway | DigitUdpPlant
                                     // | corta::ScriptedPlant, for the same graph under test ([S-46])
  auto rt = corta::compile(std::move(g), std::move(plant),
                           corta::Options{}
                             .worker("planner").worker("terrain").worker("misc")
                             .fatal_handler(on_fault)   // Stop | ContinueDegraded, [S-19]; C15
                             .command_fallback(corta::SafeCommand(zero_torque))   // ordinary [S-44]
                             .terminal_action(corta::SafeAction<ActuatorCommand>
                                                ::command(zero_torque))           // [S-45]
                             .log("run.clog"));
  rt.run();                          // library call; Ctrl-C or app logic stops it
}

The same Graph code compiles against every Plant kind (Section 5.5); the only difference in main is choose_plant. A test builds the identical graph and hands it a corta::ScriptedPlant instead, which is the level-1 rung of Section 5.10.

docs.title: 11. Reference application: perceptive humanoid locomotion
docs.text:
This application is the acceptance test for the whole design and lives under apps/ as an integrated reference application. Thin examples teach isolated APIs; they do not own humanoid behavior.

Systems and placement.

Tick thread:      ControlStack (estimator → contact credibility → locomotion
                  reference → whole-body QP), 1 kHz, inline
                  SafetyFilter, 1 kHz, inline, ordered after ControlStack
                  Plant command write (fed by SafetyFilter, check C13)
"planner" worker: footstep planner only (100 Hz, 3–8 ms, Latest)
"terrain" worker: camera-conditioned terrain processing (100 Hz dispatch,
                  frame-advanced predicate, 20–60 ms, Skip)
Python worker:    learned policy (50 Hz, 5–15 ms, Skip)
"misc" worker:    navigation (2 Hz) and non-critical background computation
Device thread:    camera driver (60 Hz, non-harmonic) → ingress mailbox
Logger thread:    replay stream + telemetry

The safety filter is a separate inline system in the first reference implementation, not a future exercise: without it, the reference application would exercise CORTA's flagship inline→inline same-tick ordering guarantee with zero edges. The internal composition of ControlStack remains plain C++ classes, unit-tested directly.

Loops the design must carry. Control↔planner closed through the deferred lane (status out, intent in, ages visible on both legs); navigation→planner→control as deferred→deferred→inline; terrain fan-out to planner and control as one pooled Block payload; policy modulating controller tasks under [S-17] reproducibility.

Required experiments (beyond the conformance suite):

  1. Planner overrun under CPU contention: no whole-tick budget exceedances on the tick thread, Latest behavior per [S-32].
  2. Skip and Latest decision traces validated against a hand-written oracle.
  3. Constant, swept, and scheduled logical completion latencies ([S-17]), including L > period and schedules fed from recorded hardware latencies.
  4. Byte-identical simulation across worker counts and worker assignments ([S-20] scope).
  5. Hardware replay using recorded cut points (mode 8.2(3)): controller demonstrably sees recorded planner/terrain/policy outputs.
  6. Logging-overflow negative control: forced overload produces counted drops, gap markers, and replay_complete = false.
  7. Large terrain fan-out: zero steady-state allocation and zero payload duplication under the probe.
  8. Qualified-target budget under the maximum simultaneous due set: zero command-latency exceedances and zero total-tick-occupancy exceedances of the declared base period in the named scenario; separately report the measured distribution without turning host scheduler noise into a portable core gate.
  9. Pool-exhaustion negative control: undeclared external retention triggers the [S-38] fault naming the lease holders; the same retention under a declared budget is safe.
  10. Parity ladder (§5.10): the reference graph runs unchanged at every level, and a level-1 replay fed the complete level-3 boundary event stream, manifest seed, logical schedules, TickInfo, sampled ingress, and declared cut outputs reproduces that run's command sequence exactly—the cross-check that levels 1 and 3 are testing one system, not two.

Acceptance criteria: the identical graph runs against all four v1 Plants — ScriptedPlant, MuJoCoPlant, DigitGateway, DigitUdpPlant ([S-46], §5.5); a full simulation run is bit-reproducible under the [S-20] scope; a hard-compatible hardware log with replay_complete == true replays through mode 8.2(2) with zero divergence downstream of declared cuts until any intentional code change; experiments 1–10 pass.

docs.title: 12.1 Conformance suite
docs.text:
Every runtime-visible guarantee has focused executable evidence; one table-driven witness may cover several rules. Application/reference obligations use review or measurement evidence, with a negative control only when CORTA can observe the violation. The flat conformance index lists every S-1…S-49 and C1…C18 exactly once with one fixed status: pass, deferred-core, deferred-app, or obligation; every pass row names an existing evidence path. It has no facet tree or computed aggregation. Required controls include: C4 rejection of an immediate inline cycle; per-residue ordering and strict pre-tick unit delay; identical post-inline snapshot vintage for ordinary and retained-demand dispatch; Skip/Latest oracle traces; ingress initial/unchanged generation; fallback and HoldLast expiry; interruptible logical wait; callback/vector-exhaustion fault routing; log gaps; declared-retention pool exhaustion; hard manifest refusal versus soft counterfactual override; and strict replay stop on user-state divergence.

The suite runs almost entirely against ScriptedPlant and conforming CallbackPlant instances (§5.9), keeping it fast and free of physics tolerances. Plant controls cover the C18 kind/time/liveness matrix; environment-index +1 after each successful ordinary Simulator/Callback write; miss-threshold rejection before tick creation; both stop safe-points; exactly one terminal-action invocation attempt after successful open; no terminal environment advancement; bounded-call obligations classified for target-host evidence; open/start/read/write unwind; and script exhaustion as normal completion.

docs.title: 12.2 Allocation probe
docs.text: A malloc-interposing probe asserts zero allocations across N steady-state ticks of the tick thread — including boundary transactions with ingress traffic and Block fan-out — and, as its own negative control, that it detects one deliberately planted allocation. A probe that can only report zero proves nothing.

docs.title: 12.3 Determinism harness
docs.text: Run the reference application twice in simulation mode from identical state under the [S-20] scope conditions (same binary, same machine, fixed FP environment); diff every logged edge byte-for-byte. Repeat across worker counts and named-worker assignments: still identical. Repeat with L > period on one system: identical, including overrun counters. The run manifest ([S-43]) records the scope conditions, so a failed diff on a different platform is triaged as scope, not as a semantics bug, until proven otherwise.

docs.title: 12.4 Migration parity (when porting an existing app)
docs.text: When moving an existing application onto CORTA, gate each slice on counter parity (end-of-run telemetry counter values, Section 8.3) against a rebuilt run of the pre-change tree, so a deviation has one candidate cause. This methodology is inherited deliberately from the port migration that validated the predecessor runtime.

docs.title: 13. Prior art and claimed contributions
docs.text:
Positioning (provisional — a dedicated comparison must establish the exact guarantees and limitations of each named system before publication). Synchronous-dataflow rate transitions (Simulink) provide [S-11]–[S-13] but no deferred lane and no code-level library ergonomics. Logical Execution Time (Giotto and successors) provides publish-at-boundary semantics but applies it to everything, inserting delay on exactly the fast path where same-tick data is the point. Drake's systems framework offers declared ports and deterministic simulation but is simulation-first: no allocation-free 1 kHz hardware loop, no tagged latest-completed lane for slow computation. ROS 2 solves distributed component communication; it has no shared logical clock, executor-order nondeterminism, and per-edge serialization cost — the right tool outside the Section 7 boundary, the wrong one inside. Orocos RTT and GXF are component middlewares with heavier programming models aimed adjacent to this niche. Rust runtimes with deterministic logging (e.g., copper-rs) share the record/replay goal; verifying their current scope is part of the comparison task.

Central claims (the paper's spine):

  1. Hybrid graph-visible time semantics. Same-tick, topologically ordered execution for tightly coupled fast computation and tick-boundary, latest-completed publication for slow computation, coexisting in one typed graph, with each edge's behavior derived from its endpoints' execution attributes.
  2. Logical completion simulation. A deterministic model of asynchronous computation — admission, overruns, commitment — under declared logical completion latencies, which degrades on hardware to recorded completion timing rather than to undefined behavior. One application, two time modes, one semantics.
  3. Replayable temporal provenance with declared cuts. Trigger ticks, commitment ticks, boundary-arrival ticks, generations, initial-value provenance, and declared replay classes ([S-40]) are sufficient to reproduce exactly the graph-visible execution downstream of the declared cuts — enabling full-graph replay, cut-point replay, and regenerable diagnostics ([S-30], Section 8.3) — without claiming that arbitrary computation can be regenerated.

Supporting design elements (evidence and engineering, not standalone claims): the single inline/deferred execution attribute as the compositional API that makes claim 1 declarable; the degenerate fast path as an engineering acceptance criterion; pure skip predicates as a simplification of event triggering; the application-owned library inversion with incremental migration.

Evaluation centers on the reference application demonstrating that the semantics solve a real humanoid software problem: the 1 kHz loop stays bounded under maximum due sets; planner, perception, and Python computation run concurrently on named workers; data age is explicit end to end; simulation traces are reproducible across placements; hardware failures replay; and the application definition stays compact.

An honest falsification clause carried over from the requirements: if a spike (recommended: the reference application ported to Drake) delivers Section 3's guarantees with comparable simplicity, the claims narrow to what remains — expected residue: claims 2 and 3.

docs.title: 14. Deliberately excluded (do not implement)
docs.text: Parameter/configuration frameworks; message IDLs or general serialization (field-wise encoders exist only for logging and wires); runtime rewiring; a general application lifecycle framework beyond the fixed System/Runtime transitions required by [S-37]/[S-39]; event-trigger machinery (the Latest service discipline is not event triggering: demand is clock-defined, Section 3.6); in-runtime visualization or telemetry streaming servers (viewers attach at the converter level); lossless ingress queues in core semantics (adapter concern, [S-34]); a universal bus or endpoint abstraction spanning Plant, adapters, and telemetry; RPC or acknowledged delivery; per-band threads or any priority-ordered execution; worker pools with migration (post-v1 at earliest); distributed clock sync or offset estimation; process supervision; QoS; discovery; application algorithms inside a Plant ([S-48]); a universal observation or command schema (§5.1); unified bridge/telemetry/replay wire envelopes; speculative endpoint manifests; wall-clock pacing in Test Plants ([S-49]); free-running simulators sampled asynchronously (§5.8); first-class support for every simulator — Simulator Plants are application code, and MuJoCo is the reference implementation, not a dependency of the core (§5.5). Each of these is how seven concepts become thirty. A proposal to add one must show a requirement in Sections 1–8 that cannot be met without it.

docs.title: 15. Open decisions
docs.text:
Resolved in this revision and folded into the spec: unit-delay implementation (previous-value slot, [S-7]); storage model and large-payload ownership (Section 2.3); simulation late-job behavior ([S-17]); output transactions and error semantics ([S-33], [S-19]); logger overflow and replay completeness ([S-36]).

Remaining:

  1. Python Block layout adapters — Value inputs and outputs cross today; exact read-only numpy views over retained Block leases remain deferred until a real consumer requires them.
  2. Python-implemented Plants — [S-23] puts the Plant on the tick thread and [S-26] keeps Python off it, so a Python Plant is currently unrepresentable. The case that wants one is the gym-style RL environment driven by rt.step() from Python (§6.1), where the tick thread is the Python thread and the objection weakens. Non-blocking for v1: that case is served today by a C++ Simulator or Test Plant stepped from Python.

docs.title: Appendix A: Glossary
docs.text: Tick — one completed increment of the logical clock, paced by an accepted Plant read and ordinary write. Due — t % k == phase for a system's declared divisor. Inline — runs to completion on the tick thread within its due tick. Deferred — snapshots post-inline at dispatch, executes on a named worker, and commits at a later boundary transaction. Boundary transaction — the single atomic step-2 transaction of [S-9] committing the Plant observation, eligible deferred results, and sampled ingress; defines tick membership and freezes tick t's external world ([S-31]). Latch — the runtime-owned instant immediately before update() at which a system's input readers atomically take their values. Immediate edge — inline→inline edge with same-tick visibility under ordering. Unit-delay edge — inline→inline edge whose latch at tick t returns the newest commit strictly before t, via two slots and commit-tick comparison ([S-7]). Trigger tick — tick at which a deferred job's inputs were snapshotted; carried on its result. Logical completion latency (L) — positive declared simulation delay from dispatch to commitment, with explicit finite-schedule exhaustion ([S-17]). Ingress mailbox — initialized latest-value cell written by a device thread and sampled once per boundary; replay records the graph-visible sample ([S-34]). Egress — an unpaired graph sink that copies or retains a typed value into preallocated off-thread storage after a successful ordinary Plant write. Adapter — one free-running in-process thread owning one external connection and binding N ingress writers plus M egress readers. Bridge — the adapter-level composition of one or more unpaired ingress and egress boundaries; never a core paired channel. Block pool / lease — output-owned fixed pool for large immutable payloads; edges and snapshots carry counted lease handles and final release atomically returns an index ([S-38]). Output transaction — invocation-local staging of publishes, committed atomically on successful return ([S-33]). Startup publication — generation-0 start() publication with publication_tick == Initial and origin == Startup ([S-14]). Publication origin — Startup, Reset, or Update provenance ([S-14], [S-39]). replay_complete — false iff any required replay record was dropped ([S-36]). Plant — typed synchronous boundary of one Runtime: one accepted observation and ordinary command per completed tick, owning pacing/exchange and containing no application algorithm ([S-45], [S-48]). Plant descriptor — immutable pre-open kind, time-mode, liveness, write-budget, and advancement claims validated by C18. TickInfo — exchange sequence, misses, clock/source identity, source timestamp, and optional environment index validated before tick creation. Plant kind — Simulator/Gateway/Hardware/Test rule binding recorded in the manifest ([S-46]). SafeAction — immutable compiled terminal command or device-native action. write_safe(action) — distinct non-advancing terminal-action attempt, invoked exactly once after a successful open and callable when ordinary exchange is broken ([S-45]). Substepping — exact-base-period Simulator/Callback integration hidden inside ordinary write() ([S-47]). Test Plant — wall-clock-free ScriptedPlant, CallbackPlant, or ReplayPlant shipped by CORTA ([S-49]). Parity ladder — level-0-to-5 escalation from class test to hardware (§5.10). ClockDomainId — shared time-basis identifier; cross-domain comparison has no result. SourceInstanceId — process/device/session identity; zero fails closed ([S-28]). Telemetry channel — declared offline diagnostic stream invisible to [S-20] ([S-30]). Frontend — C++ or Python graph construction; execution remains C++ core. Demand — clock-generated deferred release request; Latest retains at most one ([S-32]). External-lease budget — declared Block leases retained beyond an invocation ([S-38]). Reset — opt-in Degraded recovery with next-boundary Reset publications ([S-39]). Replay class — Deterministic or authoritative-cut RecordOutput ([S-40]). Run manifest — hard structural/schema/capacity and soft build/environment compatibility record ([S-43]). Command fallback policy — compile-materialized ordinary step-5 HoldLast(max_ticks) or SafeCommand ([S-44]). Quarantine — timeout escalation retaining a stuck thread's complete reachability closure until process exit ([S-37]). PredicateContext — metadata of the previously dispatched snapshot supplied to a pure dispatch predicate ([S-21]).

docs.title: CORTA adapters and external boundaries
docs.text: CORTA connects computation to the outside world through three boundaries with different responsibilities: a Plant paces observation/command exchange, adapters carry asynchronous semantic input and output, and observers consume telemetry. This reference explains the implemented separation and how to choose a boundary for a new device. The runtime overview introduces the execution model; the CORTA design specifies its rules. The current core contract, adapter contract and conformance index own implementation and evidence.

docs.title: Three boundaries, three responsibilities
docs.text:
flowchart TB
  peer["Simulator or robot"] <--> plant["Plant: clock and exchange"]
  plant <--> runtime_graph["CORTA graph"]
  device["Asynchronous device or process"] <--> adapter["Adapter thread"]
  adapter --> ingress["Ingress: latest boundary sample"]
  ingress --> runtime_graph
  runtime_graph --> egress["Egress: bounded queue"]
  egress --> adapter
  runtime_graph --> rings["Telemetry rings"]
  rings --> writer["Storage writer"]
  writer --> hdf5["HDF5"]
  writer --> queue["Bounded observer queue"]
  queue --> viewer["Rerun observer"]
Boundary Use it when What it owns What remains application-owned Plant A peer participates in the synchronous observation/command exchange that defines a tick Exchange, pacing and the declared terminal-action contract Robot mapping, controller algorithms and device-specific integration Adapter with ingress/egress Data arrives independently of the tick, or semantic output must leave the graph A connection/thread lifetime and bounded transfers Message meaning, device mapping, link-loss response and transport configuration Telemetry observer Data is for inspection or recording Bounded observation delivery and drop accounting Visualization schemas, dashboard and interpretation

A simulator behind a lockstep gateway is still a Plant. A joystick is an adapter input. A robot drawing in a viewer is an observation. Similar wire protocols do not make these responsibilities interchangeable.

docs.title: What is implemented
docs.text:
The original proposal's missing Egress and S-28 work is complete within the current software evidence boundary. Egress<T> is implemented, and S-28 is marked pass in the conformance index. This does not imply distributed clock synchronization, a qualified physical device or a general middleware bridge.

Surface Current implementation Example or consumer Adapter kernel AdapterSession, one connection and SDK-owned thread, placement reporting, counters and bounded stop/join Loopback example Typed egress Value and Block output, preallocated queue, drop-newest overflow and Block lease accounting Core egress implementation Keyboard input POSIX descriptor, application byte mapping, state/events and terminal restoration Keyboard example Joystick input Linux joystick records, axis/button snapshot, application mapping and optional keepalive Joystick example Datagram input Whole datagrams from a borrowed socket, application format, size bound and mapper rejection Datagram example; Digit browser operator over loopback UDP Rerun observation HDF5-first fan-out, bounded observer queues, exact stream selection and optional schema-specific encoder Rerun example; Digit scene and telemetry

A two-CORTA-application UDP bridge and ROS 2 topic integration remain deferred. The implemented datagram input is narrower: it delivers application-defined operator input to Digit. It provides no acknowledgement, retry or general network-delivery guarantee.

docs.title: Input is sampled at a runtime boundary
docs.text:
An adapter thread may perform device reads, decoding, allocation and transport work. It writes through an IngressWriter<T> rather than modifying graph state. Runtime samples ingress into the coherent tick boundary. A faster producer may replace several state updates before a consumer observes one; that is intentional latest-value behavior.

Fixed-size trivially copyable Value ingress is not restricted to the target's native atomic width. The implementation coordinates copying against Runtime sampling. Do not infer that the entire boundary is wait-free: the conformance index retains the S-23 limitation for coherent publication sections that can spin behind a preempted producer.

Source identity and clock identity have different meanings. A clock domain names a time basis; a source instance identifies a device/process/session epoch. Zero identities are rejected, cross-domain timestamp comparison has no result, and a changed source instance exposes restart provenance. Assigning an identifier does not synchronize clocks.

docs.title: Output leaves through a bounded queue
docs.text:
An egress is an independent graph sink, not one half of a required paired channel. After a successful ordinary Plant write, Runtime captures a new producer generation, stamps its publication provenance and tries to enqueue it. A full queue refuses the newest sample and increments its counter. Encoding and transport happen on the adapter thread.

The tick-side push is the operation with the allocation-free, wait-free evidence and target lock-free-atomic requirement. That evidence does not establish a deadline for the complete runtime or application. A Block egress retains leases; queue capacity and declared adapter in-flight leases must both be included in the C16 storage plan. Value/Block storage semantics remain core-owned.

One adapter can bind several ingress writers and egress readers. The adapter owns any pairing or connection-wide protocol. Core has no universal endpoint registry, discovery layer, QoS model or robot message schema. Egress remains a C++ surface; a Python binding is not implied by Python graph construction support.

docs.title: State and events have different delivery needs
docs.text:
Data Implemented helper Overflow and receiver behavior Durable state, such as requested velocity LatestState<T> Capacity one; intermediate updates coalesce Discrete requests, such as a mode change BoundedEvents<Event, N> A rolling sequenced batch; oldest entries drop when full, with accounting Repeated event batches crossing latest-value ingress BoundedEventReceiver<Event, N> De-duplicates overlap, detects sequence gaps and respects source-instance epochs

For example, keyboard bytes can update a desired velocity and append a stop request during one read burst. Publishing only the last raw byte would lose the earlier request. The state/event helpers preserve their different meanings within explicit capacity limits; they do not promise lossless or exactly-once delivery. See the delivery helpers.

docs.title: Lifecycle and command authority
docs.text:
AdapterSession exposes a DeviceThread so its stop/join participates in Runtime shutdown ordering. Adapters report placement and failures. Concrete input adapters borrow their descriptors; the owner creates the connection and remains responsible for its lifetime. Keyboard idle polling and join timeout must be configured consistently so an idle device cannot prevent bounded shutdown.

In Digit, keyboard, joystick and browser input map onto the same app-owned axes and request messages. The inline operator supervisor owns command shaping, modes and link-loss behavior. A mapper or viewer is not a controller or safety authority. The Digit operator contract describes the integrated behavior.

docs.title: Recording and visualization
docs.text:
The storage writer remains the sole consumer of each original telemetry ring. It appends HDF5 first, then copies selected rows into independent bounded Rerun queues. Viewer backpressure can drop visualization copies without changing stored rows or feeding commands into control. HDF5 retains exact declared types and metadata; a Rerun projection is an observation of them.

The generic encoder produces numeric time series. An application may provide an exact-schema encoder for semantic objects such as the Plant scene. The implemented Digit observer selects servo state, planner command and Plant-scene streams. Its launcher selects native or browser viewing and the dashboard; the C++ path owns live telemetry delivery. No generic VisualizationFrame egress was needed for these views.

Record/replay captures the graph-visible receiver ingress samples, not every transport arrival. Loopback evidence checks that receiver-visible sequence. It does not establish transport determinism, remote peer replay or network reliability.

docs.title: How to extend the boundary
docs.text:
Start with the closest existing example and the application message contract. Decide whether the peer defines ticks, supplies asynchronous semantics, or only observes. For an adapter, declare state/event behavior, capacity, source identity, time basis, malformed-input handling, descriptor ownership and shutdown behavior before choosing a transport SDK. Keep application fallback in the consuming app.

The adapter contract lists focused validation commands and evidence for queue behavior, restart handling, keyboard shutdown, joystick record parsing, datagram rejection, observer drops and receiver replay. Current joystick checks use synthetic kernel-format records; they do not qualify a physical controller. Software boundary checks do not qualify robot behavior, hardware timing or a new network deployment.

docs.title: Walking coordinator and planner–Servo boundary
docs.text:
Digit and TRON1 use locomotion::walking::Coordinator with both ALIP and DCM. The former WalkCoordinator is retired. The shared coordinator owns walking lifecycle and contact-event decisions on the planner side; Servo publishes evidence and executes authored references. This deep reference explains that division, the implemented event/clock behavior, and the differences between robot profiles.

Read model-based walking first for the complete loop. The locomotion contract owns the reusable API. Digit and TRON1 own their compositions; their validation records determine demonstrated behavior. Sharing a coordinator does not qualify either robot's gait or hardware operation.

docs.title: Why the planner owns walking decisions
docs.text:
A numerical planner chooses a landing and its timing; a reference author turns that choice into continuous task trajectories. Contact admission and support exchange must use the same step identity and clock. Splitting those decisions between a deferred planner and an independent Servo gait machine creates competing transition rules and makes delayed preview delivery difficult to interpret.

The implemented boundary places lifecycle, step timing, support roles and admission in the planner system. Servo remains responsible for full-rate measurements, controller realization and safety faults. The boundary is ownership, not a requirement that every calculation run at one rate.

flowchart TB
  plant["Plant observation"] --> servo["Servo: estimate and realize"]
  servo --> history["Contact history and delivered-reference acknowledgement"]
  history --> coord["Planner-owned coordinator"]
  coord --> kernel["ALIP or DCM solve"]
  kernel --> coord
  coord --> author["Reference author"]
  author --> preview["Timed futures and binary task targets"]
  preview --> servo
  servo --> plant

docs.title: Responsibility boundary
docs.text:
Servo Planner system State estimation and per-tick contact evidence Walking mode, step identity, stance and support exchange Installed-preview identity and commanded reference jets Contact admission, thresholds and dwell Reference installation, sampling and RHRS joins Numerical solve, retiming and reference authoring Applying binary activation targets through controller ramps Binary swing/support-height roles TAC-QP realization, physical constraints and controller faults Start, stop, capture assessment and recovery preparation

A Servo must not advance gait phase, select a stance from step labels, or infer a walking transition from planned timing. It receives time-indexed references and activation commands. Delivery acknowledgement is different: it reports which opaque preview/activation identity actually arrived, without interpreting the gait.

Contact force authority is also distinct from the planner's swing/support-height roles. DSG capacity and TAC-QP's contact model determine available force and release behavior at the control rate. A planner role does not certify contact or grant force authority.

docs.title: Full-rate contact evidence
docs.text:
ContactHistory is a fixed-capacity ring of 64 samples. Servo appends each tick. The planner consumes unseen samples in order, preserving the timing needed for release detection and dwell rather than receiving only a minimum, maximum or average.

Each sample includes tick/time, estimated yaw, requested vertical force, per-foot capacity/support/load and allocated force, force-bound and reference-retention information, estimated foot position/velocity, and installed activation/preview acknowledgement. These are measurements or delivery facts. Thresholding, filtering and gait decisions remain on the planner side.

At a configured 1 kHz Servo and 50 Hz planner, roughly 20 samples arrive per planner period. The 64-sample capacity provides bounded slack for delayed consumption, not unlimited history. The cursor detects a gap in newly consumed tick indices, non-increasing new-sample time, malformed storage and an epoch change without reset. A missing interval is an explicit failure rather than silent interpolation.

docs.title: One gait event per step
docs.text:
The coordinator's gait event is an admitted touchdown. It starts the next cycle on the landed foot and requests a successor solve. Until the first plan is accepted, that cycle is planless and both support-height roles remain enabled. The first accepted timing starts its execution clock and enables the next swing.

Physical double support is not a separate transfer stage inserted after every touchdown. The enum value DoubleSupport is the preparation mode used for startup or capture recovery. During an executable step, outgoing-foot release follows the authored swing reference and controller contact mechanics; there is no coordinator liftoff event or fixed transfer timer.

State or event Implemented consequence Neutral, captured startup Remain in Stand Motion request or valid capture assessment outside the standing region Enter preparation with a latched first stance Preparation ready and timing accepted Enter executable Walk Failed launch/planless successor Hold supports and retry; do not invent a successful plan Admitted touchdown Retire the outgoing cycle and request a successor Neutral touchdown gate, capture and alignment all satisfied Return to Stand

The step clock begins at the first accepted plan, so a planless wait after touchdown is not step time. Phase advances once per planner tick and remains continuous/non-decreasing through retiming. At the configured commitment phase, ordinary replanning stops until touchdown. A failed refresh does not by itself discard an existing executable plan.

docs.title: Admission uses the installed command
docs.text:
Admission starts when the evidence acknowledges installation of the swing activation. It first requires the incoming foot to have unloaded to the release threshold. The landing window then opens at a fraction of the installed step duration; capacity must meet the admission threshold for the configured dwell.

record_preview(generation) retains planner-owned timing for a published preview. With delivery-aware admission enabled, an evidence sample's installed preview identity selects that timing. A newer solve must not retroactively change the landing window for samples gathered before its preview arrived. An unmapped identity fails explicitly.

For example, if the planner has solved a shorter duration but Servo is still executing the previous preview, admission replays those samples using the previous duration. This preserves the distinction between solving a plan, publishing it and executing it. The acknowledgement does not move gait logic into Servo.

docs.title: Robot-owned settings
docs.text:
The same mechanism uses different calibration. The following values are read from the current Digit profile and TRON1 profile; they are not universal defaults.

Setting Digit TRON1 Release capacity threshold 0.50 0.50 Admission capacity threshold 0.50 0.50 Earliest contact fraction 0.60 0.85 Capacity dwell 0.005 s 0.020 s Shared-load hold fraction 0.0: disabled 0.0: disabled Neutral touchdowns required 2 2 Fore-aft Stand tolerance 0.03 m 0.03 m

The reusable coordinator supports maintaining a dwell through a per-foot capacity dip when the pair's load exceeds a configured fraction of body weight. Both app profiles disable this exception. In Digit, the outgoing foot alone can carry body weight while the incoming foot is airborne; pair load cannot establish incoming touchdown. The old description of an active 0.85-body-weight hold is therefore not the current Digit configuration.

Durations and commitment phase come from the selected planner profile; execution periods come from the app. Constructor defaults are not a substitute for the resolved application configuration.

docs.title: Standing, capture and completion
docs.text:
Capture assessment is planner-owned. For Digit it uses the available-foot support geometry and an inward-eroded standing region. Startup with unknown capture does not by itself leave neutral Stand. Loss of capture validity after an established captured stop can initiate recovery preparation. Preparation does not lift a foot until launch readiness and an accepted plan permit it.

Returning from Walk requires the configured number of touchdowns from steps that began neutral, capture inside the standing region, and fore-aft foot alignment. The planner owns any aligned final landing request. TRON1's point feet do not certify the same standing polygon; its continuous-stepping behavior must be understood through its own app contract, not copied from Digit's Stand acceptance.

Coordinator Stand is not the same as successful experiment completion. Digit continues updating standing references and permitting recovery until its app-owned measured settling gate passes. The profile currently requires planar speed at most 0.08 m/s, at least 0.15 body weight on each foot, held for one second. Physical completion and termination reasons belong to app validation.

docs.title: Planner and reference-author integration
docs.text:
The coordinator interface exposes update, plan_required, accept_timing, record_preview, elapsed and a read-only view. A consumer answers each requested solve with valid or failed timing. It owns the numerical state, geometry, model height, command interpretation and reference futures; the coordinator owns the lifecycle and clock.

DCM composes this mechanism through dcm::DcmWalkingPlanner. ALIP supplies its own numerical solve and delivered-state prediction. The shared mechanism does not make their optimization or swing-reference policy identical. App authors map coordinator roles to robot tasks and seed replacement references from the commanded jets appropriate to their delivery/join contract.

The library remains independent of robot models, numerical solver selection, task names, perception and CORTA graph composition. It covers supported biped stepping; flight, hand contacts and arbitrary contact schedules are outside its contract.

docs.title: Evidence and design rationale
docs.text:
The migration removed parallel Servo-side admission/gait logic and retired the old WalkCoordinator. Its enduring decisions are planner-owned lifecycle, ordered full-rate evidence, one touchdown event per step, explicit delivery timing and no planner-owned contact-force authority. Reintroducing a transfer timer or Servo phase branch would change that boundary and needs an owner-level design review.

Use the locomotion validation section for mechanism checks. Digit validation records shared-coordinator adoption and subsequent walking changes; TRON1 validation records its point-foot regressions and limits. Matching software transitions, an upright interval, or a shared profile does not establish physical recovery, a qualified gait or real-time deadlines.

docs.title: ALIP Footstep Planner Formulation (Angular Momentum + Conic Step Duration)
docs.text:
Status: working Formulation evidence: 2026-09-18; implementation mapping reviewed: 2026-10-18 Tags: alip angular-momentum footstep-planning mpc second-order-cone capturability

This reference retains the ALIP derivations and bounded September measurements, with the current implementation mapped below. The kernel reference, module contract and Digit app own implemented behavior and validation limits.

docs.title: Current implementation map
docs.text:
Topic Implemented behavior How to read the derivation Kernel Independent C++ ALIP planner, using one shared timing pair for both axes The conic model motivates the timing representation; it does not imply an exact nonlinear cone solve Timing Tangent relaxation or opt-in SOS2 interval enumeration, followed by exact-flow checks SOS2 is continuous timing within enumerated adjacency intervals, not a grid of fixed durations Pivot and prediction Digit latches the measured stance foot-link position and plans from measured CoM/contact momentum The CoP and fitted-bias studies in Section 5 are alternatives, not the installed pivot/predictor Constraints and recovery Executed geometry stays hard; explicit recovery can report negative viability margin certified covers the first reduced-model successor, not physical recovery or all future nodes Lifecycle and admission Shared planner-owned coordinator replays full-rate contact capacity and installed-preview timing Use the coordinator reference, not the original force-threshold proposal Deployment scope Digit's current ALIP app is blind; kernel model-height input is separate from terrain preview Disjoint-region and variable-height preview extensions below remain formulation material

The numerical constants in the derivations are reproducible fixtures. They are not live app defaults: the current Digit profile uses a 0.47 s nominal duration, 0.25–0.60 s duration bounds and 0.15–0.75 m width bounds. Its app commits at phase 0.95 and enables a 0.2 s/s late retiming bound from phase 0.4. Read the resolved run configuration for an experiment.

This note is the formulation of an angular-momentum footstep planner. Its two structural choices are:

  1. The state is angular momentum about the contact, not a divergent position/velocity mixture. Angular-momentum balance about a point contact is exact for the full articulated robot; the approximation is confined to one measurable kinematic term.
  2. Step duration is a decision variable represented exactly, as a point on a second-order cone, rather than gridded, linearized, or introduced through integers.

The decision variable is the touchdown-relative placement \(r_k = p_{k+1} - c^-_{k+1}\) — where the foot lands relative to where the body will be — with the world foothold \(p_{k+1}\) retained as a derived affine quantity so that terrain constraints are unaffected.

The document is organized the same way as the companion DCM formulation:

  1. Flat terrain baseline (Sections 1–8): one convex QP.
  2. Stepping stones (Section 9): disjoint foothold regions produce an MIQP.
  3. Variable height (Section 10): discrete region heights retain the MIQP structure with additional precomputation.

Section 11 summarizes the three levels side by side. Sections 12–20 carry the controller contract, the rejected alternatives, the implementation, failure and validation contracts, and a provenance table for every measured number quoted above.

Self-containment. Every derivation, constant, and measured number used below is stated in this document. Section 20 records where each measurement came from, so the body text needs no forward reference to a journal entry, an evidence capsule, or a prior design note in order to be read.

Relationship to the DCM formulation. The DCM reference distinguishes the current C++ kernel from its retired Python formulation. This note is a different formulation of the same problem, not a revision of that one. Where the two agree — the viable set of Section 3.2, the lateral periodic offset of Section 6.4, the cumulative progress objective of Section 7.2 — the agreement is derived here rather than imported, and Section 3.2 shows the two derivations produce the same set.

Formulation boundary. This is a numerical formulation. It owns the planning model, the optimization, the prediction, and the interface it requires of a controller. It does not own swing trajectories, contact admission, the support-transition clock, task gains, or navigation. Where it constrains those, it says so as a contract (Section 12) rather than specifying them.

Evidence boundary. The measurements in Sections 2.7, 5, and 12.6 come from 40 clean steps of one flat cruise-walking log at \(v_x \approx 0.95\) m/s, plus offline analysis of a terrain matrix. One terrain, one speed, one log for the momentum results. Those measurements predate the implemented ALIP kernel and do not qualify it or hardware. Section 17 states research validation questions; current runtime evidence belongs to the app validation record.

docs.title: 1.1) Why angular momentum is the primitive
docs.text:
For a point contact, the ground reaction force acts at the contact and therefore exerts no moment about it. Angular-momentum balance about the contact point \(p\) then involves gravity alone:

\[ \boxed{\;\dot L_y \;=\; m\,g\,q^x,\qquad \dot L_x \;=\; -\,m\,g\,q^y\;} \tag{1.1} \]

where \(q = c - p\) is the CoM position relative to the contact, \(m\) is total mass, and \(L\) is angular momentum about \(p\). Equation (1.1) is exact for the full articulated robot: no lumped mass, no constant height, no small-angle assumption, no assumption about the internal configuration. The moment arm is the true CoM offset and the only force with a moment about \(p\) is gravity acting at the CoM.

The same argument makes \(L\) conserved through the impulsive part of touchdown: the impulse acts at the new contact and has zero moment arm about it.

The approximation lives entirely in the kinematic half — the relation between momentum and the rate of change of position:

\[ \dot q^x \;=\; \frac{L_y - k_{G,y} + m\,q^x\,\dot z}{m\,H} \qquad\xrightarrow{\;k_G = 0,\;\dot z = 0\;}\qquad \dot q^x \;=\; \frac{L_y}{m\,H} \tag{1.2} \]

with \(H\) the CoM height above the contact plane and \(k_G\) the centroidal angular momentum (the angular momentum of the robot about its own CoM).

This is the reverse of the LIP/DCM split. There, the divergent coordinate \(\xi = q + \dot q/\lambda\) mixes position and velocity, and both halves of the dynamics are approximate together: the constant-height assumption enters the force balance and the kinematics at once. Here the dynamic half (1.1) is exact and the whole approximation is one term, \(k_G\), which is already computed at runtime as the angular half of the 6-D centroidal momentum. Isolating the approximation in a measurable quantity is the practical reason to change primitive; Section 2.7 measures it.

The three quantities the planner cares about separate cleanly:

quantity status across a step CoM position relative to the new contact assigned: \(q_{k+1} = -r_k\), by definition of \(r_k\) angular momentum about the contact continuous, exactly, at constant CoM height absolute CoM position never appears

The third row is structural, not an error-cancellation property. The coordinates in which the problem is posed do not contain absolute position, so no estimate of it can be wrong. This is the same property that makes the formulation insensitive to stance-foot drift, and Section 12.6 is careful about how much that is worth.

docs.title: 1.2) Scaled momentum and the two-axis normal form
docs.text:
Angular momentum and position have different units, which makes every gain in the formulation carry a scale factor and every ported constant a chance to be wrong by a power of \(\lambda\). Define the scaled momentum, a length:

\[ \boxed{\; \ell^x \;:=\; \frac{L_y}{m H \lambda}, \qquad \ell^y \;:=\; -\,\frac{L_x}{m H \lambda}, \qquad \lambda := \sqrt{g/H}. \;} \tag{1.3} \]

Index convention. Subscripts on \(L\) and \(k_G\) name a component of an angular-momentum vector. Everywhere else in this document a subscript is a step index and a superscript \(x\) or \(y\) is a horizontal motion axis. Sagittal motion is driven by \(L_y\) and lateral motion by \(L_x\), which is why the two labels appear crossed in (1.3). This matches the superscript-axis convention of the DCM formulation, where \(e_k^x\) and \(\nu_k^y\) are read the same way.

The lateral sign in (1.3) is load-bearing. With it, and with (1.1)–(1.2) at \(k_G = 0\), \(\dot z = 0\), both axes obey the same system:

\[ \frac{d}{dt}\begin{bmatrix} q \\ \ell \end{bmatrix} \;=\; \lambda \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} q \\ \ell \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \begin{bmatrix} q(T) \\ \ell(T) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \cosh\theta & \sinh\theta \\ \sinh\theta & \cosh\theta \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} q_0 \\ \ell_0 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \theta := \lambda T. \tag{1.4} \]

Without the lateral sign flip, the lateral system integrates to the same magnitudes with a reflected eigenvector. It therefore passes any test that asks "does this grow at rate \(\lambda\)" and fails only in closed loop, where the feedback pushes the wrong way. Section 15.2 makes this a required test.

Note that whenever \(k_G = 0\) and \(\dot z = 0\),

\[ \ell \;=\; \frac{v}{\lambda}, \tag{1.5} \]

so every result stated in velocity coordinates maps into this document by substituting \(v/\lambda \mapsto \ell\). The two formulations are related by a similarity transform, not by a modelling change; what differs is that \(\ell\) is defined from measured angular momentum while \(v/\lambda\) is assumed equal to it.

docs.title: 1.3) Divergent and convergent coordinates
docs.text:
The matrix in (1.4) has eigenvalues \(\pm\lambda\) with eigenvectors \((1,1)\) and \((1,-1)\). Define

\[ \boxed{\;\xi \;:=\; q + \ell, \qquad \zeta \;:=\; q - \ell.\;} \tag{1.6} \]

These diagonalize the flow:

\[ \xi(t) = \xi_0\,e^{\lambda t}, \qquad \zeta(t) = \zeta_0\,e^{-\lambda t}. \tag{1.7} \]

\(\xi\) is the divergent component of motion — the relative DCM, measured from the contact. \(\zeta\) is its convergent counterpart. They are retained as derived quantities, because the viability sets of Section 3 and the capturability conditions of Section 8 are naturally stated on \(\xi\); the state of the planner remains \((q,\ell)\).

Notation note. The DCM formulation writes the DCM as \(z\) and uses \(\eta_k\) for the DCM error rotated into node heading coordinates. This document uses \(\xi\) for the divergent coordinate and \(\zeta\) for the convergent one, and never uses \(\eta\), so the two documents can be read side by side. Under (1.5), this \(\xi\) equals that document's \(e_k = z_k - p_k\).

Two immediate consequences used throughout:

  • Monotonicity. \(\xi\) is strictly monotone in time on both axes with no sign caveat, because \(\xi(t)/\xi_0 = e^{\lambda t}\) regardless of the sign of \(\xi_0\). In contrast \(\dot q = \lambda \ell\) makes \(q\) monotone only while \(\ell > 0\), which fails laterally. Every timing bound in this document is therefore imposed on \(\xi\) (Section 4.5).
  • An invariant. \(\xi\zeta\) is constant along the flow, and \(\xi\zeta = q^2 - \ell^2\). Section 4.3 turns this into the conic representation of step duration.

docs.title: 1.4) Step-indexed variables
docs.text:
At (touchdown of) step \(k\), in the solve chart of Section 1.5:

  • Contact point \(p_k \in \mathbb{R}^2\); \(p_1\) is the current stance.
  • CoM relative to the contact \(q_k \in \mathbb{R}^2\).
  • Scaled momentum \(\ell_k \in \mathbb{R}^2\), in metres, from (1.3).
  • Touchdown-relative placement \(r_k := p_{k+1} - c^-_{k+1} \in \mathbb{R}^2\). The decision variable. The superscript \(^-\) denotes the value immediately before the support exchange at the end of step \(k\).
  • Stance-relative displacement \(u_k := p_{k+1} - p_k\). Derived, not decided.
  • Stance side \(s_k \in \{-1,+1\}\) with \(s_{k+1} = -s_k\). Positive \(s\) means the sign that folds lateral quantities so "inboard" is positive.
  • Step duration \(T_k\), with \(\theta_k := \lambda T_k\) and \(\sigma_k := e^{\theta_k}\).
  • Elapsed and remaining time in the current step, \(\tilde t\) and \(\tau := T_1 - \tilde t\).

docs.title: 1.5) The captured-yaw solve chart
docs.text:
All planar quantities are expressed in a chart whose origin is the current stance contact and whose orientation \(R\_{CW}\) is the planner's own accepted heading, captured once when the step is accepted and never refreshed mid-step.

\[ \widetilde r \;=\; R_{CW}^\top\,(r^w - p_1^w). \]

Three properties this buys, all of which the DCM formulation also relies on:

  • Every rotation is a constant of the solve. Heading is not a decision variable, so reach boxes, width bands, and progress chords stay linear.
  • Measured yaw never enters. Stance-foot yaw is distorted on uneven terrain and by single-corner contact; using it would inject that distortion into a placement command. Desired heading is planner-owned state, and the body and feet are downstream tracking systems.
