\[ \sum_{j=1}^{M}\delta_{k j} = 1,\qquad k=2,\dots,N+1. \]

Big-\(M\) membership constraints:

\[ A_j^w(o_1^w+Q_1p_k) \le b_j^w + M_{\text{big}}(1-\delta_{k j}), \qquad k=2,\dots,N+1,\;\; j=1,\dots,M. \]

Everything else (dynamics, kinematics, capture, and progress tracking objective) stays the same. The problem class becomes MIQP because of the binaries.

Practical notes:

  • The desired-world heading sequence is still pre-computed; without this, the heading-aligned stride constraints would become nonlinear.
  • Choose \(M_{\text{big}}\) as tightly as possible (use environment bounding boxes) to avoid weak relaxations.
  • If your solver supports indicator constraints, prefer them over big-\(M\) for numerical stability.

docs.title: 4) Extension: variable height terrain (discrete heights per region)
docs.text: Assume each region/stone has an associated height \(h_j\) (stairs, platforms, uneven stepping stones). The key modeling question is how height changes the DCM constant.

docs.title: 4.1) Step-dependent DCM constant
docs.text:
A common approximation is

\[ \lambda_k = \sqrt{\frac{g}{z_{c,k}}}, \]

where \(z_{c,k}\) is the effective CoM height above the stance foot during step \(k\).

Important modeling choice: if the controller enforces an (approximately) constant CoM height relative to the current stance foot, then \(z_{c,k}\) can be treated as constant and \(\lambda_k \approx \lambda\) even on stairs/platforms. In that case, “variable height” mainly enters through 3D kinematics/collision and region feasibility, not through the 2D DCM constant. If instead \(z_{c,k}\) varies with terrain (or you want a conservative bound), then \(\lambda_k\) becomes step-dependent as below.

If heights are discrete and tied to region selection, you can precompute per-region parameters \((\lambda_j,\sigma_{j,\min},\sigma_{j,\max})\) and then activate them according to the selected region.

docs.title: 4.2) Region-dependent timing bounds (MIQP-friendly)
docs.text:
Precompute for each region \(j\):

\[ \sigma_{j,\min} = e^{\lambda_j T_{\min}},\qquad \sigma_{j,\max} = e^{\lambda_j T_{\max}}. \]

docs.title: 4.2.1) Optimized current timing and fixed-preview region dynamics
docs.text:
Keep the command-dependent preferred time \(T_{\text{pref}}\) fixed for future steps, giving the per-region factors

\[ \sigma_{j,\text{pref}} := e^{\lambda_j T_{\text{pref}}}, \]

while retaining the ordinary optimized current-step factor.

For \(k=1\), the current stance region \(j_1\) and \(\lambda_{j_1}\) are known. Optimize \(\sigma_1\) with the corresponding region-specific timing bounds and elapsed-time floor, and impose directly

\[ z_2=\sigma_1 z_1+(1-\sigma_1)p_1. \]

This remains affine because \((z_1,p_1)\) are known. No \(\delta_{1j}\) is introduced.

For future \(k=2,\dots,N\), the planned stance \(p_k\) has the region indicator \(\delta_{kj}\) already defined in Section 3. Activate the fixed-preview dynamics component-wise:

\[ -M_{\text{big}}(1-\delta_{k j}) \le z_{k+1} - \sigma_{j,\text{pref}} z_k - (1-\sigma_{j,\text{pref}})p_k \le M_{\text{big}}(1-\delta_{k j}), \qquad j=1,\dots,M,\;\;k=2,\dots,N. \]

This keeps the problem MIQP (or MILP plus quadratic objective): \(\sigma_1\) remains the sole timing decision, while no \(\sigma_{k\ge2}\) decision variables are introduced. Region-conditional optimization of future \(\sigma_k\) is a different extension; combined with free \(z_k,p_k\) it reintroduces the bilinearity described in Section 2.8 and is not part of this MIQP baseline.

docs.title: 4.3) Height-dependent straight-heading invariant envelopes
docs.text:
For \(\alpha=0\), define the region-dependent fresh lower factor

\[ \sigma_{k,\mathrm{fresh}} :=\max(\sigma_{k,\min},e^{\lambda_k\Delta T}). \]

The scalar quantities of Section 2.5(c) become step-dependent:

\[ B_{x}^{(k)} = \frac{L_{\max}}{\sigma_{k,\mathrm{fresh}}-1}, \qquad L^{(k)}= \frac{\sigma_{k,\mathrm{fresh}}W_{\min}-W_{\max}} {\sigma_{k,\mathrm{fresh}}^2-1}, \qquad U^{(k)}= \frac{\sigma_{k,\mathrm{fresh}}W_{\max}-W_{\min}} {\sigma_{k,\mathrm{fresh}}^2-1}. \]

Region-selection binaries activate the corresponding precomputed hard outer and soft nominal envelopes. Both hard axes remain slack-free; both nominal axes may use operating-envelope slack. For nonzero heading this retains the same finite-horizon, not recursive-turning-invariance, interpretation.

Cross-height note: viability at touchdown \(k+1\) is naturally expressed using the next stance parameters (height, \(\lambda\), timing bounds) because the next admissible control is chosen from that stance.

docs.title: 4.4) Vertical kinematic constraints (minimal set)
docs.text:
If heights are part of region definitions, add at least a step-to-step height change limit:

\[ |h_{k+1} - h_k| \le H_{\max}, \]

or asymmetric bounds for up/down steps.

For discrete regions, this can be enforced via pairwise region transitions (big-\(M\) on \((\delta_{k,i},\delta_{k+1,j})\)) if needed.

docs.title: 5) Summary by complexity level
docs.text:
Setting Heading Timing Terrain Problem class Flat continuous bounded, precomputed optimize \(\sigma_1\), fix preview continuous QP Stepping stones continuous bounded, precomputed optimize \(\sigma_1\), fix preview union of polytopes MIQP Discrete heights continuous bounded, precomputed optimize \(\sigma_1\), region-fixed preview union plus heights MIQP

For flat terrain, zero heading, translating turns, and turn-in-place all use the first row with identical QP dimensions. The outer longitudinal/lateral envelope is hard for the reconstructed initial state and executable successor; the nominal-cadence envelope is soft in both axes over the preview. For nonzero heading, the scalar derivation is a finite-horizon contract rather than a proof of recursive turning invariance.

docs.title: 6) Implementation checklist
docs.text:
1. Initialize desired world heading to zero on reset. Permit explicit app or navigation assignment while inactive; never initialize it from measured body or stance-foot yaw.
  2. Form the frozen solve chart from captured stance translation and the planner-owned desired heading. Mid-step replans retain that chart.
  3. Back-propagate the latest measured DCM to step start: $$ z_1=p_1+e^{-\lambda\tilde t}\left(\xi(\tilde t)-p_1\right). $$
  4. Validate finite state, command, limits, and hard-set tolerance. Admit the reconstructed state only inside the timing-controlled outer envelope; negative \(q_1\) inside \([L,U]\) is passed through unchanged.
  5. Build the fixed preview duration/factor, current timing bounds, and the continuous bounded heading sequence from one command snapshot.
  6. Precompute node axes, midpoint axes, constant-twist progress chords, the hard \(T_{\min}\) invariant envelope, and the soft \(T_{\mathrm{nom}}\) operating envelope.
  7. Update the numeric data for the fixed-dimension QP: current-step timing, fixed preview timing, hard gait/outer-envelope rows, soft nominal and swing rows, the fixed last-admitted-step boundary, terminal schedule, and heading-aware objectives.
  8. Solve through the runtime dual active-set adapter and independently postcheck hard reach, width, executable-successor viability, dynamics, and terminal rows. Record solver status, dimensions, timing, both envelopes and slacks, swing demand, and lateral progress.
  9. Convert the accepted first foothold to world coordinates. Publish \(T_1\), \((\theta_1,\theta_2)\), \(\alpha_1\), and \(\omega_{\mathrm{real}}=\alpha_1/T_1\) atomically.
  10. Splice the C1 desired-yaw trajectory from the currently published desired yaw/rate to the accepted endpoint. Screen rate against at least \(\alpha_{\max}/T_{\min}\) and screen acceleration against its configured bound; reject an inadmissible trajectory without a second QP. Replan only before the commit phase; bypass and hold the accepted plan afterward.
  11. At admitted touchdown, advance desired heading to the accepted endpoint, promote the accepted command-relative fore-aft residual, physical width, and duration to the next solve's fixed gait boundary, and re-anchor the translation.

docs.title: 7.1) Focused formulation and module checks
docs.text:
The maintained checks must establish:

  • yaw-rate increments equal \(\operatorname{clamp}(\omega T_{\mathrm{nom}}, -\alpha_{\max},+\alpha_{\max})\) without snapping;
  • zero, positive, negative, and saturated yaw rates integrate into continuous unwrapped headings with the same per-step bound;
  • \(\alpha=0\) retains established straight behavior;
  • arbitrary finite nonzero \(\alpha\) reaches the ordinary QP without a velocity-domain or asset gate;
  • QP dimensions depend only on horizon and match for straight, translating turns, and turn-in-place;
  • every accepted preview satisfies hard reach and width, while its executable successor satisfies the hard longitudinal/lateral outer envelope;
  • nominal-envelope slack in either axis cannot cross hard gait or outer-set rows;
  • desired world heading is independent of measured body and stance-foot yaw; and
  • the accepted yaw trajectory is C1, respects the planner-coherent rate envelope and configured acceleration limit, and preserves nonzero body rate across touchdown while swing-foot yaw holds its landing endpoint independently.

docs.title: 7.2) Integrated Digit scenarios
docs.text:
Run with a static configuration and ordinary command ramps:

  • turn-in-place in both directions for at least two swing landings;
  • translating left and right arcs;
  • zero-yaw straight regression;
  • precommit yaw-rate changes and postcommit hold;
  • a multi-revolution turn generated by sustained yaw rate; and
  • uneven terrain where measured stance yaw differs from desired world heading.

Each scenario must complete the expected step sequence, keep the DCM QP solved or bypassed without unsupported-turning admission, track nonzero desired yaw in the requested direction, preserve hard viability/gait rows, and either complete terminal capture or report an explicit existing failure mode.

The focused flat-ground positive-direction turn-in-place and translating-arc runs are historical implementation evidence. They do not replace the remaining signed-rate, saturation, rough-terrain, or repeatability matrix, and they are not hardware or safety qualification.

docs.title: 7.3) Required diagnostics and pass boundary
docs.text:
Log on one clock:

  • requested scalar yaw rate;
  • accepted unwrapped \(\theta_1\), \(\theta_2\), \(\alpha_1\), \(T_1\), and \(\omega_{\mathrm{real}}\);
  • desired-yaw trajectory position/rate/acceleration and endpoint continuation;
  • measured body and foot yaws as downstream tracking signals only;
  • solve-chart origin/orientation, stance side, foothold, and plan/step identity;
  • hard reach, width, and executable-successor viability residuals;
  • hard/nominal invariant envelopes, both nominal-envelope slacks, swing demand/slack, raw initial utilization, and carried lateral-progress error; and
  • solver status, dimensions, iterations, residual, solve time, and acceptance/bypass/capture-hold outcome.

The historical DCM-planner HDF5 schema stores each raw planar QP vector once in the frozen solve chart and names that chart explicitly. It stores desired headings as unwrapped world scalars and command/published velocities in the desired-heading tangent frame. Offline analysis derives the constraint views:

\[ e_k^{\theta_k}=R(\theta_k-\theta_1)^T(z_k-p_k),\qquad u_k^{\bar\theta_k}=R\!\left(\frac{\theta_k+\theta_{k+1}}{2}-\theta_1\right)^T (p_{k+1}-p_k). \]

Thus DCM-envelope plots use each node heading, reach/width plots use each edge-midpoint heading, and closure rotates the committed \(e_2\) into the incoming node/solve heading before comparing it with the next measured \(e_1\). The file does not duplicate these derived projections or mix them into the raw preview arrays.

A scenario passes only when the hard mathematical postchecks hold and accepted heading/result identities remain coherent through replacement and commitment. Nominal-envelope slack is allowed and must be reported in both axes; the hard outer envelope has no slack. Focused QP tests and simulation artifacts establish formulation and software behavior only; application task trajectories and physical walking need separate validation.

docs.title: Running the Digit Walking Simulation
docs.text:
This page explains how to run the Digit walking simulation: choosing a scenario, overriding it from the command line, turning on live Rerun, the browser 3D viewer and virtual perception, and reading the results. The composition and its guarantees are described in APP.md, and what has been demonstrated is recorded in VALIDATION.md.

Run every command from the Digit project (apps/digit), which builds against the installed cyber-suite package; paths below are relative to it. From elsewhere, pixi run --manifest-path apps/digit/pixi.toml walk runs the same task. A module edit you want here takes pixi install in apps/digit first, which rebuilds the package incrementally; for an edit that changes a module and Digit together, the repository's root build also compiles Digit (in-tree), and its binary is passed with --binary ../../build/default/apps/digit/walking/digit_corta_walking.

docs.title: Build
docs.text:
pixi run build                                   # after every pull or C++ edit
pixi run build --target digit_corta_walking      # the walking binary only

The launcher runs whatever binary is in build/. A stale build runs old code without warning, so rebuild after pulling.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
Goal Command Canonical DCM walk in the MuJoCo viewer pixi run walk Same stack with the ALIP planner pixi run walk --config alip_walking List the scenarios pixi run walk --list Walk at one constant command pixi run walk --vx 0.5 --walk-duration 6 Walk on other terrain pixi run walk --terrain up-stairs Run without a window pixi run walk --headless Live Rerun dashboard pixi run walk --rerun Rerun in a browser pixi run walk --rerun-web Rerun plus virtual camera/lidar maps pixi run walk --rerun --perception Rerun and the MuJoCo viewer together pixi run walk --rerun --viewer Browser 3D view, also over SSH (experimental) pixi run walk --viser Show the effective config without running pixi run walk --print-resolved-config Every option, launcher and app pixi run walk --help

The viewer plays back in real time; - and = halve and double the rate (1/16× to 16×), and Space pauses. Headless runs go as fast as the stack allows.

The shared DCM/ALIP profiles enable the constant-acceleration joint observer. Controller joint position/velocity and base angular velocity use 20 Hz filters; InEKF base linear velocity has no additional controller filter. These settings are adopted defaults with remaining sustained combined-noise limits; see filtering validation. To disable observation, set state_estimation.joint_state_observer.enabled to false in an estimation profile selected by the scenario. This is also required when selecting an estimator mode other than group-velocity.

Options combine freely, for example:

pixi run walk --config alip_walking --terrain up-slope \
  --vx 0.4 --walk-duration 8 --rerun --perception --log artifacts/alip_slope.h5

docs.title: How a run is put together
docs.text:
pixi run walk runs walking/tools/walk.py. The launcher does three things itself:

  1. It turns --config NAME into walking/config/scenarios/NAME.yaml. The default is dcm_walking.
  2. With --rerun, it opens the native Rerun viewer; with --rerun-web, it serves the browser viewer. Both install the dashboard and add the flags that connect the app to it. --rerun-connect URL installs the same dashboard in an existing viewer. With --viser, it starts the browser 3D viewer and adds --scene-udp.
  3. It passes every other argument, unchanged, to the C++ executable build/walking/digit_corta_walking.

The executable then builds its configuration in two layers:

  1. The scenario YAML states the planner (dcm or alip), the terrain, the motion sequence, the simulation settings and logging. All tuning comes from the shared profiles in config/profiles/. See Configuration.
  2. Command-line flags override a small set of run choices on top of the scenario. The resolved config records each override separately.

The scenario selects the planner by default. --planner dcm, --planner alip or --planner policy overrides that choice. For a planner comparison, retain the same scenario and shared settings, and record the planner-specific profile and reference contract that deliberately change.

docs.title: Scenarios
docs.text:
pixi run walk --list reads these straight from the scenario files:

Scenario Planner What it runs Display dcm_walking (default) DCM Speed ramp 1.0 → 2.0 → 1.0 m/s over 10 s on flat ground viewer alip_walking ALIP 0.3 m/s for 24.4 s on flat ground viewer disturbance_rejection DCM 0.4 m/s with four scripted pushes (lateral, braking, high forward, a nudge train) viewer standing_push_recovery DCM Standing; a 450 N forward push at 3 s forces recovery steps viewer gate_cruise DCM Acceptance gate A: 1.0 m/s cruise for 20 s, then stop headless gate_ramp_high_speed DCM Gate B: staged ramp to 2.3 m/s headless gate_lateral DCM Gate C: lateral 0.15 → 0.30 m/s headless gate_yaw DCM Gate D: turning at 0.25 → 0.5 rad/s headless policy_hold policy M1 hold check: a zero-action policy bundle holds the stand for 5 s headless

Any scenario runs a trained policy instead with --planner policy --policy-bundle DIR; see APP.md:

pixi run walk --config gate_cruise --planner policy \
  --policy-bundle learning/checkpoints/policies/RUN-model_N --viewer

Each file's header comment explains why it exists. --config also takes a path, so for your own variant, copy a scenario into the ignored artifacts/ folder, edit it, and run the copy:

cp walking/config/scenarios/alip_walking.yaml artifacts/my_run.yaml
pixi run walk --config artifacts/my_run.yaml

The copy still reads the app's profiles. Scenario keys are strict: a misspelled or misplaced key fails at startup and names the file and key path.

docs.title: Motion from the command line
docs.text:
A scenario's motion: list is a sequence of timed velocity segments. Four flags replace the whole list with one segment:

Flags Result --vx V --walk-duration T Walk forward at V m/s for T s. vy and yaw rate are zero, not taken from the scenario --vy V --walk-duration T Walk sideways at V m/s --omega W --walk-duration T Turn at W rad/s --walk-duration T alone Keep the scenario's first segment and change only its duration

--vx, --vy and --omega each require --walk-duration. For a multi-segment profile such as a ramp or a stop, edit a scenario copy instead.

A run lasts longer than its motion. The robot first prepares to launch from measured state, and after the command ends it walks to a settled stop. The run finishes once that stop completes.

docs.title: Terrain
docs.text:
--terrain NAME replaces the scenario's active_terrain with a scene from modules/sim/terrains/:

flat, up-slope, down-slope, up-stairs, down-stairs, square-steps, waves, multi-sine, perlin

Terrain geometry lives in those scene files, not in flags. Terrain changes what the robot walks on, not what the controller knows. Unless oracle perception is on (see below), the planner and controller still assume flat ground.

docs.title: Launcher options
docs.text:
The launcher reads these itself:

Option Effect --config NAME\|PATH Scenario name, or a YAML path relative to the Digit project. Default dcm_walking --list Print the scenario table and exit --rerun Open the live Rerun viewer and connect the app. The app runs headless unless --viewer is also given --rerun-connect URL Install the same dashboard in an existing viewer and connect the app, without spawning another viewer. Mutually exclusive with --rerun --perception Record virtual camera/lidar maps (passed to the app). With --rerun, also show them live. --rerun-perception is the same flag --rerun-web Serve the Rerun viewer and dashboard to a browser on one port, http://127.0.0.1:9090. The app runs headless unless --viewer is also given --viser Serve the browser 3D view and copy the Plant scene to it. The app runs headless unless --viewer is also given --attach-only With --rerun, --rerun-connect or --viser: install the dashboard or start the viewer, print the app command, and stop, so you can start the app yourself (for example under a debugger) --port N Rerun gRPC port, default 9876. Use another port if 9876 is taken --web-port N --rerun-web browser port, default 9090: the only port to open or forward --web-bind IP --rerun-web bind address, default 127.0.0.1. 0.0.0.0 or Ubuntu's Tailscale/LAN address serves a remote browser without forwarding --viser-port N Browser viewer HTTP port, default 8080. The viewer takes the next free port if it is busy and prints the URL --viser-host ADDR Browser viewer bind address, default 127.0.0.1. 0.0.0.0 exposes the page to the network; with --operator viser that includes its controls, so anyone who reaches the page can drive the robot --scene-udp-port N Loopback UDP port from the app to the browser viewer, default 9877 --operator-udp-port N With --operator viser: loopback UDP port from the page to the app, default 9878 --binary PATH Run a different digit_corta_walking build -h, --help Print these options, then the app's own options

Everything else goes to the app.

docs.title: App options (digit_corta_walking)
docs.text:
Group Option Effect Scenario --config <yaml> Scenario file. Required when you run the binary directly --terrain <name> Replace active_terrain --planner <dcm\|alip\|policy> Replace the scenario's planner --policy-bundle <dir> The policy bundle for planner: policy --policy-base-state <truth\|estimate> What the policy sees: simulation truth or the InEKF estimate --seed <n> Replace simulation.seed, which draws simulation.sensor_noise. It changes nothing when noise is off; the Arena runner varies it (APP.md) --actuation <llapi\|ideal> How MuJoCo turns commands into joint torque, replacing simulation.actuation. llapi, the default, acts as Agility's low-level API: each command 5 ms late, drive damping at --llapi-min-damping toward --llapi-drive-target, the robot's torque limits (assets/robots/digit/config/drives.yaml). ideal applies each command's torque at once; with the undamped shins the legs then ring harder than on the robot (APP.md) Motion --vx, --vy, --omega, --walk-duration One-segment command; see Motion --operator <keyboard\|joystick\|viser> Drive the robot live instead of the motion schedule; see Driving the robot live. Refused together with the one-segment flags --operator-udp <port> The loopback port the viser page's operator controls send to; required by --operator viser, which the launcher's --viser supplies --operator-profile <yaml> Operator limits and mapping. Default walking/config/operator.yaml --joystick-device <path> Joystick device, overriding the profile's joystick.device Robot --llapi <address> Run on Agility's low-level API instead of MuJoCo: 127.0.0.1 for ar-control, 10.10.1.1 for Digit; observes only. See below --llapi-apply With --llapi: request torque once the Servo can stand on its own --llapi-min-damping <fraction> With --llapi or --actuation llapi: the least drive damping, as a fraction of each drive's limit, for every planner's commands. Default 0.75, as digit_fpp and Agility's example client use; 0 leaves the policy its trained damping and DCM/ALIP none --llapi-drive-target <predicted\|zero> With --llapi or --actuation llapi: what the drives damp DCM's and ALIP's joints toward. predicted (default) keeps a 9–12 cm swing and ALIP's 1.0 m/s walk in Agility's simulator and is untried on the robot; zero is digit_fpp's hardware-proven setting, with a low swing (about 4 cm) --llapi-base <agility\|estimator> With --llapi: the base state the controller uses. Default agility, Agility's own estimate; estimator is our InEKF, whose tilt drifts (see below) Display --viewer / --headless Show or hide the MuJoCo viewer, overriding simulation.headless --no-keep-viewer-open Close the viewer when the run ends. By default the last frame stays up until you close the window Logging --log [path] Turn on the session log, optionally at a new path --no-log Write no session log. Rerun and viser still work, from the same streams kept in memory only; --perception needs logging on --log-debug Also record TAC-QP solver internals as a separate stream Observation --rerun-connect <url> Stream to a running Rerun viewer. When using the launcher, it also installs the dashboard; the direct binary streams data only --scene-udp <port> Copy the 50 Hz Plant scene to 127.0.0.1:<port> for the browser 3D viewer. --viser supplies this for you --perception Record virtual sensor clouds, elevation, costmap and occupancy Safety --cbf / --no-cbf Force the collision CBF on or off. The safety profile is unchanged, so an A/B pair differs only in this flag --inspect-safety-geometry Open a paused viewer showing candidate CBF proxies. Cannot be combined with --headless --show-safety-geometry / --no-safety-geometry Show or hide the guarded-shape overlay in the viewer Diagnostics --print-resolved-config Print the effective configuration, with every override and file digest, then exit --write-resolved-config <path> Write that report to a file, then exit --print-tac-qp-summary Print TAC-QP variables, tasks and constraints before running --corta-introspect <path> Write the compiled CORTA graph as JSON. Render it with pixi run python -m cyber_suite.corta <path>

Precedence:

  • When a flag and its opposite are both given (--viewer/--headless, --log/--no-log, --cbf/--no-cbf), the later one wins. So does a repeated --config.
  • Retired flags such as --qp-solver or --keep-viewer-open fail with the YAML key that replaced them. Tuning has no command-line surface.

docs.title: Live Rerun
docs.text:
pixi run walk --rerun

This command:

  1. starts the native Rerun viewer that ships with rerun-sdk, on port 9876;
  2. installs the dashboard layout: a large Plant truth 3D view (robot, terrain, foot-corner contact forces) above four live plots, Base state, Estimated state, Motion command and Control; and
  3. launches the app headless with --rerun-connect rerun+http://127.0.0.1:9876/proxy.

The robot uses its visual meshes with smooth surface normals, and terrain uses the resolved MuJoCo material textures. The ground plane is displayed as a 2 km by 2 km textured surface that appears unbounded at normal walking views, against a sky-blue background (RGB 135, 206, 235). The spatial camera starts near Digit and follows its base position, keeping the view upright as the robot rolls, pitches or turns; you can still orbit and zoom. This requires the updated walking binary and launcher. The 3D view shows the current frame while the scalar plots retain their ten-second history. Rerun uses its own lighting, so the appearance is similar rather than identical to MuJoCo.

To view in a browser instead, on this computer or a Mac, add --rerun-web:

pixi run walk --config alip_walking --vx 0.3 --walk-duration 6 --rerun-web

Then open http://localhost:9090. Like --viser, it needs one port and the link never changes. When the simulation runs on Ubuntu, forward port 9090 with VS Code's Ports view or ssh -N -L 9090:127.0.0.1:9090 ubuntu-workstation. To skip forwarding over Tailscale or a private LAN, add --web-bind 0.0.0.0 (or Ubuntu's Tailscale address) and open http://<ubuntu-tailscale-name>:9090. Ubuntu serves the bundled Rerun web viewer, the current dashboard and the telemetry, so the Mac needs only a browser. The first visit downloads the 50 MB viewer, which the browser then caches.

The Rerun server itself listens only on Ubuntu loopback: telemetry on --port (default 9876) for the app, and its page on a private port. A small launcher-owned relay is the only listener on --web-bind. It forwards the page and the viewer's gRPC-web telemetry from --web-port (default 9090), so both share one origin and need no cross-origin permission. Opening / redirects to the viewer with WebGL selected and telemetry pointed at the address the browser used, so the same link works through a forward, a Tailscale name or a LAN address.

The browser server stays open after simulation completion so you can scrub the recording. Ctrl+C in the launch terminal closes that server; --rerun-web --attach-only likewise keeps serving until Ctrl+C while printing the separate app command. A port that is still held, usually by an earlier launch serving playback, is an error rather than a new link: press Ctrl+C in that launch, then run again with the same link. For two simultaneous runs, give the second its own --web-port and --port. --rerun, --rerun-web and --rerun-connect are mutually exclusive. See the remote workflow for the Mac recipe and native-viewer alternative.

Under planner: policy (for example --planner policy --policy-bundle DIR), every Rerun mode shows the same robot scene with the policy's own plots: the base velocity the policy saw, the estimate, the velocity command, mechanical power, saturated actuators, phase and fall. --perception is not supported with the policy and is refused before any viewer starts.

Browser mode adds the C++ operational flag --rerun-dashboard-only: its four plot panels receive their existing channels sampled at up to 50 Hz, and the robot scene remains at 50 Hz. The full 1 kHz Servo stream is stored in HDF5 before this presentation copy is made. Native --rerun and ordinary --rerun-connect retain their full scalar stream for drill-down. This limits browser ingestion overhead; use the HDF5 artifact or native viewer for signals faster than the browser display rate. No controller or simulator rate changes.

To use an existing viewer, including one reached through an SSH tunnel, run:

pixi run walk --config alip_walking --headless \
  --vx 0.3 --walk-duration 6 \
  --rerun-connect rerun+http://127.0.0.1:9876/proxy

The launcher sends and activates the same dashboard, including its sky-blue background and close camera, before starting the app. Without that camera an automatic view can frame the whole 2 km ground surface, making the robot too small to see. The endpoint remains unchanged, and no additional viewer is spawned. The direct C++ binary sends scene data but does not install a dashboard; use the launcher or prepare the viewer with --attach-only first.

The viewer stays open after the run ends, so you can scrub sim_time. Rerun receives a copy of the logged telemetry: each record is written to HDF5 first, then offered to Rerun. A slow or closed viewer drops only its own copy, never log data or control. The run's closing summary prints a rerun_observer line with offered, logged and dropped counts.

Useful combinations:

  • --rerun --viewer: the MuJoCo window as well.
  • --rerun --port 9877: use this when another viewer holds 9876 (the error is Rerun viewer did not bind to port 9876).
  • --rerun --attach-only: open the viewer and print the app command without running it.
  • --rerun-connect URL --attach-only: refresh the dashboard in an existing viewer without running the simulation.

docs.title: Browser view (viser)
docs.text:
Experimental. The page draws the Plant scene (robot, terrain, foot-corner contacts and forces) in any browser, so a remote session needs one forwarded TCP port and no viewer install:

pixi run walk --viser --vx 0.5 --walk-duration 8

The launcher starts tools/viser_view.py, waits until it serves http://127.0.0.1:8080, then runs the app headless with --scene-udp 9877. The app copies each Plant scene record to that loopback port after it is written to HDF5; like Rerun's copy, a missing or slow viewer drops only its own copy. The closing summary prints a scene_udp_tap line with offered, enqueued, dropped and sent counts. The page stays up after the run until Ctrl-C.

When the simulation runs on another computer, forward the port from your own machine and open http://localhost:8080 there. VS Code Remote-SSH forwards it from its Ports view; from a plain terminal:

ssh -N -L 8080:127.0.0.1:8080 ubuntu-workstation

Logging is not needed: with --no-log the app keeps its streams in memory only and still feeds the page. In a live operator session the page also shows an Operator status panel, and with --operator viser its controls; see Driving the robot live.

The page keeps every frame of the run:

  • Follow live shows the newest frame at simulation speed, which is not wall-clock speed. Headless runs go as fast as the stack and the host's load allow: terrain and perception runs are slower, and planner: policy can run faster than real time.
  • Play replays at the chosen Speed (1× is real time); the slider scrubs. Both turn off Follow live. Play at the end of a finished run restarts it.
  • Follow base keeps the base centred by sliding the world beneath it. Untick it to orbit or pan in world coordinates.

The viewer also replays any session log, without the app:

pixi run python walking/tools/viser_view.py --log artifacts/walking.h5

Started on its own (pixi run python walking/tools/viser_view.py), it waits for a run with --scene-udp 9877, and switches to each new run that arrives. It loads the resolved MJCF the run names, so it must run on the computer that ran the simulation. Robot meshes are merged on a 3 mm grid by default to shorten the first download (--mesh-cell 0 keeps full detail); flat heightfield cells are merged exactly. The first page load downloads about 3 MB on flat ground and 5 MB on the stairs; following a live run then takes about 70 kB/s.

It works with every planner. It shows no plots, perception maps or estimated state, and offers no MuJoCo-style perturbation: use --rerun or --viewer for those.

docs.title: Driving the robot live
docs.text:
--operator lets you drive any scenario instead of its motion schedule, with every planner, including --planner policy. The run is paced to the wall clock and lasts until you quit. With the browser view, drive from the page itself; logging is optional:

pixi run walk --config alip_walking --operator viser --viser --no-log

Open the page (http://localhost:8080, forwarded when remote), click into the scene so it has keyboard focus, and use the Operator controls panel or its keys. The Operator panel above it shows what the robot's supervisor decided, not what you asked for.

Page key Terminal key Effect G g Walk. Accepted once the status says ready I / K w / s (or i / k, Up / Down) Forward / backward request, one step (10 % of the limit) per press J / L a / d (or j / l) Left / right request U / O q / e (or u / o, Left / Right) Turn left / right Space Space Stop: zero the request and return to Stand P p Damp: latched joint damping. In simulation the robot collapses X x or Ctrl-C Quit: stop, settle, and end the run

The page uses the right hand because viser's camera owns W/A/S/D/Q/E and the arrow keys; those still move the camera and never reach the robot. The sliders set the same request as the keys, and the buttons send the same requests. The request latches: it stays where your presses leave it until you change it or stop. The page repeats it 20 times a second while a browser is connected, so closing the tab or losing the connection stops the robot within about half a second and returns it to Stand, after which it needs a new Walk. Ctrl-C in the launch terminal ends the session too.

--operator keyboard drives from the launch terminal instead, with the terminal keys above, and works over SSH because the app reads the terminal it was launched from. The terminal shows the same status in one line:

t   12.3s 1.00x | WALK  ready    link    deadman | req +0.60 +0.00 +0.00 | cmd vx +0.30 vy +0.00 wz +0.00

That is simulated time and real-time factor; mode (STAND, WALK or DAMP); whether the robot accepts motion yet (starting, ready, quitting); device link; deadman; your request as a fraction of each limit (forward, left, counter-clockwise); and the command the servo actually receives, rate-limited, in m/s and rad/s. A terminal reports no key releases, so the keyboard cannot tell a lost terminal from a quiet one: its request stays latched until the session ends.

--operator joystick reads a pad plugged into the computer that runs the simulation, which needs the joydev module and read access to /dev/input/js0 (membership of the input group). With the default Xbox-style mapping, hold LB (deadman) and use the left stick to move and the right stick to turn; A walks, B stands, Back damps and Start quits. Releasing LB ramps the command to zero but stays in Walk. If the pad goes silent for 0.3 s, for example unplugged or out of range, the robot returns to Stand and needs a new Walk. Other pads number their axes and buttons differently: jstest /dev/input/js0 (package joystick) shows yours, and config/operator.yaml maps them.

pixi run walk --config dcm_walking --operator joystick --viser --no-log

Limits, accelerations, the joystick mapping and the session limit are in config/operator.yaml; the defaults allow 0.5 m/s forward, 0.3 m/s backward and sideways, and 0.5 rad/s turning. A session ends when you quit, after session_limit_s (300 s), or on Ctrl-C (except with --operator keyboard, where Ctrl-C is the quit key), which still closes any log normally; a second Ctrl-C kills the process. Logging is your choice: with it on, the session log grows by about 1.4 GB per simulated minute.

docs.title: Agility's simulator or the robot (LLAPI)
docs.text:
--llapi runs the same app on Agility's low-level API, which Agility's own simulator, ar-control, serves exactly as the robot does; only the address changes. It needs a build with the live link: modules/digit_hardware builds it when Agility's sources are in ~/Projects/agility_resources/current (or $AGILITY_RESOURCES). Agility's controller holds the robot until you switch it to the low-level API, and you hand it back the same way.

  1. Start Agility's simulator, which starts the robot standing under Agility's controller, and wait for JSON message API server started:
cd ~/Projects/agility_resources/current/sdk/lowlevelapi && ~/Projects/ar_control/ar-control-2023 lowlevelapi_example.toml
  1. Run the app with --llapi-apply. Startup prints Agility's operation mode, which the app keeps reading from the JSON API, and then takeover-ready:
pixi run walk --config alip_walking --operator keyboard --llapi 127.0.0.1 --llapi-apply --no-log
  1. Hand the robot to the app. The app prints Agility's operation mode locomotion -> low-level-api and the robot obeys our commands, and its controller stands the robot:
pixi run python modules/digit_hardware/tools/agility_mode.py low-level-api

  1. Drive it from the app's terminal: g walks, each w or s adds a tenth of the forward limit (0.5 m/s in config/operator.yaml), a/d and q/e step sideways and turn, Space stops, x quits. A profile with a higher limits.forward_mps (--operator-profile) allows more speed.

  2. Hand the robot back to Agility's controller before quitting:

pixi run python modules/digit_hardware/tools/agility_mode.py locomotion

Without --llapi-apply the app only observes: the whole stack runs while Agility keeps the robot. --config dcm_walking runs DCM. At the switch the pelvis leans from Agility's upright stance to our controller's 0.05 rad (2.9°) forward pitch within a quarter second while the base moves about 4 cm back; that is our standing posture, not a fault. The closing digit_llapi_control line reports the time in control, the worst backlog, held and degraded sends, and the largest tilt. To diagnose a session, replace --no-log with --log <file.h5>: the components/hardware/digit_llapi stream holds the operation mode, the torque the robot applied beside the one requested, Agility's base estimate and the link's counters, tick by tick.

Watch the robot at http://localhost:8080/gamepad, Agility's page; the viser and MuJoCo views need the MuJoCo Plant. Only one ar-control can run: stop it with Ctrl+C, not kill, or it keeps port 8080. On the robot the address is 10.10.1.1, for both the LLAPI and agility_mode.py --address, and the computer sits on Digit's payload Ethernet; follow the safety procedures in Agility's manual first.

Defaults, and what they mean. These are the settings the app picks for --llapi; APP.md has the reasons and VALIDATION.md the evidence.

  • Base state: --llapi-base agility controls on the estimate Agility publishes with every observation, with our estimator off. The app anchors its height once, so connect while the robot stands on flat ground. --llapi-base estimator uses our InEKF, whose roll and pitch drift with the gyro bias (a degree after half a minute in the simulator); use it only to observe.
  • Drive damping: every command asks the joint drives to damp at --llapi-min-damping (default 0.75) of each drive's limit, as digit_fpp does on the robot, because the leg springs otherwise ring through the command delay. For DCM and ALIP, --llapi-drive-target predicted (default) damps toward the joint velocity the command expects; zero damps toward zero velocity, digit_fpp's proven robot setting, which lowers the swing to about 4 cm in the simulator. digit_fpp found a measured-velocity target fed the spring mode on the robot: watch for leg jitter there.
  • In Agility's simulator ALIP walked straight at up to 1.0 m/s with a 9.4 cm swing and 0.48 s steps (0.33–0.37 s at 1.0 m/s), and DCM at 0.3 m/s. Turning, sideways steps and pushes are untested.

Real-time priority. The control and link threads ask for SCHED_FIFO. On an account whose ulimit -r is 0, startup prints real-time priority refused and they run at normal priority; on a busy desktop a burst of late ticks can then cross the 15-slot backlog threshold and end the run with Plant read failed or crossed its miss threshold, releasing the robot to Damping. digit_fpp's procedure grants it: a realtime group with rtprio 95 and memlock unlimited in /etc/security/limits.d/99-realtime.conf, then a fresh login (a tmux or byobu server started earlier keeps the old limits), after which ulimit -r prints 95. A deployment computer needs it; digit_fpp measured 13.6 ms control ticks on the robot without it.

The learned policy runs the same way with its bundle:

pixi run walk --config policy_hold --operator keyboard --llapi 127.0.0.1 --llapi-apply --policy-bundle learning/checkpoints/policies/2026-10-12_20-32-06_arm-refine-r1-model_16800 --no-log

Until the switch the app holds the posture and torque Agility's controller applies, so the switch barely moves the robot, and it starts the policy within about 40 ms of seeing low-level-api. The policy stands until you press g and command motion; it stood still at 0.1 m/s (ww) and walked at 0.3 m/s (wwwwww), with less foot lift than ALIP. Its PD damping runs in the drives toward zero velocity, its trained law, raised to the 0.75 floor where lower. Handing back to locomotion ends the run, since the policy must not run blind.

docs.title: Perception
docs.text:
Two separate switches are both called "perception". They differ in whether the controller sees the result:

--perception (flag) simulation.terrain_perception: oracle (scenario YAML) What runs A virtual depth camera (61 × 45 rays) and lidar (426 beams) ray-cast from the robot's true pose, feeding an elevation map, costmap and 3D occupancy at up to 10 Hz A 20 Hz elevation map read directly from the simulated terrain Planners Both DCM only; an ALIP scenario with oracle fails at startup Affects walking? No. Observation only; control never reads it Yes. The planner uses terrain height to set swing apex and landing height Where it goes components/perception/maps in the session log, and Rerun with --rerun terrain/* channels of the DCM planner stream (terrain/status 1 = map applied) How to view Live: --rerun --perception. Afterwards: pixi run python -m cyber_suite.perception.playback LOG.h5 pixi run python -m cyber_suite.corta.telemetry LOG.h5 --list finds the channels; the walking plotter does not draw them yet Default off blind

To walk with oracle terrain, set it in a copy of a DCM scenario:

simulation:
  terrain_perception: oracle   # blind | oracle

cp walking/config/scenarios/dcm_walking.yaml artifacts/dcm_oracle.yaml
# edit simulation.terrain_perception to oracle, then:
pixi run walk --config artifacts/dcm_oracle.yaml --terrain up-stairs --vx 0.3 --walk-duration 6

The flag and the YAML key are independent. To watch the maps while the planner uses oracle terrain, pass --rerun --perception with that scenario. Oracle terrain is experimental, and the perception maps are an inspection tool, not a sensor model of the real robot. Their limits are in APP.md and the perception telemetry contract.

docs.title: Logs and after the run
docs.text:
Each scenario sets its log path. The canonical DCM run writes logs/digit_corta_walking.h5 and ALIP writes logs/digit_alip_walking.h5. --log PATH redirects the log; use artifacts/ for anything you want to keep apart. Both folders are ignored by Git.

The summary printed at the end reports run_complete=, boundary_pass= and an outcome line. The exit code is 0 when the run passes. A passing run proves only that the run executed cleanly, not that the gait was good. For gait quality, read the log:

Task Command Figures and a summary.json report, for either planner pixi run plot-walking LOG.h5 -o DIR List the figures, or write only the report pixi run plot-walking LOG.h5 --list / --summary-only Pick figures, a time window, or open windows --only NAME, --window START END, --show Compare two DCM runs pixi run plot-walking A.h5 --compare B.h5 -o DIR Numerical plots of the DCM kernel pixi run python -m cyber_suite.viz.cli locomotion LOG.h5 -o DIR --no-show Plain-language TAC-QP findings pixi run python -m cyber_suite.control.audit.walking_log LOG.h5 Per-tick timing percentiles pixi run python -m cyber_suite.corta.timing LOG.h5 List streams, or export to npz/csv/parquet pixi run python -m cyber_suite.corta.telemetry LOG.h5 --list Replay recorded perception maps pixi run python -m cyber_suite.perception.playback LOG.h5 (--inspect validates without a GUI; --save X.rrd --plot X.png exports)

docs.title: Running the binary directly
docs.text:
Scripts and matrix runners call the executable without the launcher:

build/walking/digit_corta_walking \
  --config walking/config/scenarios/gate_cruise.yaml --headless

Here --config needs the full path, because name lookup is a launcher feature. Run from the Digit project. For a live Rerun view, start a viewer yourself (for example with pixi run walk --rerun --attach-only) and pass --rerun-connect <url>.

docs.title: Common errors
docs.text: Message Meaning and fix Digit walking binary not found Build it: pixi run build --target digit_corta_walking unknown scenario 'x'; available: … Use one of the listed names, or give a path to a .yaml file --config is required for Digit walking runs The binary was run without a scenario. Use pixi run walk or pass --config --vx, --vy, and --omega require --walk-duration Add --walk-duration SECONDS --perception requires logging Remove --no-log, or enable logging in the scenario --operator viser drives the robot from the viser page; add --viser The page is the device, so the launcher must start it cannot bind operator port 127.0.0.1:9878 An earlier run still holds the port: end it, or pick another with the launcher's --operator-udp-port --scenario was replaced by --terrain On the binary, --scenario is retired. Use --config for the scenario file and --terrain for the ground --X was removed; set <key> in the Digit walking YAML configuration That tuning moved into YAML. Edit a scenario copy or profile Unknown option: --X Check pixi run walk --help Rerun viewer did not bind to port 9876 Another viewer holds the port. Close it or pass --port 9877 OSError: [Errno 98] Address already in use from viser_view.py Another browser viewer holds UDP 9877. Close it or pass --scene-udp-port 9878 simulation.terrain_perception: oracle feeds only the DCM planner Oracle terrain needs a DCM scenario --inspect-safety-geometry cannot be combined with --headless Drop --headless, and with --rerun add --viewer

docs.title: Run G1 with live visualization
docs.text:
Run these commands on Ubuntu from the G1 project (apps/unitree-g1), which builds against the installed cyber-suite package; paths are relative to that folder. Simulation and the viewer server run there; your browser can run on Ubuntu or another computer. Build after changing C++ sources:

cd apps/unitree-g1
pixi run build

docs.title: Viser
docs.text:
pixi run walk --planner alip --viser
pixi run walk --planner dcm --viser
pixi run stand --viser

Run one command at a time, then open http://localhost:8080. The launcher prints the run directory and URL. Live runs default to a fresh timestamped directory under artifacts/unitree-g1/; --out DIR selects an explicit fresh directory. The viewer stays open after the simulation. Ctrl+C closes only this launch's processes. If port 8080 is occupied, use --viser-port 8081 and open http://localhost:8081.

Follow live shows the newest frame. Turn it off to scrub Time (s) or use Play / pause replay and the speed selector. Follow base keeps the robot centered; Contacts and forces toggles recorded contact loads. These are observation controls; they do not pause or command the simulation. The page reports the actual acceptance outcome even when the robot remains standing.

docs.title: Rerun
docs.text:
pixi run walk --planner alip --rerun-web
pixi run walk --planner dcm --rerun-web
pixi run walk --planner alip --rerun

Browser Rerun uses http://localhost:9090. It shows the G1 mesh, ground, contact forces, base velocity versus command, contact loads, torque utilization and primary-QP status. Its timeline retains the run for playback. --rerun opens a native Rerun window on the simulation host and needs a working display. --viser can be combined with either Rerun mode to view the same run in both.

Only the browser port needs forwarding: Rerun's relay keeps its telemetry and asset listeners on Ubuntu loopback. Use --web-port 9091 if the browser port is occupied, and --port 9879 if the internal Rerun telemetry port is occupied. Existing servers are never replaced. Both viewer types bind to loopback by default; --viser-host or --web-bind can select an explicitly reachable private-network address.

docs.title: Remote browser
docs.text:
In VS Code Remote - SSH, forward 8080 for Viser or 9090 for Rerun through the Ports panel, then open that localhost URL on your Mac. Alternatively, run one of these on the Mac, substituting your SSH host alias:

ssh -N -L 8080:127.0.0.1:8080 ubuntu-workstation
ssh -N -L 9090:127.0.0.1:9090 ubuntu-workstation

Use the chosen alternate port on both sides if you changed it. The Mac needs only a browser and the connection; it does not need MuJoCo, Pixi or a repository checkout. Ubuntu loopback browser rendering is verified; the Mac/SSH path has not been exercised in this session.

docs.title: Recordings and headless runs
docs.text:
pixi run python walking/tools/view.py --run artifacts/unitree-g1/YOUR_RUN
pixi run python walking/tools/view.py --trace artifacts/unitree-g1/final/alip/trace.csv
pixi run walk --planner alip --headless --out artifacts/unitree-g1/headless-alip
pixi run walk --planner alip --viser --no-keep-open

--run reopens the full scene recording in Viser, including recorded forces; it can also attach while the producer runs. Existing --trace CSV playback and kinematic inspection without either flag remain available. A live Rerun launch also saves a unique view-*.rrd in the run directory. --no-keep-open drains the recording and closes the viewers automatically for bounded checks. Headless/native-only launches preserve their previous behavior; add --record-scene to record the full scene without a live viewer.

The optional recording consists of scene.mjb, scene.yaml and scene.bin: an exact compiled model, a versioned little-endian float64 layout, and append-only records. It contains reset/final poses plus 50 Hz qpos, generalized velocity, actuator effort/joint velocity, eight contact positions/forces, the planar command and primary-QP status. Completed launches write viewer_result.json; viewer_report.json checks received versus produced frame counts. An interrupted recording retains its complete records and an interruption marker. These display samples do not replace the 1 kHz walking metrics or establish peak impact loads.

Walking uses the sensor-only CORTA runtime described in APP.md. A run exits with code 2 when physical acceptance fails, including a fall, fault, torque saturation or insufficient tracking/stopping. The launcher preserves that result and keeps the viewer available. See VALIDATION.md for current evidence.

docs.title: Walking acceptance and sensor replay
docs.text:
pixi run check
pixi run walk-check
pixi run ./build/walking/g1_sensor_replay artifacts/unitree-g1/headless-alip artifacts/unitree-g1/replay-alip --planner alip

check retains the model/standing boundary; walk-check evaluates both planners with fresh artifacts and does not relax walking thresholds. Build before calling the replay executable directly. Supply the original --config when replaying a custom profile; the complete resolved configuration must agree. Replay requires a fresh output directory and exact sensor/command row counts. It compares every torque, release/fault decision and preview/activation/step identity within 1e-10 Nm. A replay pass can reproduce a failed physical run and is not walking acceptance.

The default is ALIP with a conservative 0.1 m/s forward command. That bounded flat-ground scenario passes; DCM still fails saturation acceptance. For a faster ALIP experiment, run pixi run walk --planner alip --vx 0.3 --walk-duration 6 --duration 16 --viser. It completes and stops in the recorded trial but still saturates actuators, so this is not a qualified speed setting. See the current contact-quality results in VALIDATION.md. Startup time is measured after the estimator and first preview release the simulation harness. The total duration includes estimation startup. summary.yaml records both milestones, run completion and physical acceptance separately. sensors.csv and commands.csv are the full-rate replay inputs; estimates.csv is offline diagnostic output and is never consumed by control.

docs.title: Terrain and motion scenarios
docs.text:
pixi run walk --list-terrains
pixi run walk --planner dcm --terrain flat --vx 0.10 --vy 0.0 --walk-duration 5 --viser
pixi run walk --planner dcm --terrain up-slope --vx 0.10 --walk-duration 8 --duration 16 --viser
pixi run walk --planner alip --terrain perlin --vx 0.10 --walk-duration 5 --viser
pixi run walk --planner alip --motion walking/config/motion-example.yaml --duration 20 --viser

These select experiments; they do not establish that a planner can traverse the terrain or track the requested speed. Non-flat walking is currently blind: terrain geometry stays in Plant for physics, initialization, scoring and recording. Landing heights, foot orientation and contact normals retain the flat-ground planner/controller assumptions. Terrain-aware footholds and yaw-rate commands are not implemented. Start both feet on a common horizontal pad; missing corner support or more than 2 mm of corner-height spread rejects startup.

--terrain NAME selects from the shared terrain catalog, including flat, slopes, stairs, platform, square steps, waves, Perlin and multi-sine. The terrain block in config/walking.yaml supplies catalog and source paths; a separate catalog directory can hold fully specified experimental scene files using the shared schema. The default name: source keeps the original G1 scene. Selecting flat and a non-flat scene generates both through the same composer, avoiding source-versus-generated model differences in matched comparisons. Generated MJCF/heightfield files stay under the run's terrain/ directory. Viser and Rerun display the recorded planes, boxes and heightfield triangles using flat colors; the native MuJoCo viewer also shows catalog textures.

--vx and --vy require --walk-duration; supplying either creates one complete planar command, with an omitted component set to zero. A duration alone retains the first configured velocity. --duration changes total simulation time; it must include post-release startup, all motion segments and at least two seconds for stopping, with additional room for estimator initialization and capture. Commands use the fixed initial heading frame. Negative components are accepted as experimental commands; turning is unsupported.

--motion PATH reads a YAML sequence such as config/motion-example.yaml. It cannot be combined with single-segment command overrides. Each item states positive duration_s and finite velocity_mps: [vx, vy]. Segments are contiguous after startup_s, measured from harness release, and intervals include their start and exclude their end. Zero velocity requests capture/standing; later nonzero segments request relaunch. After the final segment the command remains zero. A profile can contain this sequence under motion: instead of the legacy motion_s/velocity_mps pair; combining both forms is rejected.

Gait timing/step bounds, swing height, command acceleration/stopping ramps, normal touchdown braking, startup duration, centroidal/height gains, controller weights, friction assumption and estimation settings remain in the selected --config PATH. Terrain contact friction comes from the source MJCF/catalog; controller.friction is the controller's assumed coefficient and must be chosen deliberately for the experiment. Resolved configuration records the applied motion and selected terrain YAML. Replay uses the same scenario options, for example:

pixi run ./build/walking/g1_sensor_replay RUN_DIR REPLAY_DIR --planner dcm --terrain up-slope --vx 0.10 --walk-duration 8 --duration 16

docs.title: Contact-quality diagnostics
docs.text:
Add --audit to a physical run when investigating impact, bounce or slip. feet.csv contains pre-interval foot/corner position and velocity, post-step physical contact force for that command interval, the executed reference and estimated capacity. contact_slip_mps is the normal-force-weighted tangential velocity at actual physical contact points; sole-center speed is a different quantity. control.csv contains full-rate task activation, reference/actual jets, desired acceleration, weight and solver cost. support.csv contains per-point capacity, normal force/bound and allocator target. These files are large, optional and observation-only; they remain under ignored run artifacts. Peak loads must use the 1 kHz audit/metrics, rather than the 50 Hz viewer.

The selected profile brakes normal touchdown motion over 40 ms, reaching a 4 mm target depth before holding through the existing admission timeout. This fixes the earlier continued downward press; it does not guarantee load acquisition at every speed. The controller.centroidal block adds momentum and support-height control following Digit's composition with G1 tuning. Torque/friction/contact constraints and walking pass thresholds are unchanged.

docs.title: Train, inspect and export a policy
docs.text: A learning experiment has several distinct outputs: a valid task, a trained checkpoint, measured behavior and a deployable bundle. Treat them as separate steps. A high reward, a successful export and good walking answer different questions.

docs.title: The experiment chain
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    accTitle: From a learning task to deployment evaluation
    accDescr: Check the task and model, train a checkpoint, inspect and evaluate it, export a bundle, check replay parity, then evaluate in the target Plant.
    T["Check task and model"] --> R["Train a checkpoint"]
    R --> E["Inspect and evaluate"]
    E --> B["Export a bundle"]
    B --> P["Check replay parity"]
    P --> S["Evaluate in the target Plant"]

Training is owned by the robot app, using its learn environment. The default project environment supplies compiled deployment tools. The bundle records what observations mean, how actions become references and how references become actuator commands. The deployment design explains why those links must remain explicit.

docs.title: Choose a robot-specific starting point
docs.text:
Project Starting point Preserve when making a comparison G1 The 23-DoF velocity task Joint layout, model fingerprint, observation/action contract and timing Digit The task matching your intended actuation model Robot revision, ideal/drive assumptions, state source and policy contract TRON1 Point-foot learning configuration Robot cadence, contact geometry and point-foot landing metrics

Read the owning learning contract before choosing a task: G1, Digit or TRON1. A robot's gains, cadence and foot objectives should not transfer merely because another robot's recipe worked.

docs.title: A bounded G1 pipeline exercise
docs.text:
From the repository root, run this in a fresh output directory:

cd apps/unitree-g1
pixi run --locked -e learn task-check --device cpu --num-envs 2 \
  --steps 10 --ppo 1 --out artifacts/learning-smoke
pixi run --locked -e learn export-policy \
  --checkpoint artifacts/learning-smoke/model_smoke.pt \
  --out artifacts/learning-bundle --fixture-steps 30
pixi run --locked policy-parity artifacts/learning-bundle

This exercise checks the task, a small update, export and sampled convention parity. It is not enough training to produce a useful gait. The G1 learning validation describes the tested boundary and missing physical qualification.

For a substantive run, inspect the app's training options and resource requirements first:

pixi run --locked -e learn train --help
pixi run --locked -e learn evaluate --help
pixi run --locked -e learn play --help

Digit's OSC workflow explains container, scheduler and checkpoint ownership for cluster training. A submitted job or successful container startup is environment evidence, not a learning result.

docs.title: Preserve the comparison
docs.text:
Keep the baseline checkpoint, effective environment and agent configuration, source revision, model identity and evaluation schedule. For reward work, preserve the observation, action and PD contracts unless changing one is the explicit experiment. Use fixed evaluation conditions and report failures as well as tracking, stopping, effort and landing behavior.

An exporter can reject an old run because today's model or contract differs from the saved training configuration. Reproduce export from the matching source revision or deliberately reconcile the difference; do not remove the check just to obtain an ONNX file.

docs.title: What parity does and does not establish
docs.text: Replay parity compares the trainer's recorded observation, inference, decoding and action-realization chain with deployment. It catches frame, ordering, scaling and control-law mismatches. Physical evaluation asks whether the target Plant receives suitable commands and achieves the behavior under its timing and actuation assumptions. Both are needed before making a deployment claim.

docs.title: Evaluate an experiment
docs.text: A useful experiment answers a specific question under known conditions. Preserve a baseline, change the intended variable and decide which observations would support or reject the claim. Save enough context that someone else can explain the result without replaying the conversation that produced it.

docs.title: Completion is one measurement
docs.text:
Recorded October 1 simulation. Hollow circles are per-run plateau velocities; squares are medians of three seeds. This predates the current drive model and teaches how to read evidence, rather than rank today's controllers.

Open full-size plot

The policy's median shortfall is about 0.064 m/s, or 32% of the command, despite all three runs completing. That observation identifies a tracking question. It does not identify the cause, establish acceptable stopping or qualify the controller on other terrain. The figure capsule and retained source data make the numbers inspectable.

docs.title: Write the comparison before running it
docs.text:
Record Example Question Does a planner change improve stopping in this flat scenario? Baseline Exact source revision, resolved config and existing outcome Intended change One app profile or one owning implementation change Held fixed Model, terrain, actuation, state source, shared gains, seed and command schedule Outcomes Completion/fall/timeout, tracking, stopping, effort and constraint diagnostics Evidence location Separate ignored artifact directories for each arm

If a comparison necessarily changes several things, name them. Swapping ALIP for DCM deliberately changes a planner profile and reference contract. Running two different default scenarios also changes the motion schedule, so it cannot isolate the planner.

docs.title: Read the artifact at several boundaries
docs.text:
First compare the commanded and measured behavior. Then inspect the reference that was authored and the reference actually installed. Finally inspect estimated state, contact evidence, actuator saturation, constraint/fallback diagnostics and timing where they bear on the question.

Keep diagnostic truth separate from controller inputs. Align channels by their recorded timestamps and schema, rather than assuming row number means the same instant across streams. A viewer can reveal a suspicious event, but a decimated scene stream may omit the peak or transition needed to explain it.

For a Digit walking log, run the app-owned plotter from apps/digit:

pixi run --locked plot-walking artifacts/experiment/baseline.h5 \
  -o artifacts/experiment/baseline-plots

Use a separate output directory for the candidate. The running guide explains logging choices; the app validation records acceptance criteria and prior evidence.

docs.title: Keep evidence proportional to the claim
docs.text:
A single run can demonstrate a failure or help diagnose a mechanism. It generally cannot establish a broad operating envelope. Preserve all selected outcomes, state the number of seeds and scenarios, and distinguish a measured improvement from an untested explanation.

Working logs, plots and notebooks stay in ignored artifacts/. Promote a figure into a bounded evidence capsule when a maintained document needs it. Keep the reduced data, renderer, source revision and limitations together. A figure that survives without its conditions is easy to misuse.

docs.title: Give an agent a bounded task
docs.text:
Reproduce this Digit baseline, then compare the candidate on the same scenario and seeds. Preserve the robot model, state source, actuation, command schedule and shared calibration. Inspect commanded versus measured velocity, installed references, saturation, stopping and failures. Keep each arm's artifacts separate and report what the evidence establishes before proposing another change.

The deliverable is a result you can assess: a small set of annotated figures, a comparison table and a conclusion with a clear boundary.

docs.title: Remote development and viewers
docs.text:
Use the Ubuntu execution host for builds, simulation, GPU training and artifacts. You can work directly on that machine or connect from a Linux, Windows or macOS client through SSH. A browser viewer needs no local robot build. The examples below use ubuntu-workstation as an SSH alias; substitute the host configured for your account.

Where you work Where to run Pixi Where to open the viewer At the Ubuntu machine Its local terminal Its local browser or desktop Through VS Code Remote - SSH The remote integrated terminal Your client browser, with the reported port forwarded Through a plain SSH session The remote shell; use tmux for persistent work Your client browser, with an SSH local port forward

Evidence is stated for each viewer path below. Browser/tunnel recipes are independent of owning a MacBook; a successful SSH connection alone does not establish GPU setup or working display access. This guide covers project execution and viewing, not personal laptop or operating-system provisioning.

docs.title: Code And Agent Sessions
docs.text:
Open the Ubuntu checkout through VS Code's Remote-SSH: Connect to Host. Use the remote integrated terminal for agents and Pixi commands; verify hostname, pwd and git status --short there. Install/authenticate agent CLIs on Ubuntu. For extensions, check their documented remote support and actual execution location rather than assuming every extension runs remotely. VS Code documents remote terminals and extension placement.

Use the same Ubuntu user and checkout when working at the desktop. For a CLI session that must survive a client disconnect, run it inside tmux and reattach from the next terminal. Native agent resume can continue a saved session on that host; cross-agent continuity uses the task handoff. Reconnecting to Ubuntu does not require synchronizing source to a client-side clone.

Follow the development workflow to choose the command owner. Keep each root or project pixi.toml with its own pixi.lock in Git. On a new checkout, install the root environment with pixi install --locked and run root pixi run --locked orient; then use the owning robot project's manifest for its build, viewer and standalone check. Learning uses that project's learn environment. The root and robot default environments target macOS ARM64 and Linux x86-64; learning platform requirements remain in each project's manifest and validation.

Each host owns its environments, builds, credentials and local agent state. Project .pixi/config.toml files are tracked configuration that place environments in Pixi's cache; transfer that configuration, not the generated environments or CMake build trees. Retain essential instructions, skills and decisions in repository-owned files. Do not make correct continuation depend on plugins installed only on the other computer.

For occasional development on another supported host, transfer the task branch and handoff together using the handoff protocol. Store source references relative to the repository; record host plus path for artifacts outside Git. Keep long-run artifacts on Ubuntu or explicit artifact storage, with producing commit, command and checksums where needed for replay.

docs.title: Interactive Viewers
docs.text:
SSH supplies the terminal connection. A desktop graphics session or a streamed viewer is a separate connection. Prefer these paths:

Need Simulation/render host Client display path Full MuJoCo UI, picking and perturbations Ubuntu desktop graphics session Remote desktop with verified GPU acceleration Existing Digit walking scene and telemetry Ubuntu simulation, client browser rendering Rerun web page over one forwarded TCP port, Tailscale or a private LAN Digit walking scene only, any planner, nothing installed on the client Ubuntu simulation and viser server, client browser rendering viser web page over a forwarded TCP port Trained mjlab policy, with command sliders and checkpoint switching Ubuntu simulation and policy, client browser rendering viser web page over a forwarded TCP port Isaac Sim / Isaac Lab viewport Ubuntu NVIDIA GPU Isaac Sim WebRTC client compatible with installed version

MuJoCo rendering needs an OpenGL context. EGL/OSMesa support offscreen rendering; they do not transport an interactive window to a remote client. Qualify a GPU-capable remote desktop for the full UI instead of making X11 forwarding the default. Launch the app from a terminal inside that desktop session so it receives the correct display context. See MuJoCo visualization.

docs.title: Digit Rerun In A Browser
docs.text:
From the Ubuntu checkout's Digit project (apps/digit), add --rerun-web to any run:

cd apps/digit
pixi run walk --config alip_walking --vx 0.3 --walk-duration 6 --rerun-web

Then open http://localhost:9090 on the client, the same link every time. As with the viser page, one TCP port carries everything: forward 9090 with VS Code's Ports view or ssh -N -L 9090:127.0.0.1:9090 ubuntu-workstation. To use Tailscale or a private LAN directly instead, add --web-bind 0.0.0.0 (or Ubuntu's Tailscale address) and open http://<ubuntu-tailscale-name>:9090. The Ubuntu process serves its bundled Rerun web viewer and installs the current walking dashboard, including robot meshes, textured terrain, sky-blue background, base-following camera and telemetry plots. The client needs no repository checkout or local Rerun/Pixi installation; the first visit downloads the 50 MB viewer, which the browser caches.

The Rerun server listens only on Ubuntu loopback. A launcher-owned relay on port 9090 (--web-port) serves the page and forwards the viewer's gRPC-web telemetry from the server's loopback port 9876 (--port), so both share one origin. Its / redirects to the viewer pointed back at whatever address the browser used. Its default bind is loopback. After simulation completion, keep the launch terminal open to inspect or scrub the recording; Ctrl+C closes the server it started. If a launch reports its port in use, an earlier launch is usually still serving playback: stop it with Ctrl+C rather than choosing new ports, and the link stays the same. The app still logs HDF5 on Ubuntu. The native workflow below remains available when preferred.

The browser's plot channels are sampled at up to 50 Hz to keep ingestion manageable; its robot scene is also 50 Hz. HDF5 retains the full 1 kHz Servo telemetry. The native modes below retain full scalar drill-down; use those or the stored artifact to investigate faster signals.

Verified 2026-10-12 on Ubuntu Chrome over the workstation's private Tailscale address: the ALIP run completes and the web viewer renders the robot, terrain, background and dashboard plots. Rendering on other client platforms and network latency remain to be checked from the Mac; see the walking validation.

The one-port relay was verified the same day on Ubuntu only, with headless Chrome on loopback. http://127.0.0.1:<web-port> redirected to the viewer, which rendered the robot, terrain and live dashboard through the relay. In the same browser it ingested about as fast as the server's own page, and the 50 MB viewer download took 0.12 s against 0.10 s direct. The relay path from another client, by forward or Tailscale, is untested.

docs.title: Native Digit Rerun On A Client
docs.text:
This uses the existing launcher and observer; it is observation-only and does not provide MuJoCo mouse perturbations or interactive control. Use matching Rerun versions from compatible lockfile revisions on both hosts. Replace ubuntu-workstation with your configured SSH alias. Run the following from the client's local checkout/terminal, not a VS Code remote terminal. It uses the repository's root environment, which has Rerun, so the client does not build the Digit project:

pixi run python apps/digit/walking/tools/walk.py --rerun --attach-only

That opens the local viewer and blueprint without starting the simulation or requiring a local walking binary. In another local client terminal, keep this reverse tunnel open:

ssh -N -o ExitOnForwardFailure=yes \
  -R 127.0.0.1:9876:127.0.0.1:9876 ubuntu-workstation

From the Ubuntu checkout's Digit project (apps/digit) in the remote terminal, after building the walking target described in RUNNING.md:

cd apps/digit
pixi run walk --headless \
  --rerun-connect rerun+http://127.0.0.1:9876/proxy

The launcher activates the walking dashboard in the existing client viewer, including its close robot camera and sky-blue background, through the same endpoint used by the C++ observer. The Ubuntu observer connects to Ubuntu loopback port 9876, which SSH forwards to the client viewer. The Ubuntu SSH server must permit remote forwarding and the port must be free there. Do not add --rerun on Ubuntu for this recipe: that would spawn a viewer on Ubuntu. For simultaneous runs choose a distinct viewer/tunnel port and update all three commands consistently. Keep the client viewer and tunnel open while observing; simulation and HDF5 logging stay on Ubuntu. Re-establish the tunnel and check live delivery after reconnecting.

docs.title: Digit Walking In The Browser
docs.text:
Experimental. This shows the Plant scene only: robot, terrain and foot-corner contact forces, with no plots and no interaction with the simulation. It needs no Rerun version match and no local checkout. From the Ubuntu checkout's Digit project (apps/digit) in the remote terminal:

cd apps/digit
pixi run walk --viser --vx 0.5 --walk-duration 8

Then open http://localhost:8080 on the client, after forwarding the port with VS Code's Ports view or from a plain client terminal:

ssh -N -L 8080:127.0.0.1:8080 ubuntu-workstation

The simulation, the viewer process and the session log all stay on Ubuntu. The app copies its scene to the viewer over Ubuntu loopback UDP, and the browser receives poses over one websocket. The page binds 127.0.0.1 unless --viser-host 0.0.0.0 is given. The first load downloads about 3–5 MB of geometry; a live run then needs about 70 kB/s. The page keeps the whole run for scrubbing after it ends, and pixi run python walking/tools/viser_view.py --log RUN.h5 in apps/digit replays a saved log the same way. See the walking RUNNING.md.

Verified 2026-10-12 on Ubuntu only, with headless Chrome on the same host: DCM on flat ground and up-stairs, and the cadence policy on flat ground, drew correctly live and in replay, with zero dropped scene records. The SSH-forwarded client-browser path was not covered by that check.

docs.title: mjlab Policies In The Browser
docs.text:
The Digit project's play task can serve mjlab's viser viewer, a web page that draws the scene in the browser with WebGL. Ubuntu steps the simulation and the policy and sends body poses over a websocket, so an ordinary TCP forward carries it; no video is streamed. It shows a trained policy, not training: mjlab's training script has no live viewer.

From the Ubuntu checkout's Digit project (apps/digit) in the remote terminal:

cd apps/digit
pixi run -e learn play Digit-Velocity-Flat-1ms --viewer viser \
  --checkpoint-file learning/checkpoints/runs/digit_velocity/RUN/model_N.pt

Then open http://localhost:8080 on the client. VS Code Remote - SSH forwards the port from its Ports view. From a plain client terminal, forward it yourself:

ssh -N -L 8080:127.0.0.1:8080 ubuntu-workstation
  • Pass --viewer viser explicitly. mjlab's default picks its native MuJoCo window whenever DISPLAY is set, and on the workstation that window opens on the Ubuntu desktop's screen.
  • The page has velocity-command sliders, reward-term plots, environment switching, and the run's checkpoints to load while it plays.
  • viser listens on all interfaces (0.0.0.0:8080), so other machines on the workstation's network can reach it. Use it on a trusted network or firewall the port.
  • When the client reaches the workstation over Tailscale, use the workstation's Tailscale name or 100.x address, for the tunnel or directly as http://<tailscale-name>:8080. Its LAN address is not routable from another network: ssh -N to it hangs silently, which looks the same as a working tunnel.
  • For periodic clips during training instead, the train task accepts mjlab's --video True; it records one environment under the run's videos/train/.

Verified 2026-09-28 on Ubuntu: the server started with the M0 policy and served its page on port 8080. Verified 2026-10-06: a macOS browser over Tailscale played the cadence policy from Ubuntu. The --video option is untested.

docs.title: Isaac Streaming
docs.text:
Here, Isaac means Isaac Sim and the viewport used by Isaac Lab, not a new repository dependency.
