Use the streaming entry point documented for the installed Isaac version; check the matching Isaac Lab AppLauncher options if launching a Lab application. NVIDIA provides a macOS WebRTC client and a web viewer. The host needs a supported NVIDIA GPU/driver and NVENC for streaming.

Use the port and protocol requirements for the installed NVIDIA version. Ordinary SSH TCP forwarding does not carry a UDP media stream. Use an appropriate private LAN/VPN route and the installed version's networking instructions; keep endpoints on a trusted network. Host support, encoding and client compatibility must be checked before choosing exact launch flags. See NVIDIA livestream clients.

docs.title: First Workstation Verification
docs.text:
Record host, OS, GPU/driver, agent versions, Git revision and relevant simulator and viewer versions in the active setup handoff. Verify:

  1. The remote VS Code terminal and agent operate on the intended Ubuntu clone.
  2. The scoped Pixi install/build succeeds and orientation finds the handoff.
  3. The same agent session can be resumed after reconnecting; the other agent can recover the goal and next step from the repository handoff.
  4. The chosen viewer displays live motion. For the full UI, test camera/picking or interaction; for Rerun, test scene and telemetry receipt separately.
  5. Disconnect/reconnect behavior and artifact locations are understood. Keep viewer observations distinct from control behavior or timing qualification.

Headless internal validation and training remain appropriate. When offering commands for human inspection, include the applicable interactive display path.

docs.title: Running Digit Learning at OSC: Architecture and Workflow
docs.text: This is the orientation for someone new to running code on a cluster. It explains what the pieces at the Ohio Supercomputer Center (OSC) are, how a training run travels from the workstation to a GPU and back, and what to do after each kind of change. The exact, checked procedure is the OSC deployment guide; what has been demonstrated, with job IDs and checksums, is in VALIDATION.md. Where this document and the guide differ, the guide wins.

docs.title: The Core Idea
docs.text:
OSC is a shared building of thousands of computers. Nobody runs heavy work on them directly. You write a request: "one GPU, 8 CPU cores and 64 GB of memory for 5 hours, and run this command". A scheduler called Slurm queues the request with everyone else's and starts the command on a free machine when its turn comes. You are not watching when it runs; everything the program prints goes to a log file you read during or after the run.

On the workstation the GPU sits idle whenever nobody is using it. On a cluster the scheduler keeps every GPU busy by making jobs wait their turn. The wait is the price of having hundreds of GPUs.

docs.title: The Pieces
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    WS["Ubuntu workstation<br/>edit, commit, bundle"]
    subgraph OSC["OSC: Ascend and Cardinal share storage"]
        TR["Transfer host<br/>sftp.osc.edu, files only"]
        LN["Login node<br/>submit and monitor"]
        Q["Slurm queue<br/>waits for resources"]
        subgraph CN["Compute node, GPU or CPU"]
            C["Container image (SIF)<br/>locked Python environment"]
            W["/workspace<br/>your checkout, mounted"]
        end
        ST[("Home and scratch storage")]
    end
    WS -- "rsync" --> TR
    TR --> ST
    WS -- "ssh" --> LN
    LN -- "sbatch" --> Q
    Q -- "starts job" --> CN
    CN -- "logs, checkpoints" --> ST
Machine Analogy What you do there SSH alias on the workstation Workstation Your desk Edit and commit code, pack it, upload it, evaluate results Transfer host (sftp.osc.edu) Loading dock Copy files in and out; it cannot submit jobs osc-transfer Login node Front desk Look at files, submit and check jobs. It is shared by everyone, so never train or build here osc-ascend, osc-cardinal Slurm Booking system Holds each request until resources are free, then starts it Compute node Lab bench Runs the job. You never log in to it; Slurm puts your command there

Ascend and Cardinal are two separate clusters, each with its own login nodes and queue. Ascend's GPUs are A100s (40 GB); Cardinal's are H100s (93 GB), and Cardinal also has CPU-only nodes. They share the same home and scratch storage, so anything uploaded once is visible from both. Every request is charged to the project account pas2483.

docs.title: Where Files Live
docs.text:
Place Path Use it for Caution Home /users/PAS2483/hereidayonga (~, $HOME) Code checkouts, container images, job logs Moderate quota; backed up Scratch /fs/scratch/PAS2483/hereidayonga Training runs, checkpoints, anything large Not backed up and purged over time; copy keepers home Job temporary $TMPDIR inside a job Caches a job needs only while it runs Deleted when the job ends

Everything for this repository sits in one folder in each place, so the home directory stays readable and other projects stay separate:

~/cyber-suite/
  images/      container images, cyber-learn-<lock>.sif and its .sha256
  checkouts/   one clean Git clone per run, named <topic>-<commit>
  inbox/       bundles and files arriving from the workstation; delete once unpacked
  logs/        Slurm logs, named <job-name>-<job-id>.out
/fs/scratch/PAS2483/hereidayonga/cyber-suite/
  runs/<experiment>/<run>/   all training output, including runs to resume from

Pass --output=$HOME/cyber-suite/logs/%x-%j.out to every sbatch (%x is the job name, %j its ID) and --log-root /fs/scratch/PAS2483/hereidayonga/cyber-suite/runs to every training command, and the layout keeps itself.

docs.title: Slurm: Asking for a Machine
docs.text:
A job is submitted with sbatch. The training request of 2026-10-14, part by part:

Part Meaning sbatch Schedule this job -A pas2483 The account the hours are charged to -p gpu The partition: a queue for one kind of machine. Cardinal has gpu, cpu and debug; Ascend has nextgen, longgpu and debug-nextgen --time=05:00:00 Hard limit. At 5 hours Slurm stops the job, finished or not --cpus-per-task=8 --mem=64G CPU cores and memory. job.sh itself asks for one GPU --job-name=digit-drives-ft The name shown in the queue --output=$HOME/cyber-suite/logs/%x-%j.out Where everything printed goes; %x becomes the job name and %j the job ID --dependency=afterok:15517536 Start only after that job finished successfully job.sh IMAGE CHECKOUT -- COMMAND Run COMMAND inside the container, with CHECKOUT mounted at /workspace and the Digit project (/workspace/apps/digit) as its working folder

A job moves through these states:

State Meaning PENDING Waiting. The reason column says why: Priority (others are ahead), Resources (next in line, waiting for a machine to free up), Dependency (waiting for another job) RUNNING On a compute node now COMPLETED Finished with exit code 0 FAILED The command exited with an error; read the log TIMEOUT Hit its time limit CANCELLED Stopped with scancel (or by an administrator)

How long a job waits depends on how busy the partition is and on the account's priority. Priority drops as the account uses more hours recently ("fair share"). Shorter time limits start sooner, because the scheduler can fit them into gaps before big jobs it has already planned ("backfill"). The debug partitions take jobs of at most one hour and start them quickly; they are meant for tests, not training.

docs.title: The Container
docs.text:
OSC's machines run Red Hat Linux with OSC's software. Training needs exact versions of Python, PyTorch, CUDA, MuJoCo Warp and mjlab. The container image, a single .sif file of about 3.5 GB, is a sealed box holding that environment. Apptainer, the HPC counterpart of Docker that needs no administrator rights, opens it on the compute node.

In the image Not in the image The Digit project's learn Pixi environment, installed from apps/digit/pixi.toml and apps/digit/pixi.lock Any repository source code cyber-learn-exec, the launcher (learn-exec.sh) Checkpoints, runs, terrain banks Git, for training provenance Compiled C++ from this repository

At run time job.sh mounts a checkout at /workspace inside the container, and Python imports digit_learning from there. Two consequences follow:

  • Code changes need no new image. Only a change to apps/digit/pixi.lock, learn.def or learn-exec.sh does. The launcher compares the checkout's apps/digit/pixi.lock with the one baked into the image and refuses to start on a mismatch, so a run can never silently use different packages than its commit records.
  • The checkout is live, not copied. A queued job runs whatever its checkout holds when it starts, and a running one can import later edits. Never change a checkout a queued or running job uses; make a new checkout per run.

Images are named for the lock they bake: cyber-learn-489340876024.sif holds the Digit project lock whose SHA-256 starts 489340876024. A .sif.sha256 file beside each image lets sha256sum -c prove the bytes are intact. Several images can sit side by side in images/, one per lock still in use. Since 2026-10-17 the project-lock image serves migrated checkouts; the older cyber-learn-68b626462c4e.sif remains for the pre-project drives-5fcea50 checkout. Delete an image, with its .sha256, only once no checkout you still run has its lock.

docs.title: What Each Change Requires
docs.text: What changed What OSC needs Learning code, rewards, task configs, docs A new or updated checkout: send a Git bundle (below) job.sh Nothing more; jobs run the checkout's own copy apps/digit/pixi.lock (a dependency added or updated) A new image, built at OSC (below), and a smoke job learn.def or learn-exec.sh A new image and a smoke job Nothing, but a new run A fresh run name; reuse the checkout and image

docs.title: 1. Send the Code
docs.text:
The workstation packs committed history into a Git bundle, a single file that the transfer host carries into the inbox. A bundle holds commits only, so commit first; uncommitted edits do not travel.

git bundle create /tmp/cyber-suite-BRANCH.bundle BRANCH
rsync -a /tmp/cyber-suite-BRANCH.bundle osc-transfer:~/cyber-suite/inbox/

On a login node, clone it into a new checkout named for its topic and commit, then delete the bundle:

git clone -b BRANCH ~/cyber-suite/inbox/cyber-suite-BRANCH.bundle ~/cyber-suite/checkouts/TOPIC-COMMIT
git -C ~/cyber-suite/checkouts/TOPIC-COMMIT rev-parse HEAD

Later commits can travel as a small incremental bundle (git bundle create x.bundle OLD..BRANCH), fetched into a checkout that no job is using: git fetch x.bundle BRANCH && git merge --ff-only FETCH_HEAD. Inputs Git ignores, such as a checkpoint to resume from, go through the inbox as well; place them in the scratch run tree, where a resumed run looks for them (runs/<experiment>/<run>/model_N.pt).

docs.title: 2. Build an Image, Only When Dependencies Change
docs.text: Since 2026-10-14 the workstation cannot build the image: Ubuntu 24.04's AppArmor setting blocks the unprivileged build. It is built at OSC instead, from the checkout, in a Cardinal CPU job (about 3 minutes); the image lands in the shared home, so nothing large crosses the network. The command is in the deployment guide.

docs.title: 3. Smoke, Then Train
docs.text:
A smoke job is a one- or two-minute run on a debug partition that proves the image, the GPU, the scratch path and the task work together before hours are spent. Chaining the training to it with --dependency=afterok:SMOKE_ID queues both at once: training starts only if the smoke passes. A training command looks like the one in the worked example; every run writes to its own folder under scratch through --log-root.

Choose the time limit from the expected run length plus a margin, not a large round number: a longer limit waits longer in the queue. A run that hits its limit is not lost. It saves a checkpoint every 50 iterations and can continue with --agent.resume True --agent.load-run RUN_FOLDER --agent.load-checkpoint model_N.pt.

docs.title: 4. Watch and Collect
docs.text:
Log out freely; jobs keep running. Check them from a login node or from OSC OnDemand, OSC's web portal, whose file browser, active-jobs page and browser terminal need no setup. When a run ends, confirm COMPLETED with sacct and read the end of its log, then copy the run folder home through the transfer host:

rsync -a osc-transfer:/fs/scratch/PAS2483/hereidayonga/cyber-suite/runs/EXPERIMENT/RUN learning/checkpoints/runs/EXPERIMENT/

Evaluation and export then run on the workstation as for a local run: evaluate, export-policy, policy-parity (VALIDATION.md). The tools read the task from the run's saved configuration.

docs.title: Worked Example: the Drive Fine-Tune
docs.text:
The 2026-10-14 run fine-tuned model_16800 under the LLAPI drive model for 2000 iterations (VALIDATION.md, 2026-10-14 entries). It ran before OSC was organized into the layout above; the paths below are where its pieces live now.

Step Where What Pack Workstation Bundle of branch claude/hardware-deployment-ui-b4220c (87 MB) and model_16800.pt Upload Transfer host Both into home; SHA-256 checked on arrival Unpack Ascend login node Checkout ~/cyber-suite/checkouts/drives-5fcea50; checkpoint copied to /fs/scratch/PAS2483/hereidayonga/cyber-suite/runs/digit_velocity_cadence/2026-10-12_20-32-06_arm-refine-r1/ Image Cardinal cpu node Job 15516729 failed (apt under OSC's fakeroot); fixed in learn.def; job 15516744 built ~/cyber-suite/images/cyber-learn-68b626462c4e.sif Update Ascend login node The fix arrived as an incremental bundle; the checkout fast-forwarded to 5fcea50, clean Smoke Ascend debug-nextgen, Cardinal debug Jobs 7841114 (A100) and 15517536 (H100) passed Train Cardinal gpu Job 15517537, after the smoke. Ascend job 7841309 waited on priority and was cancelled before it started

The training command at the historical 5fcea50 checkout uses its root working directory and root-lock image. For current project paths and images, follow the deployment guide:

SRC=$HOME/cyber-suite/checkouts/drives-5fcea50
sbatch -A pas2483 -p gpu --time=05:00:00 --cpus-per-task=8 --mem=64G \
  --job-name=digit-drives-ft --output=$HOME/cyber-suite/logs/%x-%j.out \
  $SRC/apps/digit/learning/container/job.sh \
  $HOME/cyber-suite/images/cyber-learn-68b626462c4e.sif $SRC -- \
  python apps/digit/learning/tools/train.py Digit-Velocity-Flat-Cadence-1ms-Drives \
  --env.scene.num-envs 4096 --log-root /fs/scratch/PAS2483/hereidayonga/cyber-suite/runs \
  --agent.experiment-name digit_velocity_cadence --agent.resume True \
  --agent.load-run 2026-10-12_20-32-06_arm-refine-r1 --agent.load-checkpoint model_16800.pt \
  --agent.max-iterations 2000 --agent.run-name drives-ft

The run reuses the experiment name digit_velocity_cadence because mjlab looks for the checkpoint to resume inside the experiment's own folder.

docs.title: Commands at a Glance
docs.text:
Run these on a login node (ssh osc-cardinal or ssh osc-ascend) unless the column says otherwise.

Command What it does squeue -u $USER Your waiting and running jobs squeue -j JOB --start Slurm's estimated start time for a pending job sacct -j JOB -X --format=JobID,State,ExitCode,Elapsed,NodeList A job's final state, also after it ends tail -f ~/cyber-suite/logs/NAME-JOB.out Follow a log live; Ctrl+C stops watching, not the job scancel JOB Cancel a job sinfo -p PARTITION How busy a partition's nodes are sha256sum -c FILE.sha256 Prove an uploaded file arrived intact rsync -a FILE osc-transfer:~/cyber-suite/inbox/ (workstation) Upload a file to the inbox exit Log out; jobs keep running

docs.title: Rules of Thumb
docs.text:
• Never train, build or run anything heavy on a login node.
  • Keep everything for this repository under ~/cyber-suite/ and the scratch cyber-suite/runs/; empty the inbox after unpacking.
  • One checkout per run, named <topic>-<commit>; never edit a checkout a queued or running job uses.
  • Write runs to scratch with --log-root, and copy anything worth keeping home.
  • Smoke-test every new image on the GPU type that will train with it.
  • Ask for the time a run needs plus a margin; resume rather than over-ask.
  • Check a job's outcome with sacct and its log before believing it.

docs.title: When Something Goes Wrong
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix Log says "The checkout apps/digit/pixi.lock differs from this image" The checkout's dependencies differ from the image's Build an image from that checkout (step 2); never bypass the check PENDING (Priority) for hours Busy partition, low fair share Wait, shorten the time limit, or use the other cluster PENDING (DependencyNeverSatisfied) The job it depends on failed Read that job's log, fix, resubmit both; scancel the stuck one TIMEOUT The run outgrew its limit Resume from its last model_N.pt Image build: Couldn't create temporary file /tmp/apt.conf... apt under fakeroot without subordinate IDs Fixed in learn.def on 2026-10-14; rebuild from a checkout at or after 5fcea50 Workstation build: "Failed to create mount namespace" Ubuntu 24.04 blocks unprivileged user namespaces Build at OSC instead torch.cuda.is_available() is false The job has no GPU, or the container lacks --nv Submit to a GPU partition through job.sh, which passes --nv and asks for one GPU

docs.title: Digit
docs.text: Digit is the integrated worked example for Cyber Suite. Its project connects robot modeling and standing IK, model-based walking, policy learning, CORTA execution, recorded analysis and the Agility low-level interface. Use it to understand how the shared pieces compose before adapting the pattern to another robot.

docs.title: Choose a workflow
docs.text: Goal Start here Understand the full loop Student handbook Run walking with a viewer Digit running guide Understand planner and controller ownership Model-based walking Train, inspect and export a policy Learning workflow and learning contract Run learning on the cluster OSC architecture and workflow Inspect the standing solve or simple simulation composition IK contract and simulation contract

docs.title: Work from the project
docs.text:
Run Digit tasks from apps/digit or select its manifest explicitly. The default environment contains the compiled package boundary; learn contains the training environment. Use pixi task list and pixi task list -e learn to discover current tasks.

cd apps/digit
pixi run --locked build --target digit_corta_walking
pixi run --locked walk --config alip_walking --rerun-web

For a Mac browser, forward the viewer's printed port from Ubuntu. The remote guide distinguishes the simulation host from the display client.

docs.title: Simulation and deployment
docs.text:
The MuJoCo Plant and LLAPI Plant let the app reach different execution environments. LLAPI is used against Agility's simulator as well as being the interface intended for a robot. State-source selection, operation-mode handover, drive damping and command delay remain explicit parts of the experiment. Simulation/interface evidence does not establish complete simulator equivalence or physical-hardware qualification.

Current behavior belongs to the walking app contract. The walking validation and learning validation identify the controllers, revisions, conditions and remaining limits behind a result.

docs.title: A useful first contribution
docs.text: Reproduce one baseline, annotate the command-versus-response plot and identify a question at one boundary: planning, reference execution, state estimation, policy realization or Plant actuation. Put robot-specific tuning and scenarios in this project. Move reusable behavior to a shared module only when its contract and consumers justify it.

docs.title: Unitree G1
docs.text: G1 is the student-project starting point. It uses the repository's 23-DoF model and owns standing, walking, viewers and a learning pipeline in an independent Pixi project. The goal is to give a student a bounded experiment they can understand and extend, using Digit as the fuller integrated example.

docs.title: Start with a visible baseline
docs.text:
cd apps/unitree-g1
pixi run --locked stand --viser

The launcher builds and runs on the execution host. Open its printed browser URL, forwarding the port if your Mac is the client. The G1 running guide covers live walking, recordings and acceptance reporting.

Use the learning workflow for a small task/export/parity exercise before starting a longer training experiment. The app's contract is explicitly 23 DoF; a different upstream G1 asset or policy layout is a different experiment.

docs.title: Make it your project
docs.text:
The student-project guide exports the committed G1 source and licensed robot assets into an independent repository, pins shared dependencies and records provenance. The new project owns its subsequent configuration, experiments and validation. It does not require copying the whole Cyber Suite monorepo.

Good starting questions include understanding the observation/action mapping, evaluating a trained policy on a fixed command schedule, or explaining a walking tracking failure from recorded signals. Name the baseline and evidence before asking an agent to modify behavior.

docs.title: Read the qualification boundary
docs.text: The walking contract and validation distinguish model/standing evidence from walking acceptance. The learning contract and validation distinguish a bounded training/export pipeline from a qualified learned gait. Completing a visible run or passing parity is not a substitute for those physical evaluations.

docs.title: TRON1
docs.text: TRON1 explores walking and learning with six actuated joints and two point feet. It shares the project's ownership and evaluation principles, but its geometry changes what standing, stepping and landing mean. Robot-specific assumptions from Digit should be reviewed before reuse.

docs.title: Two research paths
docs.text:
The model-based walking app composes sensor-shaped observations, state estimation, the shared walking coordinator, ALIP or DCM, and whole-body control. The point-foot composition uses continuous stepping; a zero velocity request should not be interpreted as a certified flat-foot standing mode.

The learning app owns the point-foot task, rewards, training, playback and export. Landing metrics use the foot sphere's contact geometry, rather than Digit's heel/toe corners. Cadence, body height and actuator assumptions remain robot-specific.

docs.title: Work from the project
docs.text:
cd apps/tron1
pixi task list
pixi task list -e learn

Use the app's running instructions for the selected model-based or learned workflow. For policy inspection, the learning contract supplies a Viser command and checkpoint selection; the remote guide explains forwarding the browser port.

docs.title: Evaluate the physical behavior
docs.text:
Compare command tracking, direction and yaw behavior, alternation of steps, stopping and point-foot touchdown speed/load. Mean speed and upright trials alone do not establish gait quality. The walking validation and learning validation state the demonstrated boundaries; simulation torque settings are not verified hardware ratings.

A useful contribution is a matched analysis of one of those behaviors, preserving the baseline and the robot's own action/observation contract. The evaluation workflow provides the comparison structure.

docs.title: Terrain mapping
docs.text: The mapping app exercises sensing, registration, elevation fusion and geometric products independently of a walking controller. It is a useful place to study what the perception stack knows, where its errors come from and what a downstream consumer would receive.

docs.title: What the experiment contains
docs.text:
Sensors follow prescribed trajectories over known terrain. The app controls acquisition, injected pose errors, oracle comparisons and recorded output. Shared simulation code supplies sensor/terrain mechanisms; shared perception code supplies pose registration, fusion, geometric regions, costmaps and occupancy products.

This is a root-owned validation app rather than a separate robot Pixi project. Run its documented commands from the repository root. The app contract describes the composition and output, and validation gives the build/run commands, criteria and known failing cases.

docs.title: Inspect a saved result
docs.text:
After producing an output directory with the app's validation command:

pixi run python apps/perception/mapping/tools/view_results.py \
  artifacts/perception_mapping --scene up-stairs
pixi run python -m cyber_suite.perception.playback \
  artifacts/perception_mapping/up-stairs.h5 --inspect

The first command generates an overview and opens native Rerun on the execution host. Add --no-viewer when producing files remotely without a display. The second inspects the saved product timeline. Product playback preserves recorded maps; it does not rerun sensor acquisition or fusion.

docs.title: Questions this app can answer
docs.text:
Inspect observed versus oracle elevation, missing regions, registration errors, uncertainty and geometric support regions. Then check how a query behaves at observed, stale or unknown locations. Keep geometric correctness separate from contact friction/load authority and from a walking improvement.

The state and perception explanation connects these boundaries. Hardware calibration, autonomous localization and controller adoption require additional evidence beyond this standalone experiment.

docs.title: Development Workflow And Project Management
docs.text:
Cyber Suite develops a reusable package and robot projects in one repository. Use the primary checkout for serial work and reuse the current branch across related steps. Create a separate branch or worktree when isolation or review needs it, in the location the user chooses; a new branch is not required for every step. A robot project is a package consumer with its own Pixi manifest, while a worktree is a checkout of a Git branch. Creating or finishing a robot project does not require keeping a separate worktree.

This guide connects the shared agent instructions, project index, remote-development setup and handoff protocol. The owner contracts remain the authority for behavior and qualification.

docs.title: Start From The Actual Checkout
docs.text:
Read current status, then run these commands from the repository root on the execution host:

hostname
pwd -P
git status --short --branch
git worktree list
pixi run --locked orient

Read the owning MODULE.md or APP.md and its VALIDATION.md. For an unfinished task, read its one relevant handoff and compare the recorded branch, code checkpoint, dirty scope and evidence with the checkout. Orientation discovers project contracts, documentation and active handoffs in this checkout; it does not inventory unfinished work on other branches. Fetch and inspect branch relationships when preparing an integration, instead of treating an old plan or chat as current Git state.

Keep one active writer per task branch. Reuse the current task branch when continuing its work. Before switching an existing checkout to another task, inspect and preserve its dirty changes and check for running builds, viewers or training jobs that depend on its files. Keep unrelated work out of the task's commits. Creating a new worktree is an isolation choice, not a routine prerequisite for every task.

docs.title: Choose The Command Owner
docs.text:
Surface Run commands from Purpose Shared package, modules and root-owned validation apps Repository root Build reusable code, exercise in-tree integration, orient and audit documents Digit apps/digit Digit simulation, walking, IK and learning TRON1 apps/tron1 TRON1 walking, IK and learning Unitree G1 apps/unitree-g1 23-DoF standing, walking and learning; source for student exports Mapping validation Repository root apps/perception/mapping scenarios; this remains a root-owned app

Use pixi task list in the chosen folder to see its default commands and pixi task list -e learn for learning. Keep Pixi tasks for everyday build, launch, validation, plotting, learning and repository management; invoke specialist tools directly as listed below. A manifest path makes the owner explicit when invoking a project from the repository root:

pixi run --locked --manifest-path apps/digit/pixi.toml check
pixi run --locked --manifest-path apps/tron1/pixi.toml check
pixi run --locked --manifest-path apps/unitree-g1/pixi.toml check

Run these checks when the change affects project code, dependencies or runtime configuration; use the documentation checks below for prose-only edits. Project check builds against the installed cyber_suite package, which is the boundary an independent student repository uses. Root check configures, builds, runs CTest and audits the in-tree checkout. An in-tree pass alone does not establish that the installed package exposes everything a project needs.

Each project owns its manifest and lockfile. Its default environment contains the compiled package; pixi run -e learn ... uses its separate Python learning environment. Root robot launch aliases and a root learning environment are no longer the entry points. Preserve each manifest/lock pair, use --locked for reproducible checks, and deliberately regenerate the owning lockfile when dependencies change. Project environments are detached into Pixi's cache by their tracked .pixi/config.toml; do not transfer environments or reuse another checkout's CMake build directory.

docs.title: Specialist Tools
docs.text:
The task cleanup removes the aliases below, while retaining their implementations. Run the direct command from the indicated folder in its default environment unless -e learn is shown. Append the same tool arguments as before; Python script paths are relative to the owning project. Shared python -m cyber_suite... tools can also run in an installed robot-project environment, so analysis paths remain relative to that project. Use the tool's --help for its options.

Folder Former task Direct command Root or robot project corta-graph pixi run python -m cyber_suite.corta DUMP.json Root or robot project corta-timing pixi run python -m cyber_suite.corta.timing LOG.h5 Root or robot project corta-telemetry pixi run python -m cyber_suite.corta.telemetry LOG.h5 --list Root or robot project walk-audit pixi run python -m cyber_suite.control.audit.walking_log LOG.h5 Root or robot project perception-playback pixi run python -m cyber_suite.perception.playback LOG.h5 Root perception-view pixi run python apps/perception/mapping/tools/view_results.py OUTPUT_DIR Root g1-prepare-model pixi run python assets/robots/unitree_g1/tools/prepare_model.py apps/digit viser pixi run python walking/tools/viser_view.py --log LOG.h5 apps/digit sim-gap-compare pixi run python learning/tools/sim_gap_compare.py BUNDLE apps/digit (learn) sim-gap-record pixi run -e learn python learning/tools/sim_gap_record.py BUNDLE apps/digit (learn) export-hold-bundle pixi run -e learn python learning/tools/export_hold_bundle.py apps/tron1 verify-sensor-boundary pixi run python walking/tools/verify_sensor_boundary.py LOG.h5 apps/unitree-g1 view pixi run python walking/tools/view.py --run RUN_DIR

Prepare required inputs and binaries first: TRON1 sensor replay needs pixi run build, the simulation-gap tools need a policy bundle and recorded training rollouts, and model regeneration deliberately writes generated assets. Live viewers remain available through robot launch commands such as walk --viser; the direct viewer scripts serve inspection and replay. The model generator has no --help mode. Dated validation records and historical notes retain their original task names and revisions; use this table when replaying them with current tools.

docs.title: Keep Task State With Its Owner
docs.text:
Information Home How it is used Repository overview and shared rules docs/status/CURRENT.md, AGENTS.md, docs/policies/ Current orientation and authority Module behavior modules/<module>/MODULE.md and its validation Reusable API and demonstrated boundary Robot app behavior and acceptance apps/<robot>/<app>/APP.md and VALIDATION.md Project status; no duplicate per-project CURRENT.md Robot-only plans, investigations, ideas and handoffs apps/<robot>/notes/<category>/ Working or historical context Shared designs, cross-project work and repository tasks Root notes/<category>/ Working or historical context Consolidated research decisions Root notes/journal/ Historical rationale under the journal policy Bulk logs, plots, checkpoints and scratch work Ignored output owned by the producing workflow Evidence and replay inputs; preserve deliberately when transferring or retiring

Use a plan when the task needs staged work or unresolved design choices. Record its owner, dependencies, acceptance criteria and next action, and update the existing plan as those choices settle. Routine changes can proceed from the owning contract. A plan's completed phase is not a substitute for current validation, and a note never becomes authority simply by being written.

Before a requested pause, machine transfer or agent switch, update one task handoff in the owning note home using the handoff template. Record the actual revision plus any uncommitted delta, user decisions, evidence locations and next action. Commit and push only within the user's authorization; ignored evidence needs separate transfer. When the task finishes, fold lasting results into the owner and retire the handoff under the handoff rules.

docs.title: Validate The Changed Boundary
docs.text:
Change Evidence to collect Documentation or documentation organization Root pixi run --locked audit, orientation, changed links and git diff --check Shared C++ or package interface Owning module checks, affected in-tree integration and affected standalone project checks Robot project code or configuration That project's pixi run --locked check and the scenarios required by its VALIDATION.md Learning or policy export Owning learn tasks, saved configuration and the applicable policy-parity check Physical behavior App scenarios and artifact review against explicit completion, tracking, constraint and failure criteria

Use the smallest evidence that proves the change; do not add unit tests or run broad native/GPU sweeps for a documentation edit. Digit and TRON1 standalone checks run their existing CTest and Python contracts. G1 checks its installed-package build, model parity and bounded standing acceptance. Training, wider walking qualification and hardware validation remain separate.

Existing root CI runs the audit and root check on pull requests and pushes to main, with the build gate on Ubuntu and macOS. Project CI is optional. Run affected standalone checks manually before integration and report the command, platform, revision, result and remaining limits; a later project CI job can invoke the same check. Do not infer a green CI run from the workflow definition.

docs.title: Student Projects And Remote Execution
docs.text:
Unitree G1 is the student template. From the repository root, pixi run create-g1-project DESTINATION --revision COMMIT exports the committed project and its licensed asset snapshot, pins the C++ and Python dependencies to the same source revision and records provenance. Follow the student-project guide to generate a project lockfile, validate a fresh clone and upgrade dependencies. The exporter does not create or publish a remote repository, and no project CI workflow is required.

Ubuntu is the primary execution host; the MacBook normally connects through VS Code Remote - SSH. Verify the actual host and viewer connection using the remote-development guide. Code commits and lockfiles travel through Git; environments, credentials and ignored run data do not.

For Digit learning at OSC, follow the deployment guide and workflow explanation. The container must match apps/digit/pixi.lock; the former root learning lock is not the project environment. Record source revision, image checksum, input provenance, job ID and output location. Environment and GPU smokes establish deployment readiness, while training outcomes need their own evidence.

docs.title: Integrate And Retire Worktrees
docs.text:
Integration brings a branch's commits into main; removing a worktree only removes its checkout. Branch deletion and remote publication are separate actions. Keep them explicit in the requested scope.

  1. Inspect the primary checkout, task branch, remote state and uncommitted changes. Review the diff and validation for the exact commits to integrate. Preserve unrelated work before changing branches; do not replace a checkout's branch with a hard reset.
  2. Integrate through the authorized review path. The authorization rules require maintainer-approved pull requests for changes to authority. After integration, verify that the intended commits are reachable from main, check the resulting diff and run the validation warranted by any conflict resolution. Report the resulting commit and push state separately.
  3. Before removing a secondary checkout, stop or move processes that use it and move the active agent session out of it. Inventory its tracked changes, untracked files and ignored output. A clean git status does not account for ignored artifacts or commits absent from main.
  4. Preserve needed evidence, checkpoints, logs and other local files outside the checkout being retired. Keep provenance with the producing commit, command and checksums or a verified inventory. Keep bulk evidence ignored; publish a bounded capsule only when a maintained document needs its figure. A named branch or verified Git bundle can retain unmerged commits, but neither saves uncommitted files or ignored output.
  5. Run the repository's retirement report from a retained checkout, resolve its findings and separately inspect output outside its scan. Then remove only the intended secondary checkout using its managing app's archive operation or git worktree remove where appropriate. Review git worktree list afterward; prune stale registrations only after establishing that their directories are gone. Retain branch refs unless their deletion is explicitly requested.

Use the read-only report with an explicit target and comparison base:

pixi run --locked retire-worktree --worktree /absolute/path/to/secondary-checkout \
  --base main --include-data --list-files

The report checks unmerged commits, dirty/untracked files, selected evidence types under root artifacts/, logs/ and build/, and agent-history locations. It does not archive output, merge branches or delete the worktree. Its ignored-file scan does not cover every project output directory, checkpoint format or symlink target; supplement it with an inventory of the actual workflow's outputs. Its comparison base must exist. A zero-error result or a waived finding is not a backup.

For Claude history, --adopt-history previews moving transcripts into the retained checkout's history directory, and --adopt-history --apply performs that history move. --apply alone does not remove a worktree. Preserve required ignored files separately before a managed archive too. See the report's --help before using history options, and keep repository handoffs as the portable record of unfinished work.

docs.title: Maintain this website
docs.text: The website is a curated view of repository-owned Markdown. Its job is to explain architecture, design and use, with examples and evidence. The handbook remains the guided onboarding path; app and module contracts remain the authority for implemented behavior and validation.

docs.title: Build and preview
docs.text:
Run from the repository root:

pixi run --locked --manifest-path docs/pixi.toml build
pixi run --locked --manifest-path docs/pixi.toml check
pixi run --locked --manifest-path docs/pixi.toml serve

The isolated documentation environment is locked for Linux and Apple Silicon macOS. It does not install the robot or learning environments. The first build may fetch the pinned Mermaid and MathJax dependencies; the privacy plugin caches it under ignored artifacts/docs/cache/ and bundles assets into the site. The generated output is artifacts/docs/site/. These commands do not publish to an external host.

The preview binds to 127.0.0.1:8767. On a client using VS Code Remote - SSH, forward 8767 from Ubuntu and open the forwarded browser address. Keep the server terminal running. Stop the old handbook preview before starting the full site on the same port, or choose another address explicitly:

pixi run --locked --manifest-path docs/pixi.toml serve \
  --dev-addr 127.0.0.1:8768

The existing docs/handbook/pixi.toml build and serve tasks still produce the independent handbook. Both views read the same chapter source. Use HTTP serving for website search; opening index.html through a file URL is not the supported full-site preview.

docs.title: Where to edit
docs.text:
Change Owner Navigation and publication selection Root mkdocs.yml Public URL and publication mode Root mkdocs.pages.yml GitHub Pages deployment .github/workflows/docs-pages.yml Shared conceptual explanations docs/design/ Shared use and development guides docs/setup/ Robot introduction and local reference apps/<robot>/docs/ Onboarding lesson docs/handbook/chapters/ Theme customization and source bundling docs/site/ Module map categories and short labels docs/site/modules.yaml Module explanations and package boundaries docs/design/system-architecture.md Published illustrations and worked-example data docs/assets/ Research and historical figure capsules Root or project notes/evidence/ (outside the website)

Navigation entries are repository paths. The one alias is index.md, whose source is docs/index.md. The publication hook reads those files directly; do not maintain an HTML-specific copy of the prose. Each page offers its original Markdown and records its source path. Build output carries publication.json with source hashes, statuses and supporting-source inventory.

docs.title: Deep references and worked examples
docs.text:
Architecture contains a nested Deep references group for the CORTA execution design, adapter boundary, walking coordinator, and ALIP/DCM formulations. These are rendered from their original Markdown with the same theme and source download as the conceptual guides. Each distinguishes implemented behavior from design requirements, historical comparisons and proposed extensions. Learn includes the dated Digit M0 worked example; its original evidence is not relabeled as a new result.

The mathematical references use pymdownx.arithmatex and MathJax SVG output. The build localizes the pinned renderer through the privacy plugin; readers do not need a CDN connection. Follow the Material math configuration when changing the renderer. Check inline equations, display equations, diagrams and narrow-screen overflow in a browser after changing that setup.

docs.title: Visual identity and module map
docs.text:
The theme follows the Cyberbotics Lab website: muted red #a43b3b, charcoal #302b29, warm ivory #faf8f5 and a pale neutral #f2eeea. These tokens live in docs/site/project.css. Subdued category accents help distinguish module groups, with text labels carrying the same information. The vector CS monogram in docs/site/assets/logo.svg is a theme asset used for the header and favicon.

The homepage introduces the reusable package before the robot projects. Its module map and the architecture page's map are generated at <!-- cyber-suite:module-map --> markers from docs/site/modules.yaml. These are accessible HTML blocks with ordinary links, so they work without JavaScript and reflow on narrow screens. The original Markdown download retains the marker; the full module explanations remain readable Markdown in the architecture source.

The build rejects missing, duplicate or extra module entries by comparing the inventory against modules/*/MODULE.md, and takes lifecycle labels directly from those contracts. The output check verifies both rendered maps and the corresponding explanation anchors. When adding a module, update its category/short role and add an explanation with #module-<directory-name> as its anchor. Categories express responsibility, not dependency edges or execution order. publication.json records the inventory used for that build.

docs.title: Select documents deliberately
docs.text:
Before adding a page to navigation, compare it with its owning contract and current implementation. Selected guides must declare Status: working or Status: canonical; publication does not change that status. The site rejects missing selected files and unresolved local links. Follow the repository's approval rules before changing authority.

Every module's MODULE.md renders as a reference page with normal headings, lists, tables, code blocks, a table of contents and working links. The page preserves the owning contract's lifecycle label and validation statements, offers the unchanged Markdown download and links back to its module explanation. These detailed contracts stay outside the introductory navigation and guide search. Earlier source-view URLs redirect to the rendered contract, preserving section fragments.

Other linked documents outside the navigation list appear as supporting source views. Their original text and declared status remain visible, including dated validation and historical context. They are not added to the guide search index. A link to a design draft therefore does not silently turn that draft into current guidance. Code links support explanation without producing an API catalog.

The older ALIP/DCM formulations, coordinator migration document and CORTA design chronology still need owner review before becoming primary implementation explanations. Keep proposals and retired behavior out of the default reading path; preserve their original records rather than rewriting history to fit the website.

docs.title: Write explanations around a question
docs.text:
A strong page states the question it answers, shows the relevant relationship, walks through a concrete example and names evidence the reader can inspect. Explain frames, timing, assumptions and ownership where they change the interpretation. Put symbol-level details behind source links. Keep ordinary prose paragraphs on one physical Markdown line.

Use Markdown tables, code blocks, native disclosures and Mermaid for small relationship diagrams. The theme renders Mermaid diagrams and bundles its runtime locally. Use capsule-owned SVGs for durable technical illustrations and standard plots for measured results. Captions distinguish schematics from measurements and identify conditions, sample counts and limits. The evidence policy defines the capsule contract.

docs.title: Verify a change
docs.text:
Run the full-site check, the root audit and orientation, and git diff --check. If the chapter changes, rebuild the standalone handbook too. The site check walks generated links and anchors, confirms exact Markdown downloads, checks rendered sections for every module contract and checks that search contains the introductory guides rather than contracts or supporting sources. Inspect desktop and narrow layouts, search, section navigation and figures after presentation changes.

Commands in a guide must agree with current owning scripts and manifests. A successful documentation build validates publication; it does not establish that a robot simulation, training run, hardware deployment or remote browser connection was exercised.

docs.title: GitHub Pages
docs.text:
The public website is configured at cyberbotics-lab.github.io/cyber-suite-docs. Its generated files live in the public cyber-suite-docs repository; maintained sources remain in the private cyber-suite repository. mkdocs.pages.yml sets the website URL and private source-repository URL separately, and builds into artifacts/docs/pages/. The local preview remains a separate build under artifacts/docs/site/.

This separation allows GitHub Free organizations to host the website while keeping the source repository private. Publishing Pages directly from an organization-owned private repository requires GitHub Team or Enterprise; a personal GitHub Pro subscription does not apply after transfer to an organization. See GitHub Pages availability and repository transfer effects.

The public repository has its own Git history containing only website publications. Never mirror the private repository, copy its .git directory, or push a private source branch to the public destination. The publishing job receives the checked website artifact and checks out only the public destination. Its deploy key grants write access only to that public repository.

docs.title: Publication contents
docs.text:
The public build includes the selected guides, rendered module contracts, their Markdown downloads, embedded evidence assets and theme files. Other repository references become links to the build's Git commit on GitHub. Implementation files, app contracts, notes and directory listings are not copied into public supporting-source pages; visitors need repository access to follow those private links. The local preview continues to bundle supporting sources for convenient review. Existing module source-view aliases contain only redirects to the rendered contracts.

Build and check the exact public artifact before deployment:

pixi run --locked --manifest-path docs/pixi.toml pages-check

The check verifies local links under the /cyber-suite-docs/ prefix, source downloads, search scope and the absence of bundled implementation/notes source pages. artifacts/docs/pages/publication.json records the selected pages and build revision. Public documentation can itself contain examples and excerpts; keep the publication list intentional.

docs.title: One-time setup
docs.text:
1. Create the public Cyberbotics-Lab/cyber-suite-docs repository with an independent main branch. Initialize it from the checked public artifact, including an empty .nojekyll file. Keep Cyberbotics-Lab/cyber-suite private.
  2. In the public repository's Settings → Pages, select Deploy from a branch, main, and /(root). The files are already built; .nojekyll bypasses Jekyll processing.
  3. Create a dedicated SSH deploy key for the public repository and enable write access under its Settings → Deploy keys. Store the private half as the DOCS_PUBLISH_KEY Actions secret in the private source repository. Do not use a personal SSH key or a token with access to other repositories. See GitHub's deploy-key instructions.

docs.title: Publish a revision
docs.text:
1. Merge the reviewed documentation into the private source repository's main branch. Open Actions → Documentation Pages, choose Run workflow, select main, and run it.
  2. The build installs only the locked documentation environment, checks the public build and uploads artifacts/docs/pages/ as the public-documentation artifact. The separate publish job verifies the artifact's public-build flag, source revision and site URL, then replaces the public repository's generated files with it. An unchanged artifact needs no new commit; updates use an ordinary push that preserves publication history.
  3. Check the public repository's Pages workflow and open the website. A successful source workflow confirms the public files were pushed; the destination's successful Pages deployment confirms hosting completed.

The workflow is manual: ordinary source pushes do not publish the site. The source repository's GITHUB_TOKEN has read-only access; the dedicated deploy key supplies the cross-repository push. GitHub's publishing-source guide explains branch publication. If using a custom domain later, update the public repository's Pages setting, the complete site_url and the workflow's URL check together, then rebuild and check the artifact.

If publication fails, distinguish the source build, cross-repository push and destination Pages deployment. A missing or revoked DOCS_PUBLISH_KEY blocks the push. A successful build followed by an HTTP 422 Pages rejection can reflect repository eligibility or configuration; inspect the destination's Settings → Pages and deployment log. Pages stays disabled in the private source repository under GitHub Free.
